ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking; notice of additional date for public hearing.
SUMMARY:
This document provides a notice of an additional date for the public hearing on the notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-119986-25) published in the
Federal Register
on Friday, September 4, 2026. The proposed regulations would provide that a private school is not described as an organization exempt from Federal
(
printed page 74133)
income tax if it discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin in administration of its educational, admissions, scholarship, athletic, or other policies, based on the fundamental public policy of the United States against such practices.
DATES:
The telephonic hearing is scheduled to be held on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. ET and Thursday, December 3, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. ET.
ADDRESSES:
On Wednesday, December 2, 2026, and Thursday, December 3, 2026, the public hearing is being held telephonically. The hearing will include only those speakers that submitted requests to speak on or before the November 3, 2026 deadline. Comments and requests to speak were collected via the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
(at IRS and REG-119986-25) and paper submissions were received at: CC:PA:01:PR (REG-119986-25), Room 5503, Internal Revenue Service, P.O. Box 7604, Ben Franklin Station, Washington, DC 20044.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Concerning the proposed regulations, Office of Associate Chief Counsel (Employee Benefits, Exempt Organizations, and Employment Taxes) at (202) 317-6000 (not a toll-free number); concerning comments or the hearing, the Publications and Regulations Section at (202) 317-6901 (not a tollfree number) or by email at
publichearings@irs.gov
(preferred).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The subject of the hearing is the notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-119986-25) published in the
Federal Register
on September 4, 2026 (
91 FR 56811
). To accommodate all persons who wished to present oral comments at the public hearing, the public hearing scheduled Wednesday, December 2, 2026, has been extended an additional day to be Wednesday, December 2, and Thursday, December 3. The start time of the telephonic hearing both days is 10:00 a.m. ET.
The rules of
26 CFR 601.601(a)(3)
apply to the hearing. Persons who wished to present oral comments at the public hearing were required to submit an outline of the topics to be discussed as well as the time to be devoted to each topic by November 3, 2026. The due date for requests to testify has not been extended. Persons who made timely requests to testify will receive the telephone number and access codes for the public hearing. A period of 10 minutes will be allotted to each person testifying.
An agenda showing the scheduling of the speakers will be prepared prior to the hearing. Copies of the agenda will be emailed to those who requested to speak or attend the hearing and available via
www.regulations.gov
under the title of Supporting & Related Material.
Individuals who wish to attend the public hearing without testifying must send an email to
publichearings@irs.gov
to receive the telephone number and access code for the hearing. The subject line of the email must contain the regulation number (REG-119986-25) and the language “ATTEND Hearing Telephonically.” For example, the subject line may say: Request to ATTEND Hearing Telephonically for REG-119986-25. Requests to attend the hearing must be received by November 30, 2026.
Hearings will be made accessible to people with disabilities. To request special assistance during a hearing please contact the Publications and Regulations Section by sending an email to
publichearings@irs.gov
(preferred) or by telephone at (202) 317-6901 (not a toll-free number) by November 27, 2026. Any additional questions regarding the hearing may also be emailed to
publichearings@irs.gov
.

Federal Register Liaison, Publications and Regulations Section, Associate Chief Counsel, (Procedure and Administration).

AGENCY:
Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Treasury.
ACTION:
Final regulations.
SUMMARY:
This document sets forth final regulations that provide guidance with respect to the automatic enrollment requirements that apply to certain retirement plans. The regulations reflect statutory changes made by the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 requiring that certain cash or deferred arrangements and salary reduction agreements be eligible automatic contribution arrangements that satisfy additional specified requirements. The regulations affect participants in, beneficiaries of, employers maintaining, and administrators of certain retirement plans that include cash or deferred arrangements or annuity contracts purchased under salary reduction agreements and other retirement plans that include eligible automatic contribution arrangements.
DATES:
Effective date:
These regulations are effective on January 19, 2027.
Applicability date:
These regulations generally apply to plan years that begin after December 31, 2027. However, see § 1.414A-1(f)(2) and the Applicability Date section later in this preamble for additional details regarding applicability dates.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jamie L. Dvoretzky at (202) 317-4102 (not a toll-free number) or Kara M. Soderstrom at (202) 317-6799 (not a toll-free number).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority
These regulations are promulgated under section 7805(a) of the Internal Revenue Code (Code), which provides
(
printed page 74091)
that “the Secretary shall prescribe all needful rules and regulations for the enforcement of [the Code], including all rules and regulations as may be necessary by reason of any alteration of law in relation to internal revenue.” In addition, section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0 Act), enacted on December 29, 2022, as Division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023,
Public Law 117-328
, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022), instructs the Secretaries of the Treasury and Labor (or their delegates) to adopt regulations related to the consolidation of notices required for defined contribution plans under the Code and the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, Public Law 93-406, 88 Stat. 829, as amended (ERISA).
Background
This document sets forth a regulation under section 414A of the Code that is added to the Income Tax Regulations (
26 CFR part 1
). Section 414A, which was added to the Code by section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, provides that certain retirement plans must automatically enroll employees.
In addition to adding a new regulation under section 414A of the Code, this document sets forth amendments to the Income Tax Regulations under section 414(w). These amendments to § 1.414(w)-1 reflect the application of section 414A and the exception to the notice requirements for unenrolled participants set forth in section 414(bb), as added to the Code by section 320 of the SECURE 2.0 Act. The amendments to § 1.414(w)-1 also address section 402A(e)(5)(C) of the Code, which was added to the Code by section 127 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, as well as section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act. Section 402A(e)(5)(C) of the Code and section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act permit the consolidation of certain notices required under the Code and ERISA.
I. In General
A. Cash or Deferred Arrangements and Salary Reduction Agreements
Section 401(k)(1) provides that a profit-sharing, stock bonus, pre-ERISA money purchase, or rural cooperative plan will not fail to qualify under section 401(a) merely because it includes a cash or deferred arrangement (CODA)
[
1
]
that is a qualified CODA. Under section 401(k)(2), a CODA is a qualified CODA only if it satisfies certain requirements. These requirements include that elective contributions under the CODA are subject to the section 401(k)(2)(B) restriction on when distributions may be made, and that the arrangement satisfies the actual deferral percentage (ADP) test in section 401(k)(3)(A)(ii).
[
2
]
Section 403(b)(1) of the Code provides for an exclusion from gross income of certain contributions that are used to purchase an annuity contract, including contributions that are made under a salary reduction agreement. Although there is no direct definition of salary reduction agreement in section 403(b), several provisions of the Code set forth rules that apply to the use of a salary reduction agreement to purchase an annuity contract described in section 403(b). For example, section 403(b)(11) provides distribution restrictions that apply to “contributions made pursuant to a salary reduction agreement.”
B. Automatic Enrollment
Section 902 of the Pension Protection Act of 2006,
Public Law 109-280
, 120 Stat. 780 (PPA '06), added sections 401(k)(13) and 414(w) to the Code to facilitate automatic contribution arrangements (also referred to as automatic enrollment) in qualified CODAs under section 401(k). Section 414(w) also applies to automatic contribution arrangements under section 403(b) plans; section 457(b) plans maintained by governmental employers described in section 457(e)(1)(A); simplified employee pensions, the terms of which provide for a salary reduction arrangement described in section 408(k)(6); and SIMPLE individual retirement accounts described in section 408(p). An automatic contribution arrangement is a CODA or other similar arrangement that includes a default election under which an eligible employee is treated as having elected to have a specified contribution made on the employee's behalf under the plan unless the employee makes an affirmative election to have contributions made in a different amount on the employee's behalf (including no contributions).
[
3
]
1. Qualified Automatic Contribution Arrangements Under Section 401(k)(13)
Section 401(k)(13) provides a design-based safe harbor for a CODA that provides for automatic enrollment at a specified level and meets certain employer contribution, notice, and other requirements. A CODA that satisfies these requirements, referred to as a qualified automatic contribution arrangement (QACA), is treated as satisfying the ADP test.
Section 401(k)(13)(C)(ii) provides that the default election in a QACA ceases to apply to any eligible employee if the employee makes an affirmative election to not have any elective contributions made on the employee's behalf or to have elective contributions made in a specified amount or percentage of compensation on the employee's behalf. Reflecting that provision, § 1.401(k)-3(j)(1)(ii) provides that the default election ceases to apply with respect to an eligible employee for periods of time with respect to which the employee has an affirmative election that is currently in effect to have elective contributions made in a different amount on the employee's behalf (in a specified amount or percentage of compensation) or not have any elective contributions made on the employee's behalf.
Section 401(k)(13)(C)(iii) sets forth a series of minimum default contribution percentages (based on the plan year that the arrangement first applies to an employee) that an automatic contribution arrangement must satisfy to be a QACA and requires that the default contribution percentages apply uniformly. Under § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iii), a plan does not fail to satisfy this uniform percentage requirement merely because: (1) the percentage varies based on the number of years or portions of years an eligible employee has participated in the automatic contribution arrangement intended to be a QACA; (2) the rate of elective contributions under a cash or deferred election that is in effect immediately prior to the effective date of the default percentage under the QACA is not reduced; (3) the rate of elective contributions is limited so as not to exceed the limits of sections 401(a)(17), 402(g) (determined with or without catch-up contributions), and 415; or (4) the default election is not applied during the period an employee is not permitted to make elective contributions pursuant to section 414(u)(12)(B)(ii).
Section 401(k)(13)(C)(iv) provides an exception from the application of the default election under a QACA for eligible employees who were eligible to participate in the CODA (or a
(
printed page 74092)
predecessor CODA) immediately before the effective date of the QACA and who have an election in effect on that effective date. Reflecting that provision, § 1.401(k)-3(j)(1)(iii) provides that an automatic contribution arrangement does not fail to be a QACA merely because the default election is not applied to an employee who was eligible under the CODA (or a predecessor arrangement) immediately prior to the effective date of the QACA and on that effective date had an affirmative election in effect (that remains in effect) to have elective contributions made on the employee's behalf (in a specified amount or percentage of compensation) or not have elective contributions made on the employee's behalf.
Section 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv) provides that minimum percentages in a QACA are determined without regard to whether an employee has continued to be eligible to make contributions under the plan. However, § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv) provides that a plan is permitted to treat an employee who for an entire plan year did not have contributions made pursuant to a default election under a QACA as if the employee also had not had such contributions for any prior plan year.
2. Eligible Automatic Contribution Arrangements Under Section 414(w)
Section 414(w) facilitates automatic enrollment by providing relief from the distribution restrictions under section 401(k)(2)(B), 403(b)(7), 403(b)(11), or 457(d)(1)(A) in the case of an eligible automatic contribution arrangement (EACA). Under this relief, a plan may permit an employee who was automatically enrolled under an EACA to take a distribution within a limited period after the initial default elective contribution with respect to the employee was made.
Under section 414(w)(1) and (2), an applicable employer plan
[
4
]
that contains an EACA is permitted to allow employees to elect to receive a distribution, called a permissible withdrawal, equal to the amount of default elective contributions (and attributable earnings) made with respect to the employee beginning with the first payroll period to which the EACA applies to the employee and ending with the effective date of the election. The election must be made within 90 days after the date of the first default elective contribution with respect to the employee under the arrangement.
[
5
]
Section 414(w)(3) defines an EACA as an arrangement under which: (1) a participant may elect to have the employer make payments as contributions under the plan on behalf of the participant, or to the participant directly in cash; (2) the participant is treated as having elected to have the employer make such contributions in an amount equal to a uniform percentage of compensation provided under the plan until the participant specifically elects not to have such contributions made (or specifically elects to have such contributions made at a different percentage); and (3) participants are provided a notice that satisfies the requirements of section 414(w)(4).
Section 414(w)(4) provides that the administrator of a plan that includes an EACA must, within a reasonable period before each plan year, provide each employee to whom the arrangement applies for the plan year written notice of the employee's rights and obligations under the arrangement that is sufficiently accurate and comprehensive to apprise the employee of the employee's rights and obligations. Section 414(w)(4)(A)(ii) requires that the notice be written in a manner calculated to be understood by the average employee to whom the arrangement applies. Section 414(w)(4)(B) provides that the notice must explain: (1) the employee's rights under the arrangement to elect not to have elective contributions made on the employee's behalf (or to elect to have contributions made at a different percentage), and (2) how contributions made under the arrangement will be invested in the absence of any investment decision by the employee. In addition, the employee must be given a reasonable period after receipt of the notice and before the first elective contribution is made to make an election described in the notice.
On February 24, 2009, a final regulation under section 414(w) was published in the
Federal Register
(TD 9447,
74 FR 8200
). Section 1.414(w)-1(b)(2) includes rules that address the uniform percentage requirement of section 414(w)(3)(B), including rules that incorporate the exceptions to the uniform percentage requirement for a default elective contribution under a QACA set forth in § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iii).
II. New Automatic Enrollment Requirements and Other Changes Regarding EACAs Under the SECURE 2.0 Act
A. Section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act
Section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act added section 414A to the Code. Under section 101(c) of the SECURE 2.0 Act, the amendments made by section 101 apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024.
Section 414A(a)(1) of the Code generally provides that a CODA will not be treated as a qualified CODA described in section 401(k) unless the CODA satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b). Similarly, section 414A(a)(2) generally provides that an annuity contract otherwise described in section 403(b) that is purchased under a salary reduction agreement will not be treated as described in section 403(b) unless the salary reduction agreement satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b).
Under section 414A(b)(1), a CODA or salary reduction agreement satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b) if the CODA or salary reduction agreement is an EACA (as defined in section 414(w)(3)) that satisfies the additional requirements of section 414A(b)(2) through (4). Section 414A(b)(2) requires the EACA to allow employees to make permissible withdrawals (as defined in section 414(w)(2)). Under section 414A(b)(3)(A)(i), the minimum initial default contribution percentage under the EACA must be at least 3 percent (but not more than 10 percent), and under section 414A(b)(3)(A)(ii), the default contribution percentage must increase by one percentage point for each plan year beginning after each completed year of participation under the EACA, up to a maximum default contribution percentage of at least 10 percent (but not more than 15 percent).
[
6
]
Section 414A(b)(4) provides that amounts contributed pursuant to the EACA for which no investment is elected by a participant must be invested in accordance with the requirements of
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
[
7
]
(or any successor regulations).
Section 414A(c) sets forth certain exceptions to the requirements of
(
printed page 74093)
section 414A(a). In general, section 414A(a) does not apply to any: (1) SIMPLE 401(k) plan described in section 401(k)(11); (2) qualified CODA established before December 29, 2022 (the date of enactment of the SECURE 2.0 Act); (3) section 403(b) plan established before December 29, 2022; (4) governmental plan described in section 414(d); (5) church plan described in section 414(e); (6) plan maintained by a new business as described in section 414A(c)(4)(A); or (7) plan maintained by a small business as described in section 414A(c)(4)(B).
Certain of the exceptions in section 414A(c) include special rules for plans maintained by more than one employer. Section 414A(c)(2)(B) provides rules that apply in the case of an employer that, after December 29, 2022, adopts a plan maintained by more than one employer. Under that provision, the exception to section 414A(a) for a qualified CODA or 403(b) plan established before December 29, 2022, will not apply to that adopting employer, and the rules of section 414A(a) will apply with respect to that employer as if the plan were a single plan. In addition, under section 414A(c)(4)(C), the new business and small business exceptions to section 414A(a) are applied separately to each participating employer in a plan maintained by more than one employer, and all participating employers to which section 414A(a) applies (after the application of the new business exception in section 414A(c)(4)(A) and the small business exception in section 414A(c)(4)(B)) are treated as maintaining a separate plan for purposes of section 414A.
On December 20, 2023, the Department of the Treasury (Treasury Department) and the IRS released Notice 2024-2, 2024-2 IRB 316, which provides guidance on certain provisions of the SECURE 2.0 Act including initial guidance in the form of questions and answers regarding certain issues related to section 414A of the Code.
B. SECURE 2.0 Act Changes Regarding EACA Notices
1. Notice Requirements for Unenrolled Participants
Section 320(b) of the SECURE 2.0 Act added section 414(bb) to the Code, effective for plan years beginning after December 31, 2022. Section 414(bb)(1) provides that, with respect to any defined contribution plan, no disclosure, notice, or other plan document is required to be furnished under the Code to any unenrolled participant if the unenrolled participant is furnished: (1) an annual reminder notice (as defined in section 414(bb)(3)) of the participant's eligibility to participate in the plan and any applicable election deadlines under the plan, and (2) any document requested by the participant that the participant would be entitled to receive notwithstanding section 414(bb).
Under section 414(bb)(2), an unenrolled participant is an employee who: (1) is eligible to participate in a defined contribution plan, (2) has been furnished a summary plan description pursuant to section 104(b) of ERISA for the plan and any other notices related to eligibility under the plan and required to be furnished under the Code or ERISA in connection with the participant's initial eligibility to participate in the plan, (3) is not participating in the defined contribution plan, and (4) satisfies any other criteria the Secretary of the Treasury may determine appropriate, as prescribed in guidance issued in consultation with the Secretary of Labor. The last sentence of section 414(bb)(2) of the Code provides that any eligibility to participate in the plan following any period for which the employee was not eligible to participate is to be treated as initial eligibility.
Section 414(bb)(3) provides that the annual reminder notice required under section 414(bb)(1) is the notice described in section 111(c) of ERISA (as added by section 320(a) of the SECURE 2.0 Act).
2. Combining EACA Notices With Other Notices
Section 127 of the SECURE 2.0 Act provides for the creation of pension-linked emergency savings accounts (PLESAs) effective for plan years beginning after December 31, 2023. Among other changes, section 127 of the SECURE 2.0 Act redesignates section 402A(e) of the Code as section 402A(f) and adds a new section 402A(e) regarding PLESAs.
[
8
]
Section 402A(e)(5)(A) requires the plan administrator of a plan with a PLESA feature to furnish initial and annual notices to participants describing certain information regarding the PLESA that meet the requirements of section 402A(e)(5)(B). Section 402A(e)(5)(C) permits the initial and annual notices required under section 402A(e)(5)(A) to be included with any other notice under ERISA, including under section 404(c)(5)(B) or 514(e)(3) of ERISA, or under section 401(k)(13)(E) or 414(w)(4) of the Code, if the other notice is provided to the participant at the time required for that notice.
The Department of Labor has provided frequently asked questions regarding PLESAs, including with respect to the permitted consolidation of notices under section 801(d)(3)(C) of ERISA (which is a parallel provision to section 402A(e)(5)(C) of the Code).
See
Q&A-18 of “FAQs: Pension-Linked Emergency Savings Accounts,” available at
www.dol.gov/​agencies/​ebsa/​about-ebsa/​our-activities/​resource-center/​faqs/​pension-linked-emergency-savings-accounts
.
Section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act permits a plan (as defined in section 3 of ERISA) to consolidate two or more of the notices required under sections 404(c)(5)(B) and 514(e)(3) of ERISA and sections 401(k)(12)(D), 401(k)(13)(E), and 414(w)(4) of the Code into a single notice, provided that the combined notice satisfies certain requirements. Section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act does not prevent the consolidation of any other notices required under ERISA or the Code to the extent otherwise permitted by the Secretary of Labor or the Secretary of the Treasury (or their delegates), as applicable.
On October 24, 2007, the Department of Labor published in the
Federal Register
(
72 FR 60452
) a final regulation,
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
, providing relief from certain fiduciary responsibilities under ERISA for investments made on behalf of participants or beneficiaries who fail to direct the investment of assets in their individual accounts. The preamble to that final regulation indicates that the Department of Labor anticipates that the notice requirements of sections 404(c)(5)(B) and 514(e)(3) of ERISA and sections 401(k)(13)(E) and 414(w)(4) of the Code could be satisfied in a single disclosure document.
See
72 FR 60455
(regarding the notice requirements under section 404(c)(5)(B) of ERISA and sections 401(k)(13)(E) and 414(w)(4) of the Code) and
72 FR 60466
(regarding the notice requirements under sections 404(c)(5)(B) and 514(e)(3) of ERISA).
To aid plan sponsors for the 2008 plan year (the first plan year that a plan could have included a QACA or EACA), the IRS coordinated with the Department of Labor to post a sample “Automatic Enrollment Notice,” available at
www.irs.gov/​pub/​irs-tege/​sample_​notice.pdf
.
This sample notice is intended to satisfy the notice requirements of sections 404(c)(5)(B)
(
printed page 74094)
and 514(e)(3) of ERISA and sections 401(k)(13)(E) and 414(w)(4) of the Code.
On April 29, 2008, the Department of Labor issued Field Assistance Bulletin 2008-03. Q&A-10 of Field Assistance Bulletin 2008-03 explains that the notice required under section 401(k)(12)(D) also may be combined with the notice required under section 404(c)(5)(B) of ERISA.
Q&A-18 of “FAQs: Pension-Linked Emergency Savings Accounts” explains that, with respect to section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, the Department of Labor retains its position regarding the consolidation of notices required under sections 404(c)(5)(B) and 514(e)(3) of ERISA and sections 401(k)(12)(D), 401(k)(13)(E), and 414(w)(4) of the Code. Q&A-18 also explains that, under section 801(d)(3)(C) of ERISA, the initial and annual notices that must be furnished to PLESA participants may be included with any other notice under ERISA, including under section 404(c)(5)(B) or 514(e)(3) of ERISA, or under section 401(k)(13)(E) or 414(w)(4) of the Code, if such other notice is provided to the participant at the time required for such notice.
III. Proposed Regulations
On January 14, 2025, a notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-100669-24) containing a proposed regulation under section 414A and proposed amendments to the regulations under section 414(w) that would reflect section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, and relevant provisions of sections 127, 320, and 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, was published in the
Federal Register
(
90 FR 3092
). Comments received in response to Notice 2024-2 were considered in the preparation of the proposed regulations. Eighteen comments were received in response to the notice of proposed rulemaking, and a public hearing was held on April 8, 2025.
After consideration of the comments received in response to the notice of proposed rulemaking and testimony at the public hearing, the proposed regulations are adopted by this Treasury decision with certain changes described in the Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions section of this preamble.
Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions
This Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions addresses the comments that the Treasury Department and the IRS received in response to the proposed regulations and describes the revisions included in the final regulations. Unless otherwise indicated in this Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions, provisions of the proposed regulations for which no comments were received (or for which the only comments received were in support of those provisions) are adopted without substantive change. Several comments were unrelated to tax law or otherwise outside the scope of the proposed regulations. Some comments also expressed support or disapproval for the new section 414A, rather than the regulations, and were therefore also outside the scope of the proposed regulations. Additionally, comments that merely summarize the proposed regulations, recommend statutory revisions to section 414A, or other statutes, or address issues that are outside the scope of this rulemaking (including issues addressed in other guidance, proposed changes to such guidance, and enforcement) are beyond the scope of these regulations. For example, the application of the Employee Plans Compliance Resolution System (EPCRS), Rev. Proc. 2021-30, 2021-31 IRB 172, is beyond the scope of these regulations. The final regulations include non-substantive modifications, including non-substantive changes in response to comments and modifications that promote consistency across rules and examples and improve the overall clarity of the guidance. Such non-substantive modifications are not addressed in this Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions.
I. Section 1.414A-1
A. Employees Required To Be Covered Under the Eligible Automatic Contribution Arrangement
The proposed regulation would clarify that a CODA or salary reduction agreement under a plan satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A only if the plan provides for an EACA that covers all employees in the plan who are eligible to elect to have contributions made on their behalf under the CODA or pursuant to the salary reduction agreement. One commenter agreed with the language of the proposed regulation, but several other commenters requested that the final regulations provide that certain categories of employees need not be covered by an EACA for section 414A(b) to be satisfied. In particular, commenters requested that an EACA in a plan need not cover (1) employees who are covered by a collective bargaining agreement or (2) employees who were eligible to participate in a CODA or salary reduction agreement included in the plan before the CODA or salary reduction agreement became subject to the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b). Although section 414A(c) provides several exceptions to the requirements of section 414A(a) for certain types of plans, no provision in section 414A (or in section 101(c) of the SECURE 2.0 Act) excludes any category of employee from the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b) of the Code if the plan is subject to section 414A(a). Accordingly, § 1.414A-1(c)(1)(ii) retains the rule from the proposed regulation and clarifies that each employee who is eligible to elect to have contributions made on the employee's behalf under a CODA or pursuant to a salary reduction agreement must be covered by the EACA, which includes an employee who was eligible to participate in the CODA or salary reduction agreement before the CODA or salary reduction agreement became subject to the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b).
B. Timing Rules for Applying the Default Election
To reflect the minimum contribution percentage requirements of section 414A(b)(3), the proposed regulation would provide that an EACA satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A only if the default election made on behalf of an employee under the EACA is equal to a uniform percentage of the employee's compensation that is subject to a cash or deferred election or salary reduction arrangement under the plan. A commenter requested confirmation that, after an EACA notice is distributed, a plan may begin to apply the default election after a reasonable election period. The commenter also requested flexibility on the timing for automatically enrolling long-term, part-time employees in the EACA. Another commenter noted the importance of giving employees prior notice of their right to opt out of any default contributions and automatic increases.
Section 1.414A-1(c)(1)(i), like the proposed regulation, reflects the provisions of section 414A(b)(1) by requiring that the automatic contribution arrangement under section 414A be an EACA. An EACA is subject to the requirements of § 1.414(w)-1(e)(2), which requires that the default election begin to apply no earlier than a reasonable period of time after receipt of the notice describing the EACA. The changes made by the SECURE 2.0 Act do not affect this existing rule. Thus, an EACA that is subject to section 414A must also meet this timing requirement.

printed page 74095)
Additionally, § 1.414(w)-1(b)(3)(iii) provides timing rules for giving the EACA notice, which are not affected by the SECURE 2.0 Act, and which also would apply to an EACA that is subject to section 414A. Under these timing rules, the notice generally must be provided within a reasonable period before the beginning of each plan year (generally, at least 30 days (and no more than 90 days) before the beginning of each plan year). However, in the plan year an employee is first eligible to make a cash or deferred election (or first becomes covered under the automatic contribution arrangement as a result of a change in employment status), the notice must be provided within a reasonable period before the employee becomes a covered employee (generally, no more than 90 days before the employee becomes a covered employee, and no later than the date that affords the employee a reasonable period of time after receipt of the notice to make an affirmative election). These automatic enrollment timing rules, including the time period for giving the notice, apply to each employee covered under the EACA and do not contain any special rules for long-term, part-time employees. Accordingly, no changes were made to the final regulation in response to these comments.
C. Timing and Default Percentage Rules for Applying Automatic Increases
As described in section II.A of the Background portion of this preamble, section 414A(b)(3)(A)(ii) generally requires automatic increases of one percentage point to an employee's minimum default contribution percentage for each plan year beginning after each completed year of participation under the EACA, up to a maximum default contribution percentage of at least 10 percent (but not more than 15 percent). The proposed regulation would provide that, for each plan year beginning after an employee's initial period, the percentage contribution under the default election must be increased by one percentage point until the percentage is at least 10 percent.
Commenters requested clarification that the one percentage point increase to the percentage contribution under the default election could occur on a day other than the first day of a plan year. With respect to the timing of automatic increases, some of those commenters requested that the minimum escalated percentage for a plan year be permitted to be applied earlier than the first day of the plan year, thus allowing the escalation to be applied earlier but not later than the first day of the plan year. Additionally, one commenter asked for clarification that an automatic increase to the percentage contribution under the default election could be greater than one percentage point.
In response to the comments, § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(B) clarifies the language of the proposed regulation by providing that, not later than the first day of each plan year beginning after an employee's initial period, the percentage contribution under the default election applicable to the employee on the first day of the prior plan year must be increased by at least one percentage point. This clarification allows for flexibility in the timing and amount of the increase. The final regulation also provides that annual increases must occur until the employee's percentage contribution is at least 10 percent. Under the final regulation, a plan may provide that the annual increases continue after the employee's percentage contribution is 10 percent but may not provide for the annual increases to continue after the employee's percentage contribution is equal to 15 percent.
D. Redetermination of the Initial Period Used To Determine an Employee's Default Contribution Percentage
The proposed regulation would provide rules, based on the rules for a QACA under § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv), that address the default percentage that would apply for an employee who did not have default elective contributions made for an entire plan year. The proposed regulation would provide different rules that could be used depending on whether the employee was not eligible to have contributions made on the employee's behalf under a CODA or salary reduction agreement or had made an affirmative election to have contributions made in a different amount (including an election not to have contributions made).
Specifically, the proposed regulation would permit a plan to provide that if, after an employee's initial period began, the employee did not have default elective contributions made on the employee's behalf for an entire plan year, then the employee's initial period is redetermined. If no default elective contributions were made solely because the employee was not eligible to elect to have contributions made on the employee's behalf under a cash or deferred election or salary reduction agreement for that entire plan year, then a plan would be permitted to provide that the employee's initial period would be redetermined so that it begins on the date the employee is again eligible to elect to have contributions made on the employee's behalf under the plan. An employer would likely adopt this provision to determine the default contribution rate that applies to an employee who was rehired more than one plan year after the employee terminated employment.
However, if no default elective contributions were made solely because the employee made an affirmative election to have contributions made on the employee's behalf under a cash or deferred election or salary reduction agreement in a different amount (including an election not to have contributions made), then a plan would be permitted to provide that the employee's initial period would be redetermined so that it begins on any date specified under the plan that is later than the date the employee's original initial period ended. For example, a plan would be permitted to be amended to provide that, as of a specified date, the default election would apply to all employees who previously made an affirmative election that had been in effect for a period of at least one plan year to have contributions made on behalf of the employees under the plan at a rate that is below the uniform percentage that applies during an initial period (so that the uniform percentage that applies during the initial period will apply unless the employee makes a new affirmative election). An employer might adopt such an amendment to facilitate an increase in the rate of contributions made on behalf of its employees.
Commenters asked that the proposed regulation be modified to eliminate the requirement that a rehired employee must have been ineligible for at least an entire plan year before the plan can redetermine the rehired employee's initial period for purposes of implementing the default election applicable under the plan for the initial period. A commenter requested that plans be permitted to provide that employees who have made an affirmative election to contribute less than the default rate and have not had an entire plan year elapse since that election was implemented are not subject to increases based on the original initial period. Another commenter requested that the proposed regulation be modified to provide that an employee's initial period may be redetermined under the same rules currently applicable to a QACA under § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv).
Section 1.414A-1(c)(3)(iv) retains the requirement of the proposed regulation requiring an entire plan year of ineligibility or an entire plan year of
(

contributions made pursuant to an affirmative election, regardless of whether the affirmative election contribution percentage is less than the default percentage, before the plan can implement the initial default percentage by redetermining the rehired employee's initial period. This language is intended to parallel, not modify, the rules currently applicable to a QACA under § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv), which states that for purposes of determining the date the initial period begins, a plan is permitted to treat an employee who for an entire plan year did not have contributions made pursuant to a default election under the QACA as if the employee had not had such contributions made for any prior plan year as well. In addition, the final regulation balances the requirement of automatic increases at regular intervals with concerns regarding the administrative feasibility of determining an individual's default contribution percentage based on older data.
Another commenter requested clarification whether the plan document would need to be amended to reflect this rule if the plan chooses to reflect the provision in the preamble to the proposed regulation permitting the redetermination of the initial period in the case of an employee who became eligible to participate in the plan before the first day of the 2025 plan year and who did not have default elective contributions made for an entire plan year (and the plan document does not already provide for redetermination). As explained in section I.I of this Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions regarding applicability date issues, if a plan chooses to permit the redetermination of the initial period in this situation, plan terms would need to provide for the redetermination.
E. Investment Requirements
In accordance with the investment requirements of section 414A(b)(4), the proposed regulation would provide that an EACA satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A only if amounts contributed pursuant to the EACA, and for which no investment is elected by the employee, are invested in accordance with the requirements of
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
(or any successor regulations). Section 2550.404c-5 provides rules regarding the fiduciary relief afforded by section 404(c)(5) of ERISA, under which a participant who does not give investment directions will be treated as exercising control over the participant's account with respect to assets that the plan invests in a QDIA as defined in § 2550.404c-5(e).
Commenters requested clarification that section 414A(b)(4) does not apply to, or is deemed satisfied for, an EACA (subject to section 414A(b)) that is part of a plan that does not provide for participant direction of the investment of amounts contributed pursuant to the EACA. One commenter requested that, as an alternative, a plan be permitted to satisfy section 414A(b)(4) by providing participants with the option to choose between trustee-directed investments and a QDIA as described in
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
, with any amounts for which no investment is elected by the participant automatically invested in the QDIA.
In response to the comments, § 1.414A-1(c)(4) provides that the requirements of
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
(or any successor regulations) apply to amounts contributed pursuant to an EACA only if the EACA is part of a plan that offers an employee the opportunity to direct the investment of all or a portion of the assets allocated to the employee's individual account under the plan. This is consistent with section 414A(b)(4), under which the requirements of
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
(or any successor regulations) apply if the employee chooses not to make an investment election. Section 1.414A-1(c)(4) also clarifies that the requirements of
29 CFR 2550.404c-5
(or any successor regulations) apply to amounts contributed pursuant to an EACA only if the EACA is part of a plan that is subject to title I of ERISA.
F. Exceptions for New and Small Businesses
Section 414A(c)(4)(A) provides that the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(a) do not apply to any qualified CODA, or any annuity contract purchased under a plan, while the employer maintaining the plan (and any predecessor employer) has been in existence for less than 3 years. Section 414A(c)(4)(B) provides that the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(a) do not apply to any qualified CODA, or any annuity contract purchased under a plan, earlier than the date that is one year after the close of the first taxable year of the employer maintaining the plan with respect to which that employer normally employed more than 10 employees.
1. Predecessor Employer
The notice of proposed rulemaking requested comments on whether guidance would be needed to define the term predecessor employer as used in the new business exception under section 414A(c)(4)(A). Commenters requested guidance on the definition, mentioning, among other reasons, concerns with applying the new business exception in a merger context. One of those commenters recommended that the term predecessor employer be defined by reference to § 1.415(f)-1(c)(2), which provides rules, in the context of applying limitations on benefits and contributions, for determining a predecessor employer in a situation in which a plan is not maintained by a successor. In response to these comments, § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(i) provides that, for purposes of the new business exception, a predecessor employer is a predecessor employer within the meaning of § 1.415(f)-1(c). Thus, the final regulation includes a definition of predecessor employer in the situation in which a plan is maintained by a successor as well as a situation in which a plan is not maintained by a successor.
2. Related Employers
Commenters requested clarification as to whether, for purposes of the new and small business exceptions in proposed § 1.414A-1(d)(4), the term employer includes all members of a group of employers that are treated as a single employer under the rules of section 414(b), (c), (m), or (o). Some commenters requested confirmation that the term employer would include all those members while other commenters requested that the term employer not include any of those members. In response to these comments, § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(iv) provides that, for purposes of the new and small business exceptions in the case of a plan that is not a multiple employer plan, the term employer includes all members of a group of employers that are treated as a single employer under the rules of section 414(b), (c), (m), or (o). For purposes of the new and small business exceptions, in the case of a multiple employer plan, § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(iv) provides that the term employer includes all employers treated as a single employer under § 1.413-2(a)(2)(ii).
3. Eligibility for the Small Business Exception
One commenter requested confirmation that once an arrangement first becomes ineligible for the small business exception in proposed § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(ii) because the employer maintaining the plan normally employs more than 10 employees in a taxable year, then the arrangement will remain subject to the requirements of proposed § 1.414A-1(b) even if the employer normally employs 10 or fewer employees in a subsequent year.

Another commenter requested clarification regarding the application of the small business exception if an employer normally employs 10 or fewer employees in a subsequent year, particularly in the case of a corporate event that reduces the number of employees. Section 1.414A-1(d)(4)(ii) retains the language of the proposed regulation. Thus, the requirements of § 1.414A-1(b) do not apply before the first plan year that begins at least 12 months after the close of the first taxable year of the employer maintaining the plan with respect to which that employer normally employed more than 10 employees. 4. Determining the Number of Employees for the Small Business Exception
A commenter requested that the final regulation allow an employer the flexibility to determine the number of its employees, for purposes of determining whether the employer normally employs more than 10 employees, based on either (1) the rules of Q&A-5 of § 54.4980B-2, as specified in the proposed regulations, or (2) the eligibility rules for SIMPLE IRAs and the credit for small employer pension plan startup costs under section 45E. However, because the phrase normally employed is used in section 4980B(d)(1) and Q&A-5 of § 54.4980B-2 but not in section 45E, § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(ii) retains the rule from the proposed regulation providing that the number of employees that the employer normally employs for a taxable year is determined using the rules of Q&A-5 of § 54.4980B-2 and does not permit the alternative requested by the commenter.
G. Exceptions for Plans Established Before the Enactment of Section 414A
As described in section II.A of the Background portion of this preamble, section 414A(c)(2)(A) provides an exception from the requirements of section 414A(a) in the case of a qualified CODA, or section 403(b) plan, that is established before December 29, 2022. This Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions uses the term pre-enactment plan to encompass both a qualified CODA and section 403(b) plan that is eligible for the exception under section 414A(c)(2)(A).
The proposed regulation would implement section 414A(c)(2)(A)(i) by generally providing that the requirements of section 414A(a) do not apply to any plan that includes a qualified CODA if the plan terms providing for the qualified CODA were adopted initially before December 29, 2022, even if the plan terms providing for the CODA become effective after that date. One commenter asked for clarification of the treatment of a multiemployer plan that existed before December 29, 2022, but did not add a CODA until after that date. Section 1.414A-1(e)(1)(i) retains the rule from the proposed regulation. This rule reflects section 414A(c)(2)(A)(i) and applies to multiemployer plans. Therefore, a multiemployer plan qualifies for the exception from the requirements of section 414A only if plan terms were adopted providing for the qualified CODA before December 29, 2022. If they were not, then the plan would not qualify for the exception.
H. Merger of a Plan Established on or After the Enactment of Section 414A With a Plan Established Before the Enactment of Section 414A
The proposed regulation generally would provide that a pre-enactment plan maintained by a single employer will not continue to be treated as a pre-enactment plan after a merger with a plan maintained by a single employer that is not a pre-enactment plan. However, the proposed regulation would provide an exception in this case if there is a transaction described in § 1.410(2)-2(f), the pre-merger pre-enactment plan is designated as the ongoing plan, and the plan merger occurs within the transition period described in section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii). Under section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii), the transition period begins on the date of the change in members of a controlled group (as described in section 414(b), (c), (m), or (o)) and ends on the last day of the first plan year beginning after the date of that change.
One commenter requested that the condition to designate the pre-merger pre-enactment plan as the ongoing plan be eliminated in the final regulation or, in the alternative, recommended that the preamble to the final regulations clarify that the designation can be accomplished in any written manner and need not necessarily be in the plan document. Section 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(B) retains the condition in the proposed regulation requiring that the pre-merger pre-enactment plan be designated as the ongoing plan. However, the Treasury Department and the IRS agree with the commenter that the designation of an ongoing plan under § 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(B) should be documented in writing but does not need to be in the written plan document.
Another commenter requested that the proposed regulation be modified to extend the period for a plan merger until the end of the first plan year that ends no later than eighteen months after the end of the transition period described in section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii). Section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii) provides a period for an employer to implement changes to its plans that may be needed following a transaction described in section 410(b)(6)(C). The Treasury Department and the IRS believe that this transition period is sufficient for an employer to implement a plan merger to preserve a plan's pre-enactment status under section 414A. Accordingly, § 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(C) retains the condition in the proposed regulation that the plan merger occur within the transition period described in section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii).

J. Other Matters
1. Portability of Elections
Section 414A(b)(3)(A)(i) states that an EACA meets the requirements related to automatic contribution percentage levels if the uniform percentage of compensation contributed by the participant under the EACA during the first year of participation is not less than 3 percent and not more than 10 percent (unless the participant specifically elects not to have such contributions made or to have such contributions made at a different percentage). Proposed § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(iii) would provide exceptions to the uniformity requirement, including an exception that would apply if the rate of contributions under a CODA or salary reduction agreement that is in effect for an employee immediately prior to the date that the default election under the proposed regulation first applies to the employee is not reduced. A commenter requested that the final regulations provide for an exception to the uniformity requirement to allow for an individual's deferral election under a prior 401(k) or 403(b) plan to apply under a current plan, even if the prior and current plans are maintained by completely unrelated employers and even if the individual was not immediately eligible for the current plan after being ineligible for the prior plan (which could occur when the individual switches jobs or takes some time off between jobs). As an alternative, the commenter requested that the final regulations provide for the issuance of sub-regulatory guidance that elaborates on and further interprets the uniformity requirement. Another commenter specifically requested that the final regulations provide for portability of elections for plans sponsored by entities that are going through corporate transactions.
Section 1.414A-1(c)(3)(iii) retains the rule from the proposed regulation and does not address portability of elections in the context of (1) prior and current plans that are maintained by completely unrelated employers, including situations in which an individual was not immediately eligible for the current plan after being ineligible for the prior plan, or (2) corporate transactions. The final regulations also do not provide for the issuance of sub-regulatory guidance. The Treasury Department and the IRS have concerns about the complexity of, and disclosure concerns inherent in, allowing for elections under one plan to be taken into account under another unrelated plan without an individual providing consent.

Baseline
The Treasury Department and the IRS have assessed the benefits and costs of the regulations relative to a no-action baseline reflecting anticipated Federal income tax-related behavior in the absence of these regulations.
Need for Regulation
The regulations are necessary because section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act sets out the broad rule that certain new 401(k) and 403(b) plans must use automatic enrollment but does not provide the required operational details. The regulations provide guidance on exactly who must be covered, how to calculate and increase default contribution rates, when an escalation schedule can be reset, how the investment default rules apply, and how statutory exceptions (such as for pre-enactment plans, plans maintained by new businesses, and plans maintained by small businesses) work.
The Statute and the Regulations
Section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act adds new section 414A to the Code and
(
printed page 74100)
makes automatic enrollment a required feature for many newly established 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans. Under this change, a CODA or a 403(b) salary reduction agreement will not be treated as tax-favored unless it is structured as an EACA, under which eligible employees must be enrolled automatically unless they affirmatively opt out or choose a different contribution rate.
Section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act also sets specific minimum standards for how automatic enrollment must work. The default contribution rate must be a uniform percentage between three percent and ten percent and automatically increase by one percentage point for each plan year beginning after each completed year of participation under the EACA, up to a maximum default contribution percentage of at least ten percent (but not more than 15 percent). Employees must be allowed to opt out or elect a different percentage. In addition, automatically contributed amounts must be eligible for a limited permissible-withdrawal period shortly after enrollment, giving employees a chance to reverse default contributions. In general, if an employee does not choose how to invest contributions, the amounts must be invested in accordance with the requirements of Department of Labor rules regarding QDIAs.
Section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act builds in several exceptions. The automatic enrollment requirements do not apply to 401(k) or 403(b) plans that were established before December 29, 2022, nor to SIMPLE 401(k) plans, governmental plans, or church plans. Section 101 also provides temporary relief for certain small or new employers—businesses that have been in existence for less than three years or that normally employ ten or fewer employees. Overall, section 101 amends the Code to make automatic enrollment with escalating contribution rates the default framework for many newly created defined contribution retirement plans, with the goal of increasing employee participation and retirement savings levels nationwide.
The regulations provide the operational details of how plans comply with the automatic enrollment requirement added by section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act. The regulations clarify that, unless a statutory exception applies, a 401(k) or 403(b) plan that is subject to new section 414A of the Code must include an EACA that covers all employees who are eligible to make deferrals and not just new hires or employees not covered by a collective bargaining agreement. Employees who already have an affirmative election in effect when section 414A first becomes applicable to the plan do not have to be defaulted; this protects existing elections. The regulations confirm that the plan must include the existing EACA permissible withdrawal feature—meaning an automatically enrolled employee must be allowed to withdraw default contributions (plus earnings) within a 90-day window after the first default contribution.
The regulations also provide detailed mechanics on how the automatic increases must operate. The regulations define an employee's initial period as beginning when the employee first becomes eligible to make deferrals (or, if later, when section 414A first applies to the plan) and ending on the last day of the plan year following the plan year in which eligibility begins. The regulations provide that after that period the plan must increase the employee's default rate by at least one percentage point each year, no later than the first day of each plan year, until the rate reaches at least ten percent, but not above 15 percent.
The regulations allow certain exceptions to the uniform percentage requirement. Employees at different stages of participation can contribute at different default percentages if the default percentages are based on how long the employees have been subject to the EACA. If an employee was already contributing at a certain rate before the automatic enrollment rules applied, the plan does not have to reduce that employee's contribution rate down to a new default percentage. If statutory contribution limits prevent an employee from contributing the full default percentage, the plan can cap the employee's contributions at the legal maximum.
The regulations also permit limited resets of the beginning of an initial period. A reset is allowed if, after an employee's original initial period begins, the employee has an entire plan year with no default contributions. For example, a rehired employee who was ineligible for a full plan year may have a new initial period starting when the employee is again eligible. Similarly, if an employee affirmatively elected a zero percent contribution rate (or another rate), the employee may have a new initial period if the employee has at least an entire year with no default contributions.
Under the regulations, if a plan is subject to title I of ERISA, and permits participant-directed investments, then any defaulted contributions for which the employee does not make an investment election must be invested in a QDIA under Department of Labor rules—typically a target-date fund, balanced fund, or managed account that satisfies the QDIA regulation. By contrast, if a plan does not permit participants to direct the investment of their accounts (for example, if all investments are selected and managed by a trustee or investment committee), then the requirements of the QDIA regulation need not be satisfied. In that case, the regulations allow plan assets to be invested without having to satisfy the requirements of the QDIA regulation.
With respect to the new business exception (for employers in existence for less than 3 years), the regulations define predecessor employer by cross-reference to existing tax rules, meaning prior businesses count for purposes of determining the three-year period. Additionally, the regulations provide that the automatic enrollment requirements apply for the next plan year immediately after the employer has been in existence for 3 years. For the small business exception, the regulations specify that the employer is considered to normally employ more than 10 employees using the employee counting method under the rules of Q&A-5 of § 54.4980B-2 (referred to as the COBRA
[
12
]
regulations). The regulations also clarify that the automatic enrollment requirements apply starting with the first plan year following the first taxable year of the employer with respect to which that employer normally employed more than 10 employees. The regulations also clarify that related employers that are treated as one employer under certain controlled group rules must be aggregated when applying the exception. The regulations clarify that in the case of a multiple employer plan, the exceptions for new and small businesses apply on an employer-by-employer basis.
Finally, the regulations provide detailed guidance on the statutory exception for plans established before December 29, 2022 (the pre-enactment exception). The regulations provide that the automatic enrollment requirements do not apply to any CODA if the plan terms providing for the CODA were adopted before that date, even if those plan terms were effective after that date, and to any 403(b) plan adopted before that date, without regard to the date of adoption of any salary reduction agreement provisions.
The regulations provide that if two pre-enactment plans merge, the post-
(
printed page 74101)
merger plan will be treated as a pre-enactment plan and clarify that, in the case of a multiple employer plan, the merger does not change the status of the plan for employers that were already participating before the merger. If a pre-enactment plan merges with a plan that is not eligible for the exception as a pre-enactment plan, the merged plan generally loses the exception, unless the merger occurs in connection with certain corporate transactions during a limited transition period and the pre-enactment plan is designated as the ongoing plan.
A multiple employer plan that is merged with another plan would be treated as a pre-enactment plan with respect to the employer that sponsored the merged-in plan if, with respect to the participating employer that engaged in the transaction, the plan was treated as a pre-enactment plan before the transaction. As is the case of any merger involving a multiple employer plan, the merger would not affect whether the multiple employer plan is treated as a pre-enactment plan with respect to any other employer. With respect to a merger of a multiple employer plan that is a pre-enactment plan with a multiple employer plan that is not a pre-enactment plan, the regulation provides that the merger will not affect whether the merged plan is treated as a pre-enactment plan with respect to any employer that maintained either multiple employer plan prior to the merger. If an employer joins a multiple employer plan after the date of enactment, the automatic enrollment rules apply as if the employer maintained its own separate plan (unless another statutory exception, such as the small business or new business exception, applies).
The regulations provide that other changes, such as changing plan design features or expanding eligibility, do not cause the plan to lose pre-enactment status.

Economic Effects of the Regulations
The regulations provide operational details and clarity with respect to how 401(k) and 403(b) plans comply with the automatic enrollment requirements added by section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act. Section 101 applies only to new 401(k) and 403(b) plans and provides limited scope for choices to be made about the conditions under which a new 401(k) or 403(b) plan satisfies or fails to satisfy the automatic enrollment requirements to qualify for tax-favored status.
The clarity provided by the regulations creates economic benefits for all affected taxpayers in terms of increased retirement savings and relatively small costs for affected CODAs in terms of additional investment expenses and administrative costs. The Treasury Department and the IRS used Investment Company Institute (ICI) studies; confidential tax data, including Form 5500 filings; and Treasury's Individual Tax Model (ITM) to estimate the costs and benefits of the regulations. Section 101 is estimated to increase retirement savings by $4.2 billion on average each year between 2023 and 2032, affecting about 2.2 million taxpayers and about 31,600 affected plans on average each year.

Covered Employees and Permissive Withdrawals
The regulations clarify that a CODA or a salary reduction agreement under a plan satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements only if the plan provides for an EACA that covers all eligible employees and that, while section 101 provides exceptions to this requirement for certain types of plans, it includes no provision that excludes any category of employees. Moreover, the regulations clarify that an EACA does not fail to satisfy section 101 if the default election does not apply to an employee who has an affirmative election, including an election not to have contributions made, that remains in place. The regulations also provide that an EACA satisfies the automatic enrollment requirements only if the plan provides for permissible withdrawals, as required by section 101. Hence, the regulations do not incorporate any choice in determining covered employees and permissible withdrawals.
Timing Rules
The regulations clarify that an employee's initial period begins when the employee is first eligible to elect to have contributions made under the plan and ends on the last day of the following plan year, as opposed to the initial period's beginning when the employee first has contributions made pursuant to a default election and ending on the last day of the following plan year. The timing difference between the two alternatives is at most two weeks and arises only because of coordination issues between employee start dates (some employees start in the middle of a pay period) and payroll system operations. The decision to use the approach in the regulation as opposed to the alternative would result in an increase of annual retirement savings for a new hire of up to 3 percent. Hence, the Treasury Department and the IRS expect that this rule will increase retirement savings by about $100 million per year on average relative to $4.2 billion baseline increase in retirement savings. About 25,000 plans are expected to be affected by this rule. Allowing for partial period contributions is expected to increase administrative costs by a negligible amount each year.
Default Percentage Rule
The regulations clarify that no later than the first day of each plan year beginning after an employee's initial period, the default election applicable to the employee on the first day of the prior plan year must be increased by at least one percentage point. This decision, which allows for flexibility in terms of timing and amounts of increases, reduces the administrative burden and would increase retirement savings. However, applying the minimum escalated percentage prior to the first day of the plan year is not expected to be common since plan years are typically calendar years and the effective date used by employers for annual salary increases is often January 1 or early in the first quarter of the year.
Additionally, applying an escalating percentage point greater than one percentage point is unlikely to occur for two reasons. First, research on salience and taxation
[
18
]
would suggest that doing so is likely to result in pushback from employees who are subject to automatic enrollment in the form of complaints and some employees' opting out of automatic enrollment completely due to the abrupt and significant decrease in their take-home pay. Second, employers have no discernible benefit from applying an escalating percentage-point increase greater than one percentage point.
The regulations also provide exceptions like those found in existing rules for a QACA to the uniform percentage requirement of section 101 to ensure that the automatic escalation of the default election percentage is administratively feasible. Examples include, allowing employees to contribute at different default percentages if the default percentages are based on how long the employees have been subject to the EACA and allowing the plan to cap contributions for an employee if statutory contribution dollar limits prevent them from contributing the full default percentage.
The regulations allow plans to reset an employee's initial period if an employee goes a full year without having default contributions. If the employee had no contributions because the employee made an affirmation election, the plan can reset their initial period to any future date after the employee's initial period ended. This rule gives employers the flexibility to restart an employee's initial period, including for an employee who previously made an affirmative election. For example, if the employee had no contributions because the employee terminated employment and was later rehired, the regulations allow a plan to restart the employee's initial period. While this rule would reduce the administrative costs, as plans would not have to keep track of the automatic escalation schedule of employees who terminated employment and increase retirement savings, the economic impact would be negligible as less than two percent of the U.S. workforce is composed of workers who terminated employment and were later rehired.

Investment Requirements
The regulations clarify that the investment rules in section 414A of the Code only apply to plans that allow employees to direct their investments. Given that nearly all 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans are subject to title I of ERISA, and that Form 5500 filings indicate that only about 3.5 percent of 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans do not allow participant-directed investments, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimated the proportion of the $4.2 billion baseline increase in retirement savings attributable to 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans that do not allow participant-directed investments is about $150 million. Based on Form 5500 Schedule H data, the average expense ratio is about 1.5 percent. Hence, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimate that this part of the regulations will save about $3 million in plan costs and benefit less than 80,000 taxpayers on average each year between 2023 and 2032.
Small Business and New Business Exceptions
The regulations clarify that once a business has been in existence for three years, automatic enrollment needs to begin starting the next plan year and defines a predecessor employer (which matters for determining whether a business is a new business) using existing rules under the Code. The alternative would have been to start automatic enrollment on the date of the new business's 3-year anniversary. Using US Census Bureau data on firm age,

Based on an average shift in retirement savings of six months, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimate that this rule, relative to the alternative, would reduce retirement savings over the 2023 to 2032 time period by less than $3 million a year and would affect about 19,000 taxpayers a year. Further Treasury and the IRS estimate that about 1,000 plans a year would experience small increases in associated administrative costs per year due to this rule relative to the alternative.
The regulations clarify that the number of employees that the employer normally employs for a taxable year is determined using the COBRA regulations. This clarification is necessary because section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act stipulates that businesses normally employing ten or fewer employees are not subject to the automatic enrollment requirements and the phrase normally employed is used in the COBRA regulations. Additionally, the regulations clarify that when an employer first has a year in which it normally employed more than 10 employees, the automatic enrollment rule applies starting with the next plan year that begins at least 12 months after the end of that year. Based on Form 5500 filings, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimated the proportion of the $4.2 billion baseline increase in retirement savings and the 2.2 million affected taxpayers attributable to plans with five to nine employees. Based on the assumption that about 8 percent of such firms will increase their employment beyond the 10-person threshold in the next year and an average shift in retirement savings of eighteen months, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimate that this waiting period relative to requiring such firms to begin autoenrollment once they cross the 10-person threshold would reduce retirement savings by about $4 million and affect less than 10,000 workers. The waiting period in the regulation relative to the alternative would affect about 150 plans, but the difference in plan costs between the chosen option and the alternative is estimated to be negligible on average per year between 2023 and 2032.
Exceptions for Pre-Enactment Plans
The regulations interpret what it means to establish a CODA before December 29, 2022, for purposes of section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act. The regulations provide that the automatic enrollment requirements do not apply to any plan that includes a qualified CODA if the plan terms providing for the qualified CODA were adopted initially before December 29, 2022, even if the plan terms providing for the CODA are effective after that date. The regulations could have provided an alternative interpretation and provided that the automatic enrollment requirements do not apply to any plan that includes a qualified CODA if the plan terms providing for the qualified CODA were effective initially before December 29, 2022. This alternative would have made more plans subject to the automatic enrollment requirements.
Given that plan sponsors were able to anticipate the passage of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 well in advance
[
23
]
but there was no certainty about the adoption of regulations that would exempt qualified CODAs that were adopted initially before the date of enactment from the automatic enrollment requirements, plan sponsors with a preference against automatic enrollment would have adopted their plan terms with effective dates prior to December 29, 2022. Hence, the regulations would have had little impact on the timing of the effective dates of plan terms. Hence, the Treasury Department and the IRS estimate that just 0.25 percent of the plan terms of qualified CODAs adopted before December 29, 2022, had plan terms effective after that date. Based on this assumption, this part of the regulations, relative to the alternative, would result in a one-time reduction in retirement savings of about $11 million, affecting less than 6,000 taxpayers, less than 100 plans, and total plan costs by a negligible amount.
Lastly, the regulations provide rules regarding the applicability of the pre-enactment exception in situations involving plan mergers. These merger rules are expected to benefit employers and employees by increasing flexibility and reducing the costs for the subset of plans affected by plan mergers.
