VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
I. Background
A. Infrastructure SIPs
On June 2, 2010, the EPA established a revised primary 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS with a level of 75 parts per billion (ppb), based on a 3-year average of the annual 99th percentile of daily maximum 1-hour average concentrations.
[
1
]
CAA section 110(a)(1) requires all States to submit, within three years after promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, SIP submissions to provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the NAAQS.
[
2
]
The EPA has historically referred to these SIPs as “infrastructure SIPs.” Specifically, CAA section 110(a)(1) provides the procedural and timing requirements for SIP submissions. CAA section 110(a)(2) lists specific elements that all States must meet related to a newly established or revised NAAQS, such as requirements for monitoring, basic program requirements, and legal authority that are designed to assure attainment and maintenance of the NAAQS.
Section 110(a)(2)(D)(i) of the CAA requires SIPs to contain provisions to prohibit emissions that have certain adverse air quality effects on other States due to interstate transport of pollution. Section 110(a)(2)(D)(i) includes four distinct components, commonly referred to as “prongs,” that must be addressed in infrastructure SIP submissions. The first two prongs, which are codified in section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I), require SIPs to contain adequate provisions that prohibit any source or other type of emissions activity in one State from contributing significantly to nonattainment of the NAAQS in any other State (Prong 1) and from interfering with maintenance of the NAAQS in any other State (Prong 2). These first two prongs are often referred to as the good neighbor provision. The third and fourth prongs, which are codified in section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(II), require SIPs to contain adequate provisions that prohibit emissions activity in one State from interfering with measures required to prevent significant deterioration of air quality in another State (Prong 3) and from interfering with measures to protect visibility in another State (Prong 4). This submittal and action only address CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I). The EPA has long interpreted this language to enact a “functional prohibition” on certain emissions from upwind States, necessitating the EPA's independent assessment whether those emissions will occur or have been adequately controlled in the State where they originate.
[
3
]
B. 2010 1-Hour SO
2
NAAQS Designations Background
In this proposed action, the EPA has considered information from the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS designations process, as discussed in more detail in section III.C of this publication. For this reason, a brief summary of the EPA's designations process for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS is included here.
[
4
]
After the promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, the EPA is required to designate areas as “nonattainment,” “attainment,” or “unclassifiable” pursuant to CAA section 107(d)(1) and (2). The process for designating areas following promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS is contained in CAA section 107(d). The EPA promulgated the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS on June 22, 2010.
[
5
]
The EPA Administrator promulgated the first round of designations for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS on July 25, 2013, designating 29 areas in 16 States as nonattainment for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS.
[
6
]
The
Federal Register
publications for Round 2 designations published on July 12, 2016 and on December 13, 2016.
[
7
]
Round 3 designations were published on January 9, 2018 and April 5, 2018.
[
8
]
Round 4 designations were published on March 26, 2021 and April 14, 2021.
[
9 10 11
]
(
printed page 74135)
On August 21, 2015, the EPA separately promulgated air quality characterization requirements for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS in the Data Requirements Rule (DRR).
[
12
]
The DRR required state air agencies to characterize air quality, through air dispersion modeling or monitoring, in areas associated with sources that emitted in 2014 2,000 tons per year (tpy) or more of SO
2
, or that had otherwise been listed under the DRR by the EPA or state air agencies. In lieu of modeling or monitoring, state air agencies, by specified dates, could elect to impose Federally enforceable emissions limitations on those sources restricting their annual SO
2
emissions to less than 2,000 tpy, or provide documentation that the sources had been shut down. The EPA used the information generated by implementation of the DRR to help inform Round 4 designations for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS.
For Virginia, under the DRR, the EPA identified 11 sources for which the Commonwealth was required to characterize air quality through modeling or monitoring or impose Federally enforceable controls. The EPA designated part of Giles County as nonattainment and the remainder of the County as attainment/unclassifiable in Round 4.
[
13 14
]
For the “Giles County (part)” nonattainment area, 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 81.347 sets forth the geographic coordinates, specifying the nonattainment area boundary. This is the only nonattainment area in Virginia for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS following the EPA's fourth and final round of the designations process. All other areas in the Commonwealth were designated as attainment/unclassifiable or unclassifiable (Buchanan County) during Round 3 or Round 4.
[
15
]
While in-state designations themselves are not sufficient on their own for the EPA to draw conclusions about potential out-of-state impacts, the EPA draws upon information generated under the DRR and as part of the SO
2
designations process, as well as other available relevant information, that is useful in assessing whether Virginia's SIP meets the requirements of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I).
II. Relevant Factors Used To Evaluate 2010 1-Hour SO
                    2
                     Interstate Transport SIPs
Although SO
2
is emitted from a similar universe of point and nonpoint sources as is directly emitted fine particulate matter (PM
2.5
) and the precursors to ozone and PM
2.5
, interstate transport of SO
2
is unlike the transport of PM
2.5
or ozone, which disperse over a wide area and can contribute to nonattainment or maintenance issues hundreds of miles from precursor-emitting sources or activities. SO
2
emissions usually do not undergo long-range transport in the atmosphere. The transport of SO
2
, relative to the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS, is more analogous to the transport of lead (Pb) relative to the Pb NAAQS in that emissions of SO
2
typically result in 1-hour pollutant impacts of greatest concern near the source of emissions. However, ambient 1-hour concentrations of SO
2
do not decrease as quickly with distance from the source as do 3-month average concentrations of Pb, because SO
2
gas is not removed by deposition as rapidly as are Pb particles. Emitted SO
2
has wider-ranging impacts than emitted Pb, but it does not have such wide-ranging (far downwind) impacts that treatment in a manner similar to ozone or PM
2.5
would be appropriate. Accordingly, the approaches that the EPA has adopted for ozone or PM
2.5
transport are too regionally focused, and the approach for Pb transport is too tightly circumscribed to the source, to be appropriate for assessing SO
2
transport. SO
2
transport is therefore a unique case and necessitates an approach that lies between these other approaches to assessing pollutant transport.
In this proposed rulemaking, and consistent with prior SO
2
transport analyses, the EPA focused on a 50 kilometer (km)-wide zone around sources of interest because the physical properties of SO
2
result in relatively localized pollutant impacts near an emission source that drop off with distance. Given the properties of SO
2
, the EPA believes that significant impacts in a downwind State are unlikely at distances greater than 50 km from a source and thus, we are focusing our review on areas within 50 km of the State lines. This scale of analysis is consistent with the “urban scale” which is the largest appropriate spatial scale for SO
2
monitors and is useful for assessing SO
2
transport and trends in area-wide air quality.
[
16
]
The EPA reviewed Virginia's interstate transport SIP revision pertaining to the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS, submitted on September 13, 2022. The Agency discusses the submission in section III of this document, and in further detail in the technical support document (TSD) for this action. We also have elected to review and assess other available information regarding SO
2
emissions and air quality for sources in the Commonwealth to assist in our own evaluation, including more recent air quality, emissions, and wind rose data, when available. We independently analyzed all information to determine whether the Commonwealth meets the interstate transport requirements described in the CAA.
[
17
]
Consistent with our prior evaluations of other State's SO
2
interstate transport obligations, the EPA conducted a weight of evidence (WOE) analysis evaluating several sources of information, including current air quality data from monitors and available emissions and/or source modeling for sources in Virginia and in neighboring States within 50 km of the Commonwealth's border. A WOE approach can be appropriate in instances, such as here, to determine whether or not SO
2
emissions from Viriginia contribute to nonattainment or maintenance issues in adjoining States. A WOE analysis that is based strictly on available data may not be sufficient in all instances for evaluating interstate SO
2
transport, and additional analysis may be necessary. Further, the term “WOE” does not establish the legal or technical meaning for what constitutes significant contribution to nonattainment or interference with maintenance for the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS. Rather, the term refers to the gathering and consideration of a wide range of information, on a case-by-case basis, to make a determination regarding whether a statutory or regulatory standard is met.
In other SO
2
interstate transport SIP actions, the EPA has generally been able to use a WOE analysis of available information to reach a conclusion that there are no SO
2
nonattainment or
(
printed page 74136)
maintenance issues in the relevant areas of other States, or that no sources in the upwind State are contributing to those issues. If the available evidence indicated, however, that an upwind source, sources, or emissions activities were contributing to an out-of-state SO
2
nonattainment or maintenance problem, then further analysis and a regulatory determination would be necessary concerning what amount of those emissions, if any, constituted “significant contribution” under Prong 1 or Prong 2 of the good neighbor provision.
We find that there is sufficient information to allow the EPA to make a determination that under baseline conditions and likely future emissions scenarios no Virginia sources are contributing or will contribute to any out-of-state SO
2
nonattainment or maintenance problems. Accordingly, it is not necessary here to render a determination concerning what amount of emissions would be “significant” and therefore subject to prohibition under the good neighbor provision.
[
18
]
III. Summary of SIP Revision and the EPA's Analysis
A. State Submission
On September 13, 2022, the Commonwealth of Virginia submitted to the EPA a SIP revision concerning the interstate pollution transport requirements under CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) for the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS. The September 2022 SIP submittal and this action only address CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I), or Prongs 1 and 2, of the good neighbor provision. The Commonwealth of Virginia separately submitted, and the EPA took separate action on all the infrastructure elements outlined in CAA sections 110(a)(1) and 110(a)(2) except for the interstate transport provisions of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) for the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS.
[
19
]
In Virginia's September 13, 2022 interstate transport SIP submittal, the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (VADEQ) includes a source evaluation for Virginia SO
2
emissions to demonstrate that the majority of SO
2
emissions in Virginia originate from point source fuel combustion and certain specific industrial facilities. Virginia's analysis also identifies in-state sources (emitting 50 tons per year (tpy) or more of SO
2
) within 50 kilometers of any State boundary to determine if emissions from that point source may impact nonattainment and maintenance areas in other States. Large sources (emitting 100 tpy or more of SO
2
) within 50 km of Virginia's boundaries and located in other States, or “cross-state sources,” were also identified. These individual cross-state sources were evaluated to determine if their SO
2
emissions may combine with SO
2
emissions from Virginia sources in a manner that could create attainment or maintenance issues for the 2010 SO
2
standard. Virginia's SIP revision also included monitoring data within the Commonwealth and in other States within 50 km of the Virginia border, as well as emissions trends in Virginia and nearby States.
B. The EPA's Evaluation Methodology
For this CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) evaluation of the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS, the EPA conducted a WOE analysis for Prong 1 and Prong 2 separately, evaluating available information such as air quality, emission sources, modeling and emission trends in Virginia, and the States that border the Commonwealth.
[
20
]
To identify which sources and emissions activities in Virginia could potentially impact downwind air quality in other States with respect to the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS, the EPA used information from the EPA's National Emissions Inventory (NEI) and Emissions Inventory System (EIS).
[
21 22
]
The NEI is a comprehensive and detailed estimate of air emissions for criteria pollutants, criteria pollutant precursors, and hazardous air pollutants from air emissions sources, updated every three years using information provided by the States and other information available to the EPA. For the EPA's analyses, we largely relied on data from the 2020 NEI, because it is the most recently available, complete, and quality assured dataset.
[
23
]
However, in evaluating emissions trends, both State-wide and at the facility level, the EPA also considered data from prior NEI reports and more recent EIS queries, as part of the overall WOE analysis.
As shown in table 1, in this document, in 2020 the majority of SO
2
emissions in Virginia originate from point sources. This was also noted by VADEQ in their September 2022 SIP revision, after reviewing the 2014 and 2017 NEIs. In 2020, total SO
2
emissions from point sources in Virginia comprised approximately 78 percent of the total SO
2
emissions in the Commonwealth. Non-point sources, on road and non-road emissions sources are individually much smaller and more dispersed throughout Virginia and are therefore unlikely to contribute to high ambient concentrations when compared to point source contributions. Further analysis shows that facilities with reported emissions greater than 100 tpy represent approximately seven percent of the total number of Virginia SO
2
point sources but are responsible for 89 percent (12,312 tons of SO
2
) of the total 2020 SO
2
point source emissions in the Commonwealth.
[
24 25
]
Accordingly, the EPA focused our WOE analysis on SO
2
emissions from Virginia's larger point sources (
i.e.,
point sources emitting over 100 tpy of SO
2
) that are located within 50 km of one or more of Virginia's borders.

The EPA proposes that an assessment of Virginia's fulfilment of the Prong 1 and 2 requirements of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS may be reasonably based upon several factors. These factors include the evaluation of the predicted downwind impacts in previous relevant modeling studies for a source and nearby areas, assessment of Virginia's SO
2
point source emissions from facilities that emit more than 100 tpy of SO
2
and are located within approximately 50 km of another State, assessment of other States' point sources emitting more than 100 tpy of SO
2
located within approximately 50 km of Virginia, and assessment of Federal regulations and permits affecting Virginia's SO
2
sources.
[

]
The EPA's evaluation is informed by all available data at the time of this rulemaking.
[
27
]
The EPA notes that if this information were insufficient to draw a reasonable conclusion concerning whether Virginia is “significantly contributing” or not, then it would not be possible to propose approval based only on this information. In other words, the absence of information concerning whether interstate transport is occurring is generally not in itself sufficient justification for approving a good neighbor SIP submission. For example, if there were inadequate monitoring or modeling information to characterize the effects of a large, near-border source of SO
2
emissions, it may be appropriate to conduct, or ask the State to conduct, further analysis to better characterize that source and its effects, in order to reach a determination concerning whether the good neighbor provision is being met.
[
28
]
In this case, the information available to the EPA, as analyzed in the accompanying TSD and summarized below, is fully sufficient to conclude that Virginia is not and will not emit SO
2
pollution in violation of the good neighbor provision for the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS.
1. The EPA's Prong 1 Evaluation—Contribute Significantly to Nonattainment
Prong 1 of the good neighbor provision requires States' plans to prohibit emissions that will contribute significantly to nonattainment of the NAAQS in another State. The EPA's evaluation of whether Virginia has met its Prong 1 transport obligations was completed by considering all available information, including the following: SO
2
ambient air quality in Virginia and neighboring States; SO
2
emissions trends for Virginia; potential ambient impacts of SO
2
emissions from certain facilities in Virginia on neighboring States; potential interaction with emissions from cross-state sources; and permit requirements which may reduce SO
2
emissions either directly or indirectly.
[
29 30
]
Based on the EPA's analysis, we propose to determine that Virginia's SIP satisfies the requirements of Prong 1 of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I). This proposed determination is based on the following considerations:
No SO
2
monitors located in Virginia, or within 50 km of its border, recorded above the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS of 75 ppb for the 2023 or 2024 design values (DVs).
[
31
]
With the exception of the source-specific monitor in Giles County, the DVs at Virginia's SO
2
monitors have remained below the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS from 2015-2024;
[
32
]
Downward SO
2
emissions trends in Virginia, its surrounding States (Kentucky, Maryland, North Carolina, Tennessee, and West Virginia) and the District of Columbia, when considered together with the other factors discussed as part of the EPA's WOE analysis, further support that the Commonwealth's sources will not significantly contribute to any other States' nonattainment of the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS;
Source-specific analyses of every Virginia SO
2
source emitting over 100 tpy and located within 50 km of the Commonwealth's border indicate that the sources do not contribute to nonattainment in other States. These analyses draw upon available emissions data, monitoring data, air quality modeling, controls, wind rose data, and other relevant information to assess the likelihood of air quality impacts from these sources on areas in surrounding States. A detailed discussion of each source-specific analysis is contained in section IV.B.1 of the TSD accompanying this action. Below we cover some of the principal evidence that confirms that emissions from Virginia do not contribute to nonattainment in other States.
Jewell Coke Company, Virginia's one applicable southwest facility, has stacks of relatively short heights and sits at an elevation well below surrounding significant terrain features, which act as barriers to emissions reaching to and beyond neighboring State lines.
Several facilities have closed (Wheelabrator Portsmouth) or have been emitting less than 100 tpy of SO
2
in more recent years (King George Landfill Inc and Perdue Foods LLC—Accomac Complex).
There are generally very few cross-State facilities emitting more than 100 tpy of SO
2
within 50 km of the
(
printed page 74138)
individual large point sources in Virginia.
Modeling projections indicated that it was unlikely that certain Virginia facilities (Lhoist North American—Kimballton Plant, Roanoke Cement Company, WestRock—Covington, and Dominion/ODEC Clover Power Station) would impact another State through interstate transport of the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS.
Certain Virgina facilities (Lhoist North American—Kimballton Plant and WestRock—Covington) took facility-wide SO
2
emission limits to ensure compliance with the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS.
Two Virginia facilities (Roanoke Cement Company in Botetourt County and WestRock in the City of Covington) were able to remove their DRR source-specific monitors as they were measuring less than 50% of the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS.
Further, Virginia's SIP-approved permit programs will continue to ensure that SO
2
emissions in the Commonwealth will be effectively controlled for existing and new sources or modifications.
Based on this evaluation, and as more thoroughly discussed in our TSD for this action, the EPA proposes to find that sources within Virginia will not significantly contribute to nonattainment of the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS in any other State.
2. The EPA's Prong 2 Evaluation—Interference With Maintenance
Prong 2 of the good neighbor provision requires State plans to prohibit emissions that will interfere with maintenance of a NAAQS in another State. The EPA's evaluation of whether Virginia has met its Prong 2 transport obligations was accomplished by considering all available information, with a focus on current regional air quality data (including Virginia and its neighboring States), SO
2
emissions trends for the Commonwealth and neighboring States, and how existing and future sources of SO
2
are addressed through existing regulations and permits. This evaluation builds upon the analysis conducted for significant contribution to nonattainment (Prong 1), which evaluated SO
2
ambient air quality in Virginia and neighboring States and potential ambient impacts of SO
2
emissions from certain facilities in the Commonwealth on neighboring States.
Based on the EPA's analysis, we propose to find that SO
2
levels in neighboring States near the Virginia border indicate an ability to maintain the SO
2
NAAQS, and as such the EPA proposes to determine that Virginia's SIP satisfies the requirements of Prong 2 of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I). This determination is based on the following considerations:
2023 and 2024 DVs for SO
2
monitors in Virginia within 50 km of another State's border and in neighboring States (Kentucky, Maryland, North Carolina, Tennessee, and West Virginia) and the District of Columbia within 50 km of Virginia's border are well below the standard, indicating that these areas are all currently in attainment of the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS;
State-wide emissions trends in Virginia and surrounding States indicate generally declining SO
2
emissions and consequently declining ambient air concentrations in the relevant areas;
Source-specific analyses show that facility-level emissions are decreasing as a result of emissions unit shutdowns (Wheelabrator Portsmouth) and fuel changes (International Paper Company—Franklin Mill), indicating that emissions are not anticipated to increase relative to baseline emissions;
Current emissions control programs and permits control SO
2
emissions from certain sources within Virginia (Lhoist North American—Kimballton Plant, Roanoke Cement Company, WestRock—Covington, Covanta Fairfax, King George Landfill, Dominion/ODEC Clover Power Station, and Owens-Brockway Glass Container Inc.—Ringgold).
Virginia's prevention of significant deterioration (PSD), major new source review (NSR) regulations and minor source NSR permit programs address future new and modified SO
2
sources above major and minor permitting thresholds with the intent of ensuring that the SO
2
NAAQS will not be exceeded as a result of new facility construction or existing facility modification within the State or in surrounding States.
[
33
]
Based on this evaluation, as more thoroughly discussed in our TSD for this action, the EPA proposes to find that sources within Virginia will not interfere with maintenance of the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS in any other State.
IV. Proposed Action
The EPA is proposing to approve the interstate transport SIP revision submitted by the Commonwealth of Virginia on September 13, 2022, addressing the Prong 1 and Prong 2 requirements of CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) for the 2010 1-hour SO
2
NAAQS. Based on VADEQ's interstate transport analysis and the EPA's WOE analysis, as more thoroughly discussed in the TSD, the EPA proposes to determine that emissions from Virginia will not contribute significantly to nonattainment in, or interfere with maintenance of, any other State with respect to the 2010 SO
2
NAAQS. We therefore propose to find that Virginia's SIP contains adequate provisions consistent with CAA section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I).
The EPA is soliciting public comments on the issues discussed in this document. These comments will be considered before taking final action.

Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP submission that complies with the provisions of the CAA and applicable Federal regulations. 42 United States Code (U.S.C.) 7410(k);

. Thus, in reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. abstract: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS or Department) is updating DHS Directive 023, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act, which establishes procedures for complying with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). This update is necessary in light of the recent rescission of the Council on Environmental Quality's NEPA implementing regulations, which DHS's procedures were designed to supplement. In addition, the update incorporates provisions from the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; and the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 related to the environmental review process. The updated Directive promotes collaboration and efficiencies in the implementation of NEPA and modernizes the processes and procedures for environmental review. This update enables DHS to conduct coordinated, consistent, predictable, and timely environmental reviews, thus reducing unnecessary burdens and delays. The draft Directive is being made available for public review and comment. These comments will inform development of the final Directive. Upon finalization, the Directive will rescind DHS Directive 023-01, Rev 01 and DHS Instruction 023-01-001-01, Rev 01 which were issued in 2014.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS or Department) is updating DHS Directive
(
printed page 74182)
023, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act, which establishes procedures for complying with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). This update is necessary in light of the recent rescission of the Council on Environmental Quality's NEPA implementing regulations, which DHS's procedures were designed to supplement. In addition, the update incorporates provisions from the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; and the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 related to the environmental review process. The updated Directive promotes collaboration and efficiencies in the implementation of NEPA and modernizes the processes and procedures for environmental review. This update enables DHS to conduct coordinated, consistent, predictable, and timely environmental reviews, thus reducing unnecessary burdens and delays. The draft Directive is being made available for public review and comment. These comments will inform development of the final Directive. Upon finalization, the Directive will rescind DHS Directive 023-01, Rev 01 and DHS Instruction 023-01-001-01, Rev 01 which were issued in 2014.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. Need for This Action
The National Environmental Policy Act, as amended,
42 U.S.C. 4321-4347
(NEPA), requires all Federal agencies to assess the environmental impact of their actions.
42 U.S.C. 332(2)(C)
. The Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) previously issued regulations at
40 CFR parts 1500-1508
(CEQ regulations) implementing NEPA that were binding on Federal agencies. On April 19, 2006, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS or the Department) issued Directive 5100.1, to establish the policies and procedures that DHS would use to comply with NEPA and CEQ's then operative regulations.
71 FR 16790
(Apr. 4, 2006). In 2014, DHS rescinded Directive 5100.1 and in its place issued a new internal Directive and Instruction Manual.
79 FR 70538
(Nov. 26, 2014). These documents establish the Department's current internal procedures for complying with NEPA.
Several recent developments now require DHS to revise its NEPA procedures. First, CEQ's NEPA implementing regulations were rescinded effective April 11, 2025;
see Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations,
90 FR 10610
, Feb. 25, 2025). CEQ's action was necessitated by and consistent with Executive Order (E.O.) 14154,
Unleashing American Energy
(
90 FR 8353
, Jan. 29, 2025), in which President Trump rescinded President Carter's
E.O. 11991
,
Relating to Protection and Enhancement of Environmental Quality
(
42 FR 26967
, May 24, 1977), which was the basis CEQ had invoked for its authority to issue regulations. DHS's NEPA implementing procedures, which were a supplement to, and relied on, those CEQ regulations, thus stand in need of fundamental revision. President Trump in
E.O. 14154
further directed agencies to revise their NEPA implementing procedures consistent with the E.O., including its direction to CEQ to rescind its regulations.
In addition, Congress recently amended NEPA in significant part, in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA),
Public Law 118-5
, signed on June 3, 2023, in which Congress added substantial detail and direction in Title I of NEPA, including in particular on procedural issues that CEQ and individual agencies had previously addressed in their own procedures. DHS recognized the need to update its procedures in light of these legislative changes but had been awaiting CEQ action before updating its procedures.
See
40 CFR 1507.3(c)
(2024). With CEQ's regulations now rescinded, DHS must update its NEPA procedures to account for this change.
Finally, the Supreme Court on May 29, 2025 issued its decision in
Seven County Infrastructure Coalition
v.
Eagle County, Colorado,
605 U.S. 168 (2025), in which the Supreme Court described the “transform[ation]” of NEPA from its roots as “a modest procedural requirement,” into a significant “substantive roadblock” that “paralyze[s]” “agency decision making.”
Id.
at 173, 183. The Supreme Court explained that part of that problem had been caused by decisions of lower courts, which it rejected, issuing a “course correction” mandating that courts give “deference” to reasonable agency conclusions underlying its NEPA process.
Id.
at 184-185. The Court acknowledged, and through its course correction sought to address, the effect on “litigation-averse agencies” which, in light of judicial micromanagement, had been “tak[ing] ever more time and to prepare ever longer EISs [environmental impact statements] for future projects.”
Id.
at 184. DHS, in turn, is updating its procedures to issue its own “course correction” to streamline its process of ensuring reasonable and timely NEPA decisions, consistent with the above discussed developments.
DHS has reviewed its current NEPA implementing procedures and has developed this draft Directive in consultation with CEQ. DHS is providing an opportunity for public review and comment on this draft Directive. These comments will inform development of the final Directive. DHS will publish a final notice upon signature of the final Directive.
B. Statutory Context
NEPA establishes a national environmental policy of the federal government to use all practicable means and measures to foster and promote the general welfare, create and maintain
(
printed page 74183)
conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic, and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans. NEPA Section 101,
42 U.S.C. 4331(a)
.
In general, NEPA requires federal agencies to analyze all of their major federal actions to determine whether NEPA applies and, if so, what level of environmental analysis is required. NEPA identifies three levels of environmental review—categorical exclusion, environmental assessment, and environmental impact statement. NEPA Section 107,
42 U.S.C. 4336a
. A categorical exclusion (CATEX) is a “a category of actions that a federal agency has determined normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment within the meaning of NEPA section 102(2)(C).” NEPA Section 111(1),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(1)
. If a CATEX does not apply, the agency conducts an environmental assessment (EA) or an environmental impact statement (EIS). An EA is a “concise” document “set[ting] forth the basis of [an] agency's finding of no significant impact or determination that an environmental impact statement is necessary,” prepared in connection with a proposed agency action that does not have a significant impact, or the significance of whose impact is unknown.
See
NEPA Section 106(b)(2), 111(4),
42 U.S.C. 4336(b)(2)
,
4336e(4)
. An EIS is a document analyzing a “major federal action” significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.” NEPA Section 102(C), 111(6),
42 U.S.C. 4332(C)
,
4336e(6)
;
see also Seven County,
605 U.S. at 173. An EIS must address several factors including: (1) reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed action, (2) unavoidable adverse environmental effects, (3) feasible alternatives, (4) the relationship between human use and long term protection of the environment, and (5) irreversible and irretrievable commitments of Federal resources incurred.
[
1
]
The analysis is to be based on reliable scientific data. NEPA Section 102,
42 U.S.C. 4332
.
There have been numerous statutory changes to the environmental review process since DHS last updated its NEPA procedures in 2014. In 2015, Congress directed the Department to implement a variety of reforms to streamline and accelerate its environmental review process.
See
Fixing America's Surface Transportation (FAST) Act,
Public Law 114-94
(2015). In 2023, Congress amended NEPA in the FRA,
Public Law 118-5
(June 3, 2023). Through these amendments, Congress added substantial detail and direction regarding procedural issues that CEQ and individual agencies had previously addressed in their own procedures. The FRA amendments include defining major Federal action; clarifying the requirements for determining whether NEPA applies and the appropriate level of NEPA review; and clarifying the scope of an EIS, including clarifying the alternatives to be included in an EIS. In addition, the FRA amendments established page and time limits for EAs and EISs, outlined specific roles for lead agencies, and directed agencies to prescribe procedures to allow a project sponsor to prepare an EA or EIS under the supervision of the agency. Further, the FRA provided guidelines for the use of analysis from a prior programmatic environmental review in a subsequent document for a specified time period, and a streamlined process for adopting another agency's CATEXs. In 2025, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025,
Public Law 119-21
, title VI, 60026, (July 4, 2025), adding Section 112 of NEPA, entitled “Project Sponsor Opt-in Fees for Environmental Reviews.” This provision allows project sponsors to pay a fee to obtain shortened NEPA review deadlines. DHS needs to update its NEPA procedures in light of these statutory changes.
C. Expected Outcome
This Directive revises the internal procedures of DHS, promoting consistent implementation across the Department of its responsibilities under NEPA while still allowing flexibility for each of the Department's Components to carry out its own mission. These policies and procedures provide consistency, aid efficiency, reduce duplication, and refocus agency practice on fostering informed decision making, rather than generating paperwork. The Department expects that this Directive will reduce unnecessary delays. The Department also expects these changes to increase the availability and use of CATEXs, early collaboration, coordination techniques, and to improve timely completion of the environmental review process.
The Directive outlines the Department's interpretations of existing law and provides guidelines for agency procedure and practice with respect to NEPA compliance. The Directive does not in fact, nor does it intend to, govern the rights and obligations of any party outside the federal government. Further, nothing contained in the Directive is intended or should be construed to limit the Department's other authorities or legal responsibilities.
D. Reliance Interests
In deciding to revise its Directive, the Department acknowledges that third parties may claim to have reliance interests in the Department's existing NEPA procedures. However, DHS's revised procedures will have no effect on sufficiently advanced ongoing NEPA reviews, where the Department, following CEQ guidance, has decided that it will continue to apply existing procedures. Because reliance interests are inherently backward-looking, it is unclear how any party could assert reliance interests in these
prospective
procedures.
To the extent such interests exist, the Department first notes that, as the Supreme Court recently explained, NEPA “is a purely procedural statute” that “imposes no substantive environmental obligations or restrictions.”
Seven County,
605 U.S. at 184. Therefore, the Department believes that any asserted reliance interests grounded in substantive environmental concerns, should be entitled to no weight. Moreover, the Department further finds that any cognizable reliance interests in maintaining DHS's prior NEPA procedures are “outweigh[ed]” by “other interests and policy concerns.”
Dep't of Homeland Sec.
v.
Regents of the Univ. of California,
591 U.S. 1, 32 (2020). The complex web of regulations and procedures that preexisted the 2023 amendments to NEPA and these new procedures repeatedly led to the same type of problems that the Supreme Court identified with respect to judicial review of agency NEPA decisions: “more agency analysis of separate projects, more consideration of attenuated effects, more exploration of alternatives to proposed agency action, more speculation and consultation and estimation and litigation,” which in turn has meant that “[f]ewer projects
(
printed page 74184)
make it to the finish line,” or even “to the starting line.”
Seven County,
605 U.S. at 184. Accordingly, DHS believes that a wholesale revision and simplification of its NEPA procedures is needed to ensure a more efficient and predictable NEPA review process that supports, rather than unnecessarily hinders, DHS's ability to carry out its homeland security missions. This set of policy considerations outweighs any claimed reliance interests in the preexisting procedures.
E. Authority
DHS's foundation for the updates to its NEPA procedures is NEPA itself. Now that CEQ has rescinded its NEPA implementing regulations,
see
90 FR 10610
(Feb. 25, 2025),
see also
91 FR 618
(Jan. 8, 2026) (final rule finalizing removal of CEQ's NEPA implementing regulations), DHS is issuing this draft Directive in compliance with NEPA Section 102(2)(B),
42 U.S.C. 4332(B)
, which directs all agencies of the federal government to identify and develop methods and procedures, in consultation with CEQ, to conduct the environmental analysis that NEPA requires.
The Department's procedures incorporate the 2023 statutory amendments to NEPA, the guiding principles reflected in
E.O. 14154
, and the recent decision of the U.S. Supreme Court. Before publishing these procedures, the Department consulted with CEQ to ensure the procedures conform to NEPA.
II. Summary of Revisions
DHS proposes to revise its NEPA implementing procedures in accordance with the September 2025 CEQ guidance, “Memorandum for Heads of Departments and Agencies: Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act.” Key changes are identified below.
A. Statutory Alignment
DHS's new NEPA implementing procedures implement major structural features of the 2023 amendments, such as deadlines and page limits for EAs and EISs, as directed at NEPA Section 107(e) and (g),
42 U.S.C. 4336a(e)
and
42 U.S.C. 4336a(g)
. They incorporate Congress's definition of “major Federal action” and the exclusions thereto, as defined at NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. They incorporate Congress's mandated procedure for determining the appropriate level of review under NEPA, as provided in NEPA Section 106,
42 U.S.C. 4336
. And they incorporate Congress's revision to the requirements for what an agency must address in its EISs, as provided at NEPA Section 102(2)(C),
42 U.S.C. 4332(C)
, and Congress's requirement that public notice and solicitation of comment be provided when issuing a notice of intent to prepare an EIS, as directed at NEPA Section 107(c),
42 U.S.C. 4336a(c)
. These are all crucial features of Congress's policy design and its purpose in enacting the 2023 amendments that NEPA review be more efficient and certain.
B. Identification of DHS Actions not Subject to NEPA
The Directive identifies examples of activities that do not meet the definition of a “major federal action” pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. Additionally, DHS has identified a category of actions that are administrative and routine in nature, undertaken to support the normal conduct of DHS business. The identified actions encompass routine administrative, personnel, fiscal, and management activities that are inherently limited in scope and do not alter the physical environment, infrastructure capacity, or land use. While these activities are Federal actions, they are not “major” and therefore not subject to NEPA. These can now be classified as actions where NEPA does not apply. These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion.
C. Categorical Exclusions
Under the Directive, DHS is revising its CATEX list, now found in Appendix B, in the following manner: (1) Removal of items that no longer meet the definition of a “major federal action” pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion. (2) Clarification that all CATEXs may be used by any DHS Component. (3) Correction of typographical or other non-substantive errors. (4) Elimination of duplicative CATEXs. (5) Integration of adopted CATEXs. (6) Administrative modification to CATEX L13.
III. Discussion of the Directive
Section 1: General Directive Information
This section provides general context for the Directive and establishes its applicability throughout DHS, including all components. It revokes previous DHS NEPA implementing procedures found in Directive 023-01,
Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act (2014)
and Instruction 023-01-001-01, Rev 01,
Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act
(
Revised 2017).
Section 2: Responsibilities
Section 2 establishes roles and responsibilities throughout DHS for the implementation of NEPA. Unless otherwise delegated, the Executive Director, Energy and Environment Division serves as the individual responsible for approving NEPA documentation. The Director, Environmental Planning and Historic Preservation is responsible for the day-to-day oversight and serves as the Federal NEPA Contact for DHS.
Section 3: Content and Procedures
In general, Section 3 provides detailed procedures for DHS implementation of NEPA. Elements are summarized below.
Section 3.1.
This section recognizes the policy of DHS to comply with NEPA and integrate NEPA review at the earliest planning stages for informed decision-making, public transparency, and compliance with environmental planning requirements. The sections of the Directive are separate and severable from one another. DHS retains the authority to adopt approaches on a case-by-case basis that differ from those described in the Directive as appropriate.
Section 3.2.
This section emphasizes the importance of early NEPA compliance and integration with other planning and authorization process. This section also affirmatively asserts that NEPA applies only to major federal actions with the potential to significantly impact the human environment.
This section identifies situations in which NEPA does not apply, such as non-final agency actions, actions exempted by law, nondiscretionary actions, certain regulatory actions, extraterritorial activities, presidential actions, and actions waived under Section 102(c) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA),
Public Law 104-208
, div. C, 110 Stat. 3009, 3009-546.
DHS has identified examples of activities that do not meet the definition of a “major federal action” pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. Additionally, DHS has identified a category of actions that are administrative and routine in nature, undertaken to support the normal conduct of DHS business. Although these activities are Federal actions, they are not “major” and therefore not subject to NEPA. These can now be classified as actions where NEPA does not apply. These actions have been
(
printed page 74185)
retained as Appendix A for east of reference and to avoid confusion.
To provide consistent guidance to DHS NEPA practitioners, DHS has identified thresholds for determining NEPA applicability to grants. In alignment with the statutory framework found in NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
and the definition of “major federal action”, DHS has established a minimum threshold of 15% DHS funding or $5 million in DHS investment for an action to be considered subject to DHS review under NEPA. The 15% DHS funding requirement is necessary to demonstrate sufficient federal authority or control over an action's design, implementation, or outcome. For projects where DHS funding comprises less than 15% of the total project execution cost, the DHS role is considered incidental or ancillary, and the primary authority and decision-making responsibility remain with non-DHS entities.
Similarly, DHS has determined grant actions receiving less than $5 million in DHS funding do not rise to the level of “major federal action” and do not trigger a NEPA review. In 2025, approximately 44% of the EAs prepared by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) were for projects under $5 million in funding. None resulted in a finding of significant environmental impacts. These minimum funding thresholds ensure efficient allocation of DHS resources to actions with the potential for significant environmental effects, while maintaining compliance with NEPA's statutory intent and avoiding unnecessary review of projects with only minor federal participation.
Section 3.3.
Within Section 3.3 DHS establishes a hierarchical approach to NEPA compliance. DHS will first consider application of CATEX, either through established CATEX, adopted CATEX, or establishment of a new or revised CATEX. If DHS cannot apply a CATEX, DHS will then prepare an EA if a proposed action has unknown or less than significant environmental effects. If the proposed action is likely to have reasonably foreseeable significant effects, DHS will develop an EIS.
In considering whether the reasonably foreseeable effects of a proposed action are significant, DHS will analyze the potentially affected environment, as appropriate to the action, and degree of effects, including both short- and long-term effects, both beneficial and adverse effects, effects on public health and safety, economic effects and effects on the quality of life of the American people.
Section 3.4.
This section explains that DHS seeks efficiency by integrating NEPA with other planning processes and using programmatic analyses, existing documents, and early scoping. Generally, until DHS makes a CATEX determination, issues a finding of no significant impact, or issues a record of decision, DHS will take no action concerning a proposed action that would (1) have an adverse environmental effect; (2) limit the choice of reasonable alternatives; or (3) result in an irreversible and irretrievable commitment of resources.
Section 3.5.
Due to the mission of the Department and Departmental components, DHS anticipates the need to comply with NEPA for classified actions. Classified NEPA documents are prepared and safeguarded per security requirements, with unclassified portions made public when possible and in accordance with legal requirements.
Section 3.6.
Congress has provided that the multiple agencies involved shall determine which of them will be the lead agency pursuant to the criteria identified in NEPA Section 107(a)(1)(A),
42 U.S.C. 4336a(a)(1)(A)
. When serving as the lead agency, DHS is ultimately responsible for determining and documenting the scope of the project at hand and completing the NEPA process. Section 3.6 further identifies procedures to address disputes regarding lead agency designation and join lead agency designations.
This section also identifies cooperating agency designations. Any Federal agency, including DHS, with special expertise with respect to any environmental issue may be a cooperating agency. A state, tribal, local, or territorial agency of similar qualifications may become a cooperating or participating agency by agreement with the lead agency.
Section 3.7.
This section discusses how DHS uses CATEXs. DHS establishes, revises, adopts, or removes CATEXs through consultation with CEQ and public notice. After DHS establishes or adopts CATEXs, DHS components may apply them when the action fits within the CATEX and no unmitigated “extraordinary circumstances” exist.  DHS may apply multiple CATEXs to the constituent parts of single action but must consider whether the aggregate impacts of the constituent parts could give rise to an extraordinary circumstance or result in a reasonably foreseeable significant effect. The mere presence of an extraordinary circumstance does not necessarily prevent the application of the CATEX. DHS considers the following “extraordinary circumstances”:
(1) A potentially significant effect on public health or safety.
(2) A potentially significant effect on species or habitats protected by the ESA, Marine Mammal Protection Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, or other Federal law protecting a species or habitat.
(3) A potentially significant effect on historic properties (
e.g.,
districts, sites, buildings, structures, or objects) that are listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, a potentially significant effect on traditional cultural properties or sacred sites, or lead to the loss or destruction of a significant scientific, cultural, or historical resource.
(4) A potentially significant effect on an environmentally sensitive area.
(5) A potential or threatened violation of a Federal, tribal, state, local, or territorial law or requirement imposed to protect the environment. Some examples of other requirements to consider are a local noise control ordinance; the requirement to conform to an applicable State Implementation Plan for air quality standards; Federal, tribal, state, local, or territorial, requirements to control hazardous or toxic substances; and environmental permits.
(6) An effect on the quality of the human environment that is likely to be highly controversial in terms of scientific validity, likely to be highly uncertain, or likely to involve unique or unknown environmental risks. This also includes effects that may result from the use of new technology or unproven technology. Controversy over, including public opposition to, a proposed action absent any demonstrable potential for significant environmental impacts does not itself constitute an extraordinary circumstance.
(7) Extent to which a precedent is established for future actions with significant effects.
(8) Significantly greater scope or size than normally experienced for this category of action.
(9) Potential for significant degradation of already existing poor environmental conditions. Also, initiation of a potentially significant environmental degrading influence, activity, or effect in areas not already significantly modified from their natural condition.
CATEXs designated with an asterisk (*) in Appendix B require documentation utilizing the Environmental Planning and Historic Preservation (EPHP) Decision Support System (DSS), or DHS component approved system.
Section 3.8.
This section provides for the use of a Notice of Intent (NOI) and Scoping to assist DHS with the preparation of EAs and EISs. Scoping may be used to identify substantive issues and connected actions for analysis.
Section 3.9.
This section details when and how DHS prepares EAs. DHS will prepare an EA when an action is not
(
printed page 74186)
categorically excluded and significant environmental effects are not anticipated. EAs are concise documents analyzing purpose, alternatives, effects, and mitigation. EAs are limited to 75 pages and must be completed within one year.
Section 3.10.
DHS issues a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) when an EA shows no significant effects, closing the NEPA process for that action.
Section 3.11.
DHS will prepare an EIS for actions with significant environmental effects. EISs are limited to 150 pages (300 for complex actions) and will be completed within two years.
Section 3.12.
DHS issues a Record of Decision (ROD) to summarize the final decision, alternatives analyzed in the EIS, and mitigation plans, closing the NEPA process for the action.
Section 3.13.
To enhance efficiencies in NEPA, DHS will utilize programmatic NEPA documents and tiering where appropriate. DHS encourages the use of supplemental NEPA documents and reliance on existing documentation, where appropriate. Where possible, DHS will integrate other environmental requirements, including compliance with other Federal environmental laws, with the NEPA process to streamline reviews and reduce duplication.
Section 3.14.
DHS integrates CEQ's January 21, 2026
Memorandum for Heads of Departments and Agencies: Emergencies and NEPA Guidance.
In general, DHS will take direct action to address immediate threats to life, property, or important natural, cultural, or historic resources. For actions subject to NEPA, DHS will determine the appropriate level of NEPA review—CATEX, EA, EIS. Where emergency circumstances make it necessary to take an action with reasonably foreseeable significant effects without observing these procedures, DHS will consult with CEQ about alternative arrangements for compliance with NEPA Section 102(2)(C),
42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C)
.
Section 3.15.
This section establishes DHS procedures for project sponsor-prepared NEPA documents. When project sponsors or contractors prepare DHS NEPA documents, DHS will provide appropriate supervision and guidance. DHS retains responsibility for content.
Section 3.16.
This section provides direction for DHS components wishing to prepare Component Supplemental Instructions for NEPA implementation. Supplemental Instructions must be consistent with the DHS NEPA Directive and are subject to approval by the Executive Director, DHS Energy and Environment Division. Components with approved Supplemental Instructions may also request Delegation of Authority to approve component NEPA documents.
Section 3.17.
This section identifies activities requiring notification to the Energy and Environment Division.
Section 4: Authorities
This section identifies the authorities supporting the execution of this Directive.
Modifications to DHS Categorical Exclusions
1. General
Under the Directive, DHS is revising its CATEX list, now found in Appendix B, in the following manner: (1) Removal of items that no longer meet the definition of a “major Federal action” pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion. (2) Clarification that all CATEXs may be used by any DHS Component. (3) Correction of typographical or other non-substantive errors and administrative revisions. (4) Elimination of duplicative CATEXs. (5) Integration of previously adopted CATEXs. (6) Modification of CATEX L13. The DHS CATEX substantiation documentation is available for review at
dhs.gov/nepa.
2. Removal
DHS has determined that 16 actions previously designated as CATEXs do not meet the definition of “major federal action” under NEPA Section 111(10),
42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)
. Identified actions are limited to routine or administrative functions that do not have the potential to significantly affect the quality of the human environment. Although these activities constitute federal actions, they are not considered “major federal actions” and, as such, are not subject to NEPA requirements. As such, these actions have been removed from DHS's CATEX list, found in Appendix B. However, to provide continued reference and to avoid potential confusion, these actions are listed in Appendix A of the DHS NEPA procedures.
3. Clarification
DHS is clarifying that all CATEXs may be utilized by any DHS Component or entity executing an action within the mission space of the established CATEX. While Appendix B identifies when a CATEX is more likely to be utilized by a specific Component, its use is not precluded by other Components. This clarification fosters a unified standard for compliance with NEPA, minimizes duplicative efforts, reduces administrative delays, and supports the Department's ability to rapidly respond to evolving threats and mission requirements.
4. Corrections and Administrative Revisions
The Directive makes non-substantive corrections to typographical errors identified during the review period. Additionally, in recognition of DHS's mission space, DHS has inserted “territorial” into previous references to state, tribal, and local equities. Additional non-substantive administrative revisions include, but are not limited to, updating references to DHS as opposed to a specific Component, renumbering, and modernizing terminology.
5. Duplications
To streamline DHS's CATEX listing, duplicative CATEXs have been removed. Impacted CATEXs were predominantly within the listing designated for primary utilization by the U.S. Coast Guard. Remaining CATEXs have been renumbered accordingly.
6. Integration
DHS has fully integrated previously adopted CATEXs into the CATEX table found in Appendix B. Integrated CATEXs have been assigned a DHS number for utilization. DHS will apply the extraordinary circumstances found in Section 3.7 for these actions.
7. Modification to CATEX L13 (Previously Numbered CATEX L38)
On behalf of the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), DHS proposes an administrative revision to CATEX 13, previously numbered CATEX L38. The changes are intended to clarify the scope of the CATEX. The USCG has relied on CATEX L38 for actions performed as part of the Aids to Navigation (ATON) program. The modified verbiage will provide improved clarity for field users on the scope of the CATEX and require a Record of Consideration when there is potential for extraordinary circumstances. As described, DHS has determined that the revised CATEX does not normally have significant effects and that the actions described are appropriate to include within the scope of this CATEX.
IV. Notice to the Public
This notice serves to inform the public of DHS's proposed modifications to the Department's NEPA implementing procedures, found in Directive 023-01, and to request comment on the proposed
(
printed page 74187)
modifications. Upon issuance of this notice, the draft Directive will be available on
DHS.gov
at
https://www.dhs.gov/​ocrso/​eed/​epb/​nepa
.
Tracey L. Watkins,
Chief Readiness Support Officer, Department of Homeland Security.

On September 5, 2025, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., of Alexandria, Virginia (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 1, at 1, 4. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration, N9918357, alleging that Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the Commonwealth of Virginia, the state in which [she is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
).
[
1
]
The OSC notified Registrant of her right to file a written request for hearing, and that if she failed to file such a request, she would be deemed to have waived her right to a hearing and be in default. RFAAX 1, at 2 (citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds her to be in default. RFAA, at 3.
[
2
]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
at 1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to
21 CFR 1301.43(c)
,
(f)
, and
1301.46
. RFAA, at 4;
see also
21 CFR 1316.67
.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. According to the OSC, on or about May 21, 2025, the Virginia Board of Medicine suspended Registrant from the practice of osteopathic medicine in Virginia. RFAAX 1, at 2.
According to Virginia online records, of which the Agency takes official notice,
[
3
]
Registrant's Virginia osteopathic medical license is suspended. Virginia Department of Health Professions License Lookup,
https://dhp.virginiainteractive.org/​Lookup/​Index
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia, the state in which she is registered with DEA.
[
4
]
(
printed page 74196)
Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. § 802(21).”). The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., James L. Hooper, M.D.,
76 FR 71371
,
71372
(2011),
pet. for rev. denied,
481 F. App'x 826 (4th Cir. 2012);
Frederick Marsh Blanton, M.D.,
43 FR 27616
,
27617
(1978),
Scott Hansen, A.P.R.N.,
90 FR 27338
(2025).
[
5
]
According to Virginia statute, “dispense” means “to deliver a drug to an ultimate user or research subject by or pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, including the prescribing and administering, packaging, labeling, or compounding necessary to prepare the substance for that delivery.” Va. Code § 54.1-3401 (2026). Additionally, Virginia statute defines “practitioner” as “a physician . . . or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted to distribute, dispense, prescribe and administer, or conduct research with respect to a controlled substance in the course of professional practice or research in [Virginia].”
Id.
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia. As discussed above, an individual must be a licensed practitioner to dispense a controlled substance in Virginia. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Virginia, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 824(a)
, I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. FB9918357 issued to Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O. Further, pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
, I hereby deny any pending applications of Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., for additional registration in Virginia. This Order is effective December 18, 2026.

AGENCY:
United States International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice of the scheduling of expedited reviews pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 (“the Act”) to determine whether revocation of the countervailing and the antidumping duty orders on potassium phosphate salts from China would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury within a reasonably foreseeable time.
DATES:
September 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Julie Duffy (202) 708-2579, Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov
). The public record for this proceeding may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On September 4, 2026, the Commission determined that the domestic interested party group response to its notice of institution (
91 FR 32445
, June 1, 2026) of the subject
(
printed page 74195)
five-year reviews was adequate and that the respondent interested party group response was inadequate. The Commission did not find any other circumstances that would warrant conducting full reviews.
[
1
]
Accordingly, the Commission determined that it would conduct expedited reviews pursuant to section 751(c)(3) of the Act (
19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(3)
).
For further information concerning the conduct of these reviews and rules of general application, consult the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, part 201, subparts A and B (
19 CFR part 201
), and part 207, subparts A, D, E, and F (
19 CFR part 207
).
Staff report.
—A staff report containing information concerning the subject matter of the reviews has been placed in the nonpublic record, and will be made available to persons on the Administrative Protective Order service list for these reviews on November 17, 2026. A public version will be issued thereafter, pursuant to § 207.62(d)(4) of the Commission's rules.
Written submissions.
—As provided in § 207.62(d) of the Commission's rules, interested parties that are parties to the reviews and that have provided individually adequate responses to the notice of institution,
[
2
]
and any party other than an interested party to the reviews may file written comments with the Secretary on what determination the Commission should reach in the reviews. Comments are due on or before November 24, 2026 and may not contain new factual information. Any person that is neither a party to the five-year reviews nor an interested party may submit a brief written statement (which shall not contain any new factual information) pertinent to the reviews by November 24, 2026. However, should the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) extend the time limit for its completion of the final results of its reviews, the deadline for comments (which may not contain new factual information) on Commerce's final results is three business days after the issuance of Commerce's results. If comments contain business proprietary information (BPI), they must conform with the requirements of §§ 201.6, 207.3, and 207.7 of the Commission's rules. The Commission's
Handbook on Filing Procedures,
available on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/​documents/​handbook_​on_​filing_​procedures.pdf
,
elaborates upon the Commission's procedures with respect to filings.
In accordance with §§ 201.16(c) and 207.3 of the rules, each document filed by a party to the reviews must be served on all other parties to the reviews (as identified by either the public or BPI service list), and a certificate of service must be timely filed. The Secretary will not accept a document for filing without a certificate of service.
Determinations.
—The Commission has determined these reviews are extraordinarily complicated and therefore has determined to exercise its authority to extend the review period by up to 90 days pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(5)(B)
.
Authority:
These reviews are being conducted under authority of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930; this notice is published pursuant to § 207.62 of the Commission's rules.
By order of the Commission.
Issued: November 16, 2026.
Lisa Barton,
Secretary to the Commission.

ACTION:
Request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Labor, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing collections of information in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. This program helps to ensure that requested data can be provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, and the impact of collection requirements on respondents can be properly assessed. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is soliciting comments concerning the proposed extension of the “Labor Market Information (LMI) Cooperative Agreement Application Package.” A copy of the proposed information collection request can be obtained by contacting the individual listed below in the Addresses section of this notice.
DATES:
Written comments must be submitted to the office listed in the Addresses section of this notice on or before January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Send comments to Morgan Scheinin, BLS Clearance Officer, Division of Management Systems, Bureau of Labor Statistics, by email to
BLS_PRA_Public@bls.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Morgan Scheinin, BLS Clearance Officer, at 202-691-7268 (this is not a toll free number). (See Addresses section.)
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The BLS enters into Cooperative Agreements with State Workforce Agencies (SWAs) annually to provide financial assistance to the SWAs for the production and operation of the following LMI statistical programs: Current Employment Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, and Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages. The Cooperative Agreement provides the
(
printed page 74207)
basis for managing the administrative and financial aspects of these programs.
The existing collection of information allows Federal staff to negotiate the Cooperative Agreement with the SWAs and monitor their financial and programmatic performance and adherence to administrative requirements imposed by the
Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards
(
2 CFR 200
) and other grant related regulations. The information collected also is used for planning and budgeting at the Federal level and in meeting Federal reporting requirements.
II. Current Action
Office of Management and Budget clearance is being sought for the LMI Cooperative Agreement application package. The extension of this collection of information will allow the BLS to incorporate routine annual updates to the Cooperative Agreement and work statements which define SWA deliverables and requirements and allow the BLS to carry out its responsibilities to monitor financial and programmatic performance.
The Cooperative Agreement application package being submitted for approval is representative of the package sent every year to state agencies. The work statements included in the Cooperative Agreement application also are representative of what is included in the whole LMI Cooperative Agreement package. The final Cooperative Agreement, including the work statements, will be submitted separately to the Office of Management and Budget for review of any minor year-to-year information collection burden changes they may contain.
III. Desired Focus of Comments
The Bureau of Labor Statistics is particularly interested in comments that:
Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility.
Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used.
Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected.
Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submissions of responses.

SUMMARY:
The Department of Labor's (DOL) Employment and Training Administration (ETA) is soliciting comments concerning a proposed revision for the authority to conduct the information collection request (ICR) titled, “Unemployment Insurance (UI) State Quality Service Plan (SQSP) Planning and Reporting Guidelines.” This comment request is part of continuing Departmental efforts to reduce paperwork and respondent burden in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
DOL, as part of continuing efforts to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing collections of information before submitting them to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for final approval. This program helps to ensure requested data can be provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, and the impact of collection requirements can be properly assessed.
The SQSP is a comprehensive performance management system implemented in 1995 for the UI program and the principal vehicle that state UI agencies use to plan, record, and manage program improvement efforts. SQSP also serves as the grant document through which states receive Federal UI administrative funding. SQSP links program performance with the budget and planning process. The SQSP package also includes key reports associated with workload and cost detail from states used to determine administrative funding in excess of initial funding allocations made to each state.
The SQSP, with its State Plan Narrative, Corrective Action Plans (CAPs), and Integrity Action Plan, represents the state's formal plan and schedule for improving performance. States will continue to use the State Plan Narrative to provide a general summary of the UI program in the state. Actions planned to correct deficiencies for Secretary Standards, Core Measures, and UI programs are expected to be addressed in CAPs. Each SWA is required to submit one CAP for each deficiency. Based on the most recent activity during the FY 2027 SQSP process, a total of 750 CAPs were submitted from SWAs. This is a decrease of 124 CAPs from the last OMB approval cycle and represents a significant decline in the burden associated with the SQSP information collection. ETA proposes extending this collection with a revision due to the change in estimated burden.
The Secretary of Labor is authorized to provide funds to administer the UI program and to govern the expenditures of those funds. The SQSP is a major part of the Department's program oversight and governance and administrative funding distribution process. The Social Security Act sections 302, and 303(a)(8) and (9), authorize this information collection.
This information collection is subject to the PRA. A Federal agency generally cannot conduct or sponsor a collection of information, and the public is generally not required to respond to an information collection, unless it is approved by OMB under the PRA and displays a currently valid OMB Control Number. In addition, notwithstanding any other provisions of law, no person shall generally be subject to penalty for failing to comply with a collection of information that does not display a valid Control Number.
See
5 CFR 1320.5(a)
and
1320.6
.

Submitted comments will also be a matter of public record for this ICR and posted on the internet, without redaction. DOL encourages commenters not to include personally identifiable information, confidential business data, or other sensitive statements/information in any comments.
DOL is particularly interested in comments that:
Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
Evaluate the accuracy of the Agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;

permitting electronic submission of responses).
