AGENCY:
U.S. National Science Foundation.
ACTION:
Notice of permit applications received.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is required to publish a notice of permit applications received to conduct activities regulated under the Antarctic Conservation Act of 1978. NSF has published regulations under the Antarctic Conservation Act in the Code of Federal Regulations. This is the required notice of permit applications received.
DATES:
Interested parties are invited to submit written data, comments, or views with respect to the permit applications by December 18, 2026. The applications may be inspected by interested parties at the Permit Office, address below.
ADDRESSES:
Comments should be addressed to Permit Office, Office of Polar Programs, U.S. National Science Foundation, 401 Dulany Street, Alexandria, Virginia 22314 or
ACApermits@nsf.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Andrew Titmus, ACA Permit Officer, at the above address, 703-292-4479.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The U.S. National Science Foundation, as directed by the Antarctic Conservation Act of 1978 (Pub. L. 95-541,
16 U.S.C. 2401
et seq.
), as amended by the Antarctic Science, Tourism and Conservation Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-227
), has developed regulations (
45 CFR parts 670 to 674
) for the establishment of a permit system for various activities in Antarctica related to the designation of certain animals and certain geographic areas as requiring special protection, among other purposes.
Application Details
Permit Application: 2027-006
1.
Applicant:
James Hansen, Textron Aviation, One Cessna Blvd., Wichita, KS 67215.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Waste Management (
45 CFR 671
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with waste management activities for a flight expedition from Punta Arenas, Chile to King George Island in the Antarctic Peninsula region. The applicant would conduct a single trip to King George Island using a King Air 350CER aircraft in December 2026. The aircraft would spend approximately two hours on the ground at King George Island before returning to Punta Arenas, Chile. The aircraft would not be refueled while in Antarctica and has a fuel capacity of 775 gallons. No materials are planned to be released to the environment during the expedition. All solid and liquid waste will be contained on the aircraft and returned to Punta Arenas, Chile for disposal.
Location:
Antarctic Peninsula region.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
December 5-14, 2026.
Permit Application: 2027-007
2.
Applicant:
Holly Keltner, Northern Illinois University, 1620 Wagner Rd., Batavia, IL 60510.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Take, Import into USA (
45 CFR 670
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with research into transportation of nutrients by seabirds linking marine and terrestrial ecosystems. The applicant proposes to collect up to 12 samples of two different plant species, Antarctic hair grass (
Deschampsia antarctica
) and Antarctic pearlwort (
Colobanthus quitensis
), with up to three newest-growth leaves collected per sample, leaving individual plants intact. Samples will be collected opportunistically at potential sites throughout the Antarctic Peninsula with the support of a non-governmental tour vessel. Samples will be imported into the USA for analysis.
Location:
Antarctic Peninsula region.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
November 7-December 31, 2026.
Permit Application: 2027-008
3.
Applicant:
Susan Caballero, Nova Southeastern University, 8000 North Ocean Drive, Dania Beach, FL 33004.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Take, Harmful Interference, Import into USA (
45 CFR 670
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with research into understanding the levels of genetic diversity of humpback whales (
Megaptera novaeangliae
) and leopard seals (
Hydrurga leptonyx
) in the Antarctic Peninsula. The applicant proposes to conduct photo identification of marine mammals of interest, conduct skin biopsy sampling, and analyze seawater for marine mammal environmental DNA. Particularly, the applicant proposes to collect up to 30 skin biopsy samples from humpback whales using a modified biopsy crossbow arrow. The applicant further proposes to collect up to 15 skin biopsy samples from leopard seals using small biopsy darts from a Daninject biopsy system which was developed to have minimal impact on pinnipeds. The applicant is trained and experienced in the biopsy collection methods and would be the only person conducting these activities. The applicant would conduct research with the support of a non-governmental tour vessel, and sampling would occur using small boat support opportunistically at sites throughout the Antarctic Peninsula. Samples would be imported into the USA for genetic analysis.
Location:
Antarctic Peninsula region.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
January 29, 2027-February 20, 2027.
Permit Application: 2027-009
4.
Applicant:
Jessie Creamean, Colorado State University, 1371 Campus Delivery, Fort Collins, CO 80523.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Take, Harmful Interference,
(
printed page 74220)
Import into USA (
45 CFR 670
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with research to determine how Antarctic marine and terrestrial environments vary seasonally in their production of atmospheric bioaerosols. The applicant proposes to collect up to 12 samples of mosses, 12 samples of lichens, and 12 samples of vascular plants across a range of species per year over a two-year project duration. The applicant proposes that samples may cover a range of species and the small samples would be collected and stored within 1oz whirlpak bags. Sampling would occur at pre-approved locations in the vicinity of Palmer Station and in a manner designed to minimize disturbance to surrounding vegetation. Samples would be imported into the USA for genetic analysis.
Location:
Palmer Station, Antarctica.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
November 1, 2026-May 31, 2028.
Permit Application: 2027-010
5.
Applicant:
Laura Smith, 60 South Limited, 1498 Paradise Point Rd., Oakland, MD 21550.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Waste Management (
45 CFR 671
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with waste management activities for the operation of three vessels, the “Ocean Tramp,” “Hans Hansson,” and “Meredien” in the Antarctic Peninsula region. All vessels carry 12 passengers or fewer. The applicant proposes activities that include: small boat cruising, shore landings, kayaking, polar plunge, mountaineering and skiing, coastal camping, snorkeling and freediving, filming, and transfer of passengers to commercial air services on King George Island. Wastes generated during shore-based activities would be returned to the vessel for proper disposal. The applicant also proposes the use of a small Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) for scientific, navigational, or commercial reasons. Only experienced pilots would operate UAS and appropriate mitigation measures would be implemented to reduce the risk of loss of the UAS to the environment.
Location:
Antarctic Peninsula region.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
December 1, 2026-April 15, 2031.
Permit Application: 2027-011
6.
Applicant:
Holly Fearnbach, 446 Harbor Vista Dr., Friday Harbor, WA 98250.
Activity for Which Permit is Requested:
Take, Import into USA (
45 CFR 670
). The applicant seeks an ACA permit in association with research into the health of the Antarctic trophic food web. The applicant proposes to collect photogrammetric measurements, blow samples, and fecal samples from whales in the Antarctic Peninsula region including up to 300 non-invasive samples from Killer whales (
Orcinus orca
), 200 non-invasive samples from Humpback whales (
Megaptera novaeangliae
), 100 non-invasive samples from Antarctic minke whale (
Balaenoptera bonaerensis
), and 100 non-invasive samples from Arnoux's beaked whale (
Bernardius arnuxii
). Samples would be collected using a small Unmanned Aerial System (UAS). The applicant would conduct research with the support of a non-governmental tour vessel, and sampling would occur using small boat support opportunistically at sites throughout the Antarctic Peninsula. Samples would be imported into the USA for analysis.
Location:
Antarctic Peninsula region.
Dates of Permitted Activities:
December 1, 2026-December 24, 2026.
Jean C. Allen,
Office Director, Office of Polar Programs.

The IHS is submitting the proposed information collection to OMB for review, as required by section 3507(a)(1)(D) of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. This notice is soliciting comments from members of the public and affected agencies as required by
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)

e.g.,

The Agency's 60-day notice (

) soliciting comments on the information collection was published in the
Federal Register
on August 26, 2025. No comments were received.
Title of Proposal:
Addendum to Declaration for Federal Employment (OF 306), Indian Health Service, Child Care and Indian Child Care Worker Positions.
Type of Information Collection Request:
Reinstatement, without revision, of information collection, 0917-0028, Addendum to Declaration for Federal Employment (OF 306), Indian Health Service, Child Care and Indian Child Care Worker Positions. There are no program changes or adjustments in burden hours.
OMB Control Number:
0917-0028.
Need and Use of Information Collection:
This is a request for approval of the collection of information as required by section 408 of the Indian Child Protection and Family Violence Prevention Act, Public Law (Pub. L.) 101-630, 104 Stat. 4544, 4551, codified as amended at 25 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 3207; the Crime Control Act of 1990, Pub. L. 101-647, title II, subtitle E, section 231, 104 Stat. 4789, 4808, codified as amended at
34 U.S.C. 20351
(formerly codified at
42 U.S.C. 13041
, which was transferred to
34 U.S.C. 20351
); and
42 CFR part 136, subpart K
.
The IHS is required to compile a list of all authorized positions within the IHS where the duties and responsibilities involve regular contact with, or control over, Indian children; and to conduct an investigation of the character of each individual who is employed, or is being considered for employment, in a position having regular contact with, or control over, Indian children.
25 U.S.C. 3207(a)(1)
and
(2)
. Section 3207(a)(3) of Title 25 requires regulations prescribing the minimum standards of character for individuals appointed to positions involving regular contact with, or control over, Indian children, and section 3207(b) provides that such standards shall ensure that no such individuals have been found guilty of, or entered a plea of nolo contendere or guilty to, any felonious offense, or any two or more misdemeanor offenses, under Federal, State, or Tribal law involving crimes of violence; sexual assault, molestation, exploitation, contact or prostitution; crimes against persons; or offenses committed against children.
In addition,
34 U.S.C. 20351
requires each agency of the Federal Government, and every facility operated by the Federal Government (or operated under contract with the Federal Government), that hires (or contracts for hire) individuals involved with the provision of child care services to children under the age of 18 to assure that all existing and newly hired employees undergo a criminal history background check. The background investigation is to be initiated through the personnel program of the applicable Federal agency.

Subject

Title

: The Commission will consider a Report and Order that would authorize non-federal operation of radio frequency jamming solutions in the limited context of correctional facilities, in compliance with applicable congressional statutes. Wireless Telecommunications
Title:

Title:

Wireline Competition
Title:

AGENCY:
Indian Health Service, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces the Catastrophic Health Emergency Fund (CHEF) threshold established at $20,258 for Fiscal Year 2027 CHEF requests.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Indian Health Service (IHS) administers the CHEF pursuant to section 202 of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act (IHCIA). The purpose of the CHEF is to meet the extraordinary medical costs associated with the treatment of victims of disasters or catastrophic illnesses who are within the responsibility of the Service. The CHEF was established by section 202 of the IHCIA, Public Law 94-437 (25 U.S.C. § 1621a). The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act,
Public Law 111-148
, as amended by the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010,
Public Law 111-152
(collectively, the Affordable Care Act or “the ACA”), reauthorized the IHCIA and amended the CHEF, directing the Secretary to promulgate regulations governing the administration of the CHEF. The final CHEF regulation (2024-19421 (
89 FR 70527
)) was published on August 30, 2024, in the
Federal Register
, establishing the threshold cost of $19,000 for Fiscal Year (FY) 2024. See 42 CFR § 136.503(a). The threshold amount in subsequent years is calculated from the threshold amount of the previous year, and increased by the percentage increase in the medical care expenditure category of the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers (United States city average) for the 12-month period ending with December of the previous year. See
42 CFR 136.503(b)
. The Consumer Price Index is released monthly. For FY 2027, “December of the previous year” is December 2025, because December 2026 is part of FY 2027. The “12-month period ending with December of the previous year” is therefore December 2024 to December 2025. The medical care expenditure category for this 12-month period was 3.2%, thereby increasing the threshold from $19,630 for FY 2026 to $20,258 for FY 2027 CHEF requests. See
https://www.federalregister.gov/​documents/​2026/​03/​12/​2026-04827/​catastrophic-health-emergency-fund-chef-fiscal-year-2026-threshold
for the FY 2026 CHEF Threshold Notice.

AGENCY:
Employee Benefits Security Administration, U.S. Department of Labor.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed class prohibited transaction exemption.
SUMMARY:
This document gives notice of a proposed class prohibited transaction exemption (PTE). This proposed QROAD class PTE (Proposed QROAD Class Exemption) would allow certain qualified professional asset managers (QPAMs) to continue relying on PTE 84-14, known as the QPAM Class Exemption, even after an event that would otherwise make them ineligible under Section I(g) of that exemption. To use this alternative path, the QPAM must comply with the protective conditions in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted. This proposal does not change any fiduciary duties under ERISA section 404 or expand the relief available under the QPAM Class Exemption.
DATES:
Exemption date:
If granted, this proposed exemption will be in effect 60 days after the date of publication of the final exemption in the
Federal Register
.
Comments due:
Written comments and requests for a public hearing on the proposed exemption must be received by the Department by January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
All written comments and requests for a hearing concerning the proposed PTE should be sent electronically to the Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA), Office of Exemption Determinations (OED) through the Federal eRulemaking Portal and identified by Application No. D-12126 and/or Z-RIN 1210-ZA37:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
at Docket ID number: EBSA-2026-0397. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
See
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
below for additional information regarding comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brian Mica, telephone (202) 693-8540 or email at
ClassExemptions@dol.gov
,
Office of Exemption Determinations, Employee Benefits Security Administration, U.S. Department of Labor (this is not a toll-free number).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comment Instructions
Comments should state the nature of the person's interest in the proposed exemption and how the person would be materially affected by the exemption, if granted. Any person who may be materially affected by an exemption can request a hearing on the exemption if their request includes: (1) the name, address, telephone number, and email address of the person making the request; (2) the nature of the person's interest in the exemption and the manner in which the person would be materially affected by the exemption; and (3) a statement of the issues to be addressed and a general description of the evidence to be presented at the hearing. The U.S. Department of Labor (Department) will grant a hearing request made in accordance with the requirements above when it finds that a hearing is necessary to fully explore material factual issues identified by the requestor and will publish a hearing notice in the
Federal Register
. The Department may decline to hold a hearing if it finds that: (1) the hearing request does not meet the requirements stated above; (2) the only issues identified for exploration at the hearing are matters of law; or (3) the factual issues identified in the request can be fully explored through the submission of evidence in written (including electronic) form.
[
1
]
Warning:
The Department will include all comments received in the public record without change and make them available online at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
The Department notes that it will include any personal information provided by the commenter in the public record and online, unless the commenter claims that any of the information included is confidential, or the disclosure of such information is restricted by statute. If you submit a comment, EBSA recommends that you include your name and other contact information in the body of your comment, but DO NOT submit information that you consider to be confidential or otherwise protected (such as a Social Security number or an unlisted phone number), or confidential business information that you do not want publicly disclosed. If EBSA cannot read your comment due to technical difficulties and cannot contact you for clarification, EBSA might not be able to consider your comment. Additionally, the
https://www.regulations.gov
website is an “anonymous access” system, which means EBSA will not know your identity or contact information unless you provide them in the body of your comment. EBSA encourages commenters to include supporting facts, research, and evidence in their comments. When doing so, commenters are encouraged to provide citations to the materials referenced, including active hyperlinks. Likewise, commenters who reference materials that have not been published are encouraged to upload relevant data collection instruments, data sets, and detailed findings as a part of their comment. Providing such citations and documentation will assist EBSA in analyzing the comments. EBSA reemphasizes that materials provided will be part of the public record.
Background on Administrative Exemptions Under ERISA
A fiduciary's duties under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (ERISA), are “the highest known to the law.”
[
2
]
To safeguard Plans
[
3
]
and their participants and beneficiaries from the potential for abuse that arises when Plans engage in transactions with closely connected parties, Congress enacted ERISA Section 406, which forbids ERISA fiduciaries from causing their Plans to engage in transactions with “parties in interest” to the Plans. In general terms, “parties in interest” are people or entities closely connected to a Plan, including, among others, ERISA fiduciaries and certain of their direct and indirect owners and subsidiaries.
[
4
]
Both ERISA and the Code provide statutory exemptions from these prohibited transactions, and the Department has the authority to grant administrative exemptions—either individually or by class—under ERISA Section 408(a) and Code Section 4975(c)(2). The Secretary of Labor may not grant an exemption unless he finds that such an exemption is: (1) administratively feasible, (2) in the interest of the plan and of its participants and beneficiaries, and (3)
(
printed page 74435)
protective of the rights of participants and beneficiaries of such plan.
[
5
]
Virtually all administrative exemptions granted by the Department have conditions. These conditions, which often utilize Independent Fiduciaries, as defined in Section I(h), independent auditors and/or compliance officers: (1) allow the Department to make its required findings under ERISA Section 408(a) with respect to transactions that violate ERISA Section 406; and (2) reflect the Department's view that the high standard to which ERISA fiduciaries are held is often, by itself, not sufficiently protective of affected Plans in the context of transactions prohibited by ERISA Section 406.
Background of the QPAM Class Exemption
DOL's QPAM Class Exemption
[
6
]
is an important, widely-used
[
7
]
class exemption that permits an Investment Fund, as defined in Section VI(b) of the QPAM Class Exemption, managed by a Qualified Professional Asset Manager (QPAM)
[
8
]
to engage in a broad range of transactions with parties in interest with respect to Plans that invest in the Investment Fund, subject to protective conditions. The QPAM Class Exemption also allows QPAMs to streamline compliance with the prohibited transaction provisions of Title I of ERISA and the Code. A QPAM relying on the QPAM Class Exemption does not need to keep and routinely check a list of parties in interest before engaging in a transaction to avoid inadvertently entering into a prohibited transaction with potentially hundreds, if not thousands, of parties in interest. The QPAM also does not have to seek an individual exemption or, alternatively, forgo investment opportunities that would be in the interest of Covered Plans, as defined in Section I(d), invested in the Investment Fund merely because a party in interest is involved.
In proposing the QPAM Class Exemption, the Department noted, “A QPAM, and those who may be in a position to influence its policies, are expected to maintain a high standard of integrity. Accordingly, the proposed class exemption does not cover transactions if the QPAM or various `affiliates' have been convicted of various crimes (outlined in section I(g) of the proposal), that involve abuse or misuse of a position of trust, or felonies generally described in ERISA section 411.”
[
9
]
As granted, Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption provides generally that a QPAM is ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption for a period of 10 years if the QPAM, its various Affiliates,
[
10
]
or five percent or more owners of the QPAM, engage in certain types of serious misconduct that is prohibited by the QPAM Class Exemption.
[
11
]
If an asset manager becomes ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption, its Covered Plans may miss out on investment opportunities or be required to find a new asset manager.
The preamble to the QPAM Class Exemption, as it was proposed, states that a QPAM must “maintain a high standard of integrity.” This is an important premise of the QPAM Class Exemption. Although under ERISA, the duties of fiduciaries are already high, for QPAMs, the added integrity requirement arises because: (1) the scope of Section I of the QPAM Class Exemption is expansive, permitting an Investment Fund managed by a QPAM to engage in all prohibited transactions described in ERISA Section 406(a) with virtually all parties in interest to Plans that invest in the Investment Fund (except the QPAM), with limited relief also from ERISA Section 406(b);
[
12
]
and (2) the QPAM Class Exemption is largely self-executing and requires no reporting to, or filing with, the Department, other than a one-time notification to the Department that the asset manager is relying on the QPAM Exemption. Therefore, the concept of QPAM “integrity,” as reinforced by Section I(g), is a critical underpinning for the exemptive relief provided in DOL's QPAM Class Exemption.
In addition, just as QPAMs are subject to a standard of integrity beyond the duties required of ERISA fiduciaries, QPAMs also must maintain their eligibility for the QPAM Class Exemption under a more demanding standard than that applied to fiduciaries under ERISA generally. As a result, while a person can be precluded from serving as an ERISA fiduciary due to committing violations specified in ERISA Section 411, a QPAM is also subject to the more stringent ineligibility provision in Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. However, unlike ERISA Section 411, which provides a mechanism to bar an entity that has been convicted of certain crimes from acting as an ERISA fiduciary, Section I(g) does not bar an entity from acting as an ERISA fiduciary. Section I(g) instead proactively ensures that the broad permission afforded under the QPAM Class Exemption for asset managers to engage in certain prohibited transactions does not extend to entities (or are related to entities) that have engaged (or that are related to entities that have engaged) in certain disqualifying events.
In 2024, DOL amended the QPAM Class Exemption. This amendment: (1) clarified the requirement that a QPAM have authority over investment decisions; (2) increased the required asset management and equity thresholds for all QPAMs; (3) added a new recordkeeping requirement, and (4) modified the integrity requirement in Section I(g). The 2024 amendment expanded the disqualification triggers in Section I(g) in three ways: (1) providing that certain foreign convictions are disqualifying; (2) adding certain deferred-prosecution agreements (DPAs) and non-prosecution agreements (NPAs) between QPAMs or their affiliates and Federal or State agencies; and (3) adding certain civil judgments and settlements with Federal and State agencies.
As defined in Section I(
l
) of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, the term Prohibited Misconduct has the same meaning as that same term is defined in Section VI(s) of the amended QPAM Class Exemption. It generally refers to when a QPAM, any Affiliate thereof, or any owner, direct or indirect, of a five (5) percent or more interest in the QPAM enters into a domestic NPA or DPA or is found in a court's final judgment or court approved settlement to have participated in conduct that intentionally violated the QPAM Class Exemption's conditions or provided
(
printed page 74436)
misleading information in connection with the QPAM Class Exemption's conditions.
As defined in Section I(e), the term Criminal Conviction has the same meaning as the term is defined in Section VI(r) of the QPAM Class Exemption, except that, for purposes of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, a “Criminal Conviction” includes all Criminal Convictions that arise from the same incident in that they are the same in nature, and based on the same underlying facts, circumstances and conduct. A “Criminal Conviction” includes “U.S. Convictions” and “Foreign Convictions,” as those terms are described below and generally refers to when a QPAM, any Affiliate thereof, or any owner, direct or indirect, of a five (5) percent or more interest in the QPAM is convicted in a U.S. Federal or State court for certain listed offenses described in ERISA section 411; or is convicted by a foreign court of competent jurisdiction of a crime that is substantially equivalent to the listed U.S. offenses.
Further, in the Department's view, the mere fact that an asset manager has not been barred from acting as a fiduciary under ERISA Section 411 does not equate to a demonstration that the asset manager has exhibited sufficient integrity to qualify for a self-executing class exemption that permits the asset manager to engage in a wide range of transactions that otherwise are prohibited by ERISA Section 406(a). For example, an ERISA fiduciary that admits to fraud against its Plan clients in a non-prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice would not be barred under ERISA Section 411 solely because of the non-prosecution agreement. Similarly, an ERISA fiduciary that engages in misconduct for which its corporate parent is criminally convicted would not be barred under ERISA Section 411 solely because of the Criminal Conviction of the corporate parent. Nonetheless, both instances could constitute an ineligibility event under the QPAM Class Exemption, as they would raise serious concerns regarding whether the asset manager can be expected to act with integrity if allowed to engage in a wide range of transactions otherwise prohibited under ERISA Section 406(a) essentially unsupervised by the Department. The Department was able to make its required findings under ERISA Section 408(a) when granting such relief to QPAMs under the QPAM Class Exemption, in part, by holding QPAMs to a higher standard of integrity.
Overview of This Proposed QPAM Re-Eligibility Options After Disqualification (QROAD) Class Exemption
Over the years, the Department has reviewed more than 50 requests for individual exemptions submitted on behalf of QPAMs facing ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. The requestors sought individual PTEs that would allow the QPAMs to continue to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption, notwithstanding violations of Section I(g) that would otherwise make the QPAMs ineligible to rely on the relief in the QPAM Class Exemption. Based on this experience that the Department has had in considering and granting such individual exemptions, the Department now is proposing the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. Discussed in the preamble below are the reasons why the Department is proposing this exemption.
In requests for individual exemptions from ineligibility under the QPAM Class Exemption, the factual records supporting them include a detailed exemption application, which typically contains, among other things, court-approved pleadings, comments from interested parties, reports, and audits associated with the application. The Department reviews the nature of the underlying conduct and works with applicants and their attorneys to determine the nature of the criminal conduct or other Prohibited Misconduct. The Department has recently granted individual PTEs that do not provide relief for the full ten years of ineligibility under the QPAM Class Exemption. The QPAM then relies on an individual PTE for one, three, or five years, and must hire an independent auditor to conduct an audit of its compliance with the individual PTE. The Department receives a copy of that audit and uses it to determine whether to grant another exemption to cover more of the initial ten-year period. A few QPAMs have faced multiple convictions over a ten-year period, and the Department has granted new individual PTEs to provide relief for the additional ineligibility events, as they arose, and to impose new conditions.
The experience the Department gained from processing this type of exemption request, and from reviewing the subsequent audits performed in connection therewith, has led the Department to tentatively conclude that it would be appropriate to grant a class exemption that conditionally permits, in certain instances, an asset manager facing ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption to continue to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption. As discussed below, this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption also reflects the view that, in certain other instances, exemptive relief for asset managers facing ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption is more appropriately considered under the Department's individual exemption process.
The Department believes that this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption will remove a great deal of the uncertainty affecting Covered Plan
[
13
]
fiduciaries whose prudently selected asset manager of choice is subject to potential ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. In this regard, when the Department receives an individual exemption application involving a potential ineligibility event, the Department must consider the entire record attributable to the application prior to granting the requested exemption, including comments received following publication of a proposed exemption. The Department granted 30 Section I(g) individual exemptions during the period 2016 through 2025. During the same period, the Department denied 4 additional applications for relief from the ineligibility provision in Section I(g) and another 5 applications were withdrawn by the applicants. Withdrawals in these circumstances typically occur in anticipation of an impending denial of an application during review. Accordingly, until the application is reviewed, the proposed individual exemption is published for comment, the comments are reviewed and the proposed exemption is finalized, the Department cannot guarantee that an exemption request ultimately will be granted. Therefore, Covered Plan fiduciaries will not know with certainty whether their asset manager will continue to have relief until the individual exemption is granted. Even where the record indicates a likelihood that the Department will grant an individual exemption the Department cannot typically guarantee that the exemption will be granted prior to a lapse in the relief afforded by the QPAM Class Exemption. Under the QPAM Class Exemption, the timing of ineligibility is
(

generally set by a court. Section I(h) provides that a QPAM becomes ineligible upon the judgment of a court or the date of an NPA or DPA. Section I(i) provides a One-Year Transition Period,

which allows a QPAM continued relief for up to one year, subject to additional conditions. However, an exemption is not granted until it is published in the
Federal Register
, and the timing for publication depends on when the application is submitted, the completeness of that application, the public comments the Department receives, and various other factors. This creates additional uncertainty for QPAMs facing even a short-term lapse of relief. It is the Department's understanding that these uncertainties are disruptive to Covered Plans. This Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would remove many of these uncertainties by providing a clear, reliable path to exemptive relief in applicable cases.
Further, the Department believes that, under the circumstances described in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, a procedurally streamlined approach designed to reduce costs and administrative friction to allow QPAMs to continue relying on the QPAM Class Exemption is appropriate. Based on the Department's consideration of its experience with individual exemption applications from QPAMs otherwise facing ineligibility under the QPAM Class Exemption, as described below, the conditions of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption are more carefully tailored to the ineligibility events and arrangements that give rise to QPAM ineligibility under the QPAM Class Exemption than the conditions found in the Department's individual exemptions, which, for the most part, have applied a more “one size fits all” approach to these sorts of exemption requests. If this largely self-executing Proposed QROAD Class Exemption is granted, eligible QPAMs will be saved the time and expense of submitting a detailed exemption application, thus alleviating the uncertainty of the individual exemption process.
As noted above, Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption provides generally that a QPAM is ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption for a period of 10 years if the QPAM, its Affiliates, or five percent or more owners of the QPAM, engage in serious misconduct that is prohibited by the QPAM Class Exemption. As explained further below, Section VI(d) of the QPAM Class Exemption defines the term “Affiliates” for purposes of Section I(g) to include: entities that Control or are Controlled
[
15
]
by the QPAM; and certain entities that do not Control or are not Controlled by the QPAM. This distinction is relevant to this proposal because the existence of Control or lack thereof between a QPAM and an entity that is the subject of a Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct (a Misconduct Entity) will determine what Section of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption a QPAM may rely on for conditional relief.
Under the terms of this proposal, an arrangement involving a QPAM that Controls or is Controlled by a Misconduct Entity will generally be subject to more conditions than an arrangement involving a QPAM that neither Controls nor is Controlled by a Misconduct Entity. The Department believes that imposing additional conditions when there is direct control is appropriate and also aligns with the expressly stated essential premise of the QPAM Class Exemption noted above, that “a QPAM, and those who may be in a position to influence its policies, are expected to maintain a high standard of integrity.” This also reflects the Department's view that the mandate in ERISA Section 408(a) with respect to exemptions that provide expansive self-executing relief from ERISA's prohibited transaction provisions, for QPAMs that Control or are Controlled by an entity that has engaged in serious misconduct, requires greater oversight (audits and compliance officers, for example) than the same relief for QPAMs that do not Control or are not Controlled by such Misconduct Entity.
Moreover, since the relief in both the QPAM Class Exemption and the relief proposed herein is mostly self-executing, the Department believes that, with respect to arrangements involving QPAMs that Control or are Controlled by a Misconduct Entity, the requirements of Section 408(a) warrant not only conditions that are similar to the conditions set forth in the Department's recent individual exemptions, but also warrant Independent Fiduciary oversight, as discussed below. This oversight is important, given that the Department will not be reviewing an exemption application.
Department's Note:
As noted above, the Department developed the definitions and conditions in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption based on its experience processing numerous individual exemption applications involving QPAMs facing ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. The Department is aware that comments on the associated individual exemptions have stated that the conditions contained in those exemptions are burdensome, unnecessary, and/or expensive. This proposal addresses many of those concerns with respect to the relief described herein for QPAMs that do not Control or are not Controlled by a Misconduct Entity, because the conditions in this proposal applicable to those circumstances do not include many of the conditions required by the Department's recent individual exemptions.
However, as noted above, this proposal does include many of the conditions set forth in the Department's recent QPAM Section I(g) individual exemptions with respect to QPAMs that Control or are Controlled by a Misconduct Entity. The Department continues to believe that the conditions described below, such as requiring a compliance officer and an auditor to confirm compliance with this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption and the QPAM Class Exemption, are necessary for the Department to make its required findings under ERISA Section 408(a), including that the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption is sufficiently protective of Plans, given that this proposal would provide relief in circumstances where, for example, a Misconduct Entity that Controls a QPAM has engaged in fraudulent activity against its own clients.
Commenters to the Department's recent QPAM Section I(g) individual exemptions have suggested that such exemptions are not “administratively feasible” for the QPAMs and Covered Plans. However, the conditions proposed herein were developed with due consideration of whether this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would be administratively feasible for the Department, consistent with the meaning of ERISA Section 408(a).
[
16
]
Nearly all the exemption conditions described herein are largely self-executing and do not pose an unreasonable burden to the Department.
Some commenters to the Department's recent QPAM Section I(g) individual exemptions have further
(
printed page 74438)
suggested that the conditions contained therein provide no benefit to affected Covered Plans.
[
17
]
However, in the Department's view, conditions requiring maintenance and adherence to a QPAM's policies, specialized QPAM training, checks on QPAM compliance, and among other things, the provision of information to Covered Plans so that ERISA fiduciaries can make prudent decisions regarding their retention of their asset manager of choice, are protective of the rights of the participants and beneficiaries of the Covered Plans. The conditions described in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption help to further empower Covered Plan fiduciaries to make prudent fiduciary decisions, by requiring, in certain situations, their QPAM to indemnify the Covered Plans against any actual losses resulting directly from, among other things, a violation of the conditions of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. The indemnification and hold harmless conditions permit Covered Plan fiduciaries to exercise prudence when deciding to retain a new asset manager, without fear of incurring substantial charges, lock-ups, or other disincentives that could otherwise impair their ability to exercise prudence.
However, the indemnification provisions in this proposal are narrower and more targeted than the indemnification provisions in the Department's recent QPAM Section I(g) individual exemptions. This Proposed QROAD Class Exemption limits the QPAM's indemnification obligations to plan losses resulting directly from: the QPAM's violation of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption; loss of QPAM relief due to failure to satisfy Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption; or prohibited transactions or ERISA fiduciary breaches connected to the misconduct that gave rise to the need for reliance on this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. Recent individual exemptions have had a larger indemnification scope than this, and include plan losses resulting from the QPAM's violation of its ERISA fiduciary duties and the prohibited transaction provisions of ERISA and the Code, whether or not such violations are tied to a violation of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, failure to satisfy Section I(g), or prohibited transactions or ERISA fiduciary breaches connected to the misconduct that gave rise to the need for reliance on this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.
This proposal would require confirmation from an Independent Fiduciary that certain requirements of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption have been met. The Department believes that the broad self-executing relief afforded by this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption warrants independent oversight of certain of its terms, not merely representations by a QPAM. Equally, the Department believes that Independent Fiduciary oversight reduces the likelihood that Covered Plans would incur substantial harm in situations where the conditions of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption subsequently were determined not to have been met, following their QPAM's reliance on the relief in this exemption. Further, the Department considers the Independent Fiduciary requirement more efficient than the process it would replace (application analysis by the Department) because the Independent Fiduciary requirement described herein would involve coordination between the Independent Fiduciary and a senior QPAM officer who is knowledgeable of the misconduct that necessitated reliance on this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted.
The Department is aware that stakeholders view Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption as too broad. The Department believes this proposal addresses many of these concerns and does so in a streamlined fashion. As discussed below, the alternative route to relief that the Department proposes here is closely tied to the Department's experience with individual exemption applications, and it will more quickly and effectively address stakeholder concerns than would amending the QPAM Class Exemption itself. The Department invites comments on whether the relief afforded by the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, offers sufficiently streamlined paths to relief from stakeholder concerns about the breadth of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption, while doing so in a manner still sufficiently protective of Plans. This Proposed QROAD Class Exemption does not require an amendment to the QPAM Class Exemption generally, nor Section I(g) in particular, because it does not change the terms of ineligibility; rather, for QPAMs otherwise facing ineligibility under the existing QPAM Class Exemption, the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption offers egress from such ineligibility along two clearly navigable paths. The two alternative paths to relief, each with protections and requirements that were developed in careful consideration of whether control existed between a Reliance QPAM and a Misconduct Entity, are designed to deliver the highest level of protections to Plans. Moreover, under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, any QPAM remains free to submit an individual exemption application.
Further, the records attributable to, and the Department's experience with, several individual PTE requests appear to support a wide scope to Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption, by clearly demonstrating that misconduct even by a “far flung” affiliate of a QPAM with no apparent Control over the QPAM, may nonetheless involve numerous personnel spread across the QPAM's organizational structure.
Given the gravity, prolonged duration, and complex nature of misconduct associated with many Criminal Convictions, the Department believes the protections described in this proposal are warranted. However, nothing in this proposal precludes a QPAM from submitting an exemption request with fewer conditions than those described herein. Such a request should clearly demonstrate why an exemption with fewer conditions would be in the interest of, and protective of, Covered Plans, and administratively feasible, as required under ERISA Section 408(a).
The Department understands that interested parties may have unique insight as to how the Department could revise the terms of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption to strengthen its protections for Covered Plans and/or lessen unnecessary burdens on Covered Plans, their fiduciaries, and/or their asset managers of choice. The Department welcomes these comments and also welcomes comments from QPAMs that currently rely on individual exemptions due to ineligibility under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. In this regard, this proposal requires that QPAMs that have received current individual exemptions, in order to continue relying on the QPAM Class Exemption, must continue to comply with those individual exemptions until the date they are in compliance with all applicable conditions of this exemption. The Department welcomes comments regarding QPAMs' ability to coordinate their individual exemption compliance with the conditions outlined in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, including any difficulties they may anticipate. Additionally, the Department welcomes comments regarding the regulatory alternatives it considered, as discussed in section 10 of the Regulatory Impact Analysis below.

Layout and Structure of This Proposed QROAD Class Exemption
In general terms, QPAMs that do not Control and are not Controlled by a Misconduct Entity (that itself is not a QPAM) may rely on the relief in Section II of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if the conditions in Section II are met. QPAMs that Control or are Controlled by a Misconduct Entity may generally rely on the relief in Section III of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if the conditions in Section III are met. However, in certain instances, if the applicable conditions are met, QPAMs that do not Control and are not Controlled by a Misconduct Entity, and that are not eligible for the relief in Section II of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, may nonetheless be eligible for the relief in Section III.
The Proposed QROAD Class Exemption has four other sections: a definitions section (Section I); a phase-out section (Section IV); a recordkeeping section (Section V); and a date section (Section VI). This preamble summarizes those sections; however, it does not fully describe all the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption's definitions and conditions. See the specific sections below to view all of the proposal's governing terms and conditions.
Section I: Definitions
QPAM
For purposes of this proposal, the term “QPAM” has the same meaning as in the QPAM Class Exemption, and means an Independent Fiduciary that is a bank, savings and loan association, insurance company, or investment adviser registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (Advisers Act) that meets certain equity, net worth, and assets under management requirements, and acknowledges in a written management agreement its ERISA fiduciary status with respect to each Plan that retains it as a QPAM. Upon the occurrence of a triggering event, Section I(g) imposes ineligibility on a QPAM based on the misconduct by (1) the QPAM itself, (2) any Affiliate, and (3) any owner, direct or indirect, of a five (5) percent or more interest in the QPAM.
Misconduct Entity
The term “Misconduct Entity” means an entity that is the subject of a Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct, each as defined in the QPAM Class Exemption. Except as expressly allowed, relief in this exemption does not extend to any QPAM that is the subject of a Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct.
Affiliated QPAMs
Section I(b) of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption provides that a QPAM is an “Affiliated QPAM” if it is an Affiliate of the Misconduct Entity. The definition of “Affiliate” is the same as the definition of “Affiliate” in Section VI(d) of the QPAM Class Exemption. Thus, for purposes of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, a QPAM is defined as an “Affiliated QPAM” with respect to a Misconduct Entity, if the Misconduct Entity:
(1) directly or indirectly through one or more intermediaries, Controls, is Controlled by, or is Under Common Control with the QPAM;
(2) is any director of, Relative of, or partner in, the QPAM;
[
18
]
(3) is a corporation, partnership, trust or unincorporated enterprise of which the QPAM is an officer, director, or a five percent or more partner or owner; or
(4) is any employee or officer of the QPAM who:
a. is a highly compensated employee (as defined in Code Section 4975(e)(2)(H) or officer (earning ten (10) percent or more of the yearly wages of such person); or
b. has direct or indirect authority, responsibility, or control regarding the custody, asset management or disposition of Plan assets.
The term “Affiliated QPAM” has been used regularly in individual exemptions for QPAMs ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption. Notably, the definition of Affiliated QPAM is not limited to entities that Control or are Controlled by a Misconduct Entity. Whereas some Affiliated QPAMs may Control or be Controlled by the Misconduct Entity and may be eligible for the relief in Section III, others will not have that specific Control relationship and may be eligible for the relief in Section II.
Related QPAM
The term “Related QPAM” has been used regularly in individual exemptions for QPAMs ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption. The term refers to QPAMs with respect to which a Misconduct Entity directly or indirectly owns a five percent or more interest in the QPAM but does not “Control” the QPAM.
[
19
]
These QPAMs are not Affiliated QPAMs because they do not meet any part of the definition of Affiliate.
As further described below, Related QPAMs are generally subject to fewer conditions than Affiliated QPAMs because of the Misconduct Entity's more attenuated relationship to a Related QPAM and limited ability to influence a Related QPAM's policies and management of plan assets. The Department understands that a Misconduct Entity's investments in Related QPAMs are often passive investments, and Related QPAMs maintain their own information and technology infrastructure and are operationally separate and distinct from the Misconduct Entity. In fact, various applicants for individual exemptions have represented that a Misconduct Entity's relationship to a Related QPAM may be so minimal that the Misconduct Entity does not know if the Related QPAM is relying on the QPAM Class Exemption. These factors provide comfort to the Department that different, less robust, conditions are needed to protect Covered Plans of Related QPAMs from a Misconduct Entity. Nonetheless, because a Misconduct Entity's Criminal Conviction
[
20
]
or Prohibited Misconduct
[
21
]
causes a
(
printed page 74440)
Related QPAM to become ineligible under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption, this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would provide relief to those Related QPAMs, subject to the special rule for Related QPAMs described below.
Reliance QPAM
A single Criminal Conviction or instance of Prohibited Misconduct could cause several QPAMs (Affiliated QPAMs and/or Related QPAMs) to be ineligible, and each of those QPAMs may seek to rely on the relief in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. Historically, in requests for individual exemptions for relief from Section I(g), the applicants have requested an exemption on behalf of all Affiliated QPAMs and Related QPAMs located within an affected corporate family. However, Proposed QROAD Class Exemption is structured such that a QPAM that relies on the relief in this exemption (a Reliance QPAM) is generally responsible only for its own compliance with the terms of the exemption. In other words, if a Related QPAM and an Affiliated QPAM each reside within the same corporate organizational structure as a Misconduct Entity, and the Related QPAM fully complies with the terms of this exemption but the Affiliated QPAM does not, the Related QPAM will remain eligible for the relief provided by this exemption notwithstanding the non-compliance of the Affiliated QPAM.
However, there is one condition in the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption that requires compliance by all QPAMs under the same corporate organizational structure. Under Section II(b)(3) of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if any QPAM in the corporate organizational structure exercised authority over the assets of any plan in a manner that it knew, or should have known, would further the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct, then no Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM can rely on Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. Each QPAM connected to that Misconduct Entity would need an individual exemption to continue operating as a QPAM. This requirement protects Plans and IRAs by ensuring that no QPAM assets within the same organizational structure are used in conduct underlying a Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct.
Reliance Date
A QPAM that becomes ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption does not become a Reliance QPAM under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption until the “Reliance Date.” The Proposed QROAD Class Exemption defines Reliance Date as the date on which a QPAM first relies on this exemption with respect to a Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct.
The Reliance Date may not be earlier than the associated Ineligibility Date
[
22
]
under the QPAM Class Exemption. This provides Affiliated and Related QPAMs with flexibility to determine when they will begin complying with the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. An Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM, for instance, could first rely on the One-Year Transition Period in Section I(i) of the QPAM Class Exemption for 10 months and then rely on the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption for the remaining 9 years and 2 months of its ineligibility period.
The conditions in the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption must be complied with as of the QPAM's Reliance Date, not its Ineligibility Date. Thus, an Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM that does not immediately come into compliance with this exemption as of its Ineligibility Date will not inadvertently miss its opportunity to rely on this exemption.
Independent Fiduciary
This Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would require the oversight of a prudently selected Independent Fiduciary. The term “Independent Fiduciary” has the same meaning as in the Department's Procedures Governing the Filing and Processing of Prohibited Transaction Exemption Applications,
[
23
]
and generally means an individual or entity that has appropriate training, experience, and facilities to act on behalf of the Plan regarding the exemption transaction in accordance with the fiduciary duties and responsibilities prescribed by ERISA, and that is independent of and unrelated to any party in interest engaging in the exemption transaction.
Criminal Conviction
Under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, multiple convictions are treated as one single “Criminal Conviction” if the convictions arise from the same incident in that they are based on the same underlying facts, circumstances, and conduct, and were perpetrated by the same person (or group of people) during the same time frame or where the same defective control function enabled the same type of misconduct to occur during the same general time frame. For example, if a Misconduct Entity is convicted in U.S. district court on two charges that are part of the same scheme, such as embezzlement and fraudulent concealment directly related to said embezzlement, then these would be treated as one single “Criminal Conviction” if the convictions are based on the same underlying facts, circumstances, and conduct, and were perpetrated by the same person (or group of people) during the same time frame or where the same defective control function enabled the same type of misconduct to occur during the same general time frame. Likewise, if a Misconduct Entity is convicted in U.S. district court and separately in a State court, and both charges stem from the same incident in that they are based on the same underlying conduct, those two convictions would be treated as one for purposes of this exemption. However, if the charges underlying the State conviction were brought because the Misconduct Entity continued engaging in the illegal conduct after the Federal conviction, the Federal and State convictions would be considered two separate convictions.
Two convictions also would not be treated as one when the types of misconduct are distinct and/or there is no direct connection between the misconduct underlying the two separate convictions. For example, if a Misconduct Entity is convicted for fraud in U.S. district court and for tampering with a witness with respect to the fraud proceedings, the two convictions will be treated as distinct. In that example, while some of the facts associated with the two convictions might be the same, the charged conduct underlying each conviction is different. For purposes of this proposal, a Criminal Conviction includes U.S. Convictions and Foreign Convictions, as those terms are described below.
The Department invites comments on whether this approach towards counting Criminal Convictions is appropriately calibrated and whether the proposed
(
printed page 74441)
approach should be modified in the final exemption.
Section II: Exemptive Relief Where No Control Relationship Exists Between the Reliance QPAM and the Misconduct Entity
Section II relief extends to an Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM that is ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption as a result of: (1) a single Criminal Conviction described in Section VI(r)(1) of the QPAM Class Exemption
[
24
]
(a U.S. Conviction); and/or (2) one or more Criminal Convictions described in Section VI(r)(2) of the QPAM Class Exemption
[
25
]
(Foreign Convictions); and/or (3) one or more instances of Prohibited Misconduct. The Misconduct Entity must neither Control nor be Controlled by the Reliance QPAM and must not itself be a QPAM. Importantly, relief in this Section (and Section III below) is not available if the conduct that is the subject of a Criminal Conviction or the Prohibited Misconduct involved assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975.
The Department acknowledges that the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption takes a different approach to Foreign Convictions than the Department has historically taken in granting individual exemptions from the QPAM Class Exemption's ineligibility provision. The Department continues to believe that Foreign Convictions for substantially equivalent crimes raise serious integrity concerns. However, the Department believes this different treatment is warranted given that foreign criminal justice systems may differ from the U.S. system with respect to procedural rules, evidentiary standards, prosecutorial practices, judicial independence, appellate review, and other due process safeguards. Although Foreign Convictions remain relevant to QPAM integrity and continue to trigger ineligibility under Section I(g), the Department preliminarily believes these cross-jurisdictional differences support a more tailored approach for class-wide relief, including permitting relief for one or more Foreign Convictions under Sections II and III subject to the exemption's protective conditions. The Department invites comments on whether this treatment of Foreign Convictions is appropriately calibrated, whether additional safeguards are needed, and whether the proposed distinction between Foreign Convictions and U.S. Convictions should be modified in the final exemption.
Similarly, the Department acknowledges that this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption takes a different approach to NPAs and DPAs than the Department has historically taken in connection with the QPAM Class Exemption's ineligibility provision. The Department continues to believe that conduct underlying NPAs and DPAs can raise serious integrity concerns relevant to whether a QPAM should be able to rely on the broad, self-executing relief provided by the QPAM Class Exemption. However, the Department believes this different treatment is warranted given that, unlike Criminal Conviction, an NPA or DPA may not involve an adjudication of guilt and may include no admission of culpability by the relevant entity, even though the agreement may describe serious misconduct and impose meaningful obligations. Although NPAs and DPAs remain relevant to QPAM integrity and continue to trigger ineligibility when they constitute Prohibited Misconduct under Section I(g), the Department preliminarily believes the distinctions between NPAs and DPAs and Criminal Conviction support a more tailored approach for class-wide relief, including permitting relief for one or more instances of Prohibited Misconduct under Sections II and III, subject to the exemption's protective conditions. The Department invites comments on whether this treatment of NPAs and DPAs is appropriately calibrated, whether additional safeguards are needed, and whether the proposed distinction between U.S. Convictions and Prohibited Misconduct should be modified in the final exemption.

Neither the Foreign Conviction nor the Prohibited Misconduct (reflected in the NPA) involved assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975. Assume neither U.S. Conviction involved assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975. Because the two U.S. Convictions were the same in nature and involved the same underlying facts and circumstances, Bank B, the QPAM, would be eligible to rely on the relief in Section II of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, as a Reliance QPAM if the definitions in Section I and the conditions in Section II are met.
