Section II Conditions
Section II(b) Eligibility
Relief under Section II(b)(1) and (2) requires that, as of the Reliance Date, no officer, director, agent (other than the Misconduct Entity), or employee of the Reliance QPAM or a party engaged on behalf of the Reliance QPAM, who had responsibility for, or exercised authority in connection with, the management of plan assets, knew of or had reason to know of,
[
27
]
or Participated In,
[
28
]
received direct compensation, or knowingly received indirect compensation, in connection with the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct. In other words, by the Reliance Date, there must no longer be any association between the Reliance QPAM and any individuals who were aware of the misconduct during the time the misconduct was ongoing or profited from the misconduct. The Department considered whether, when a person at the Reliance QPAM knew or had reason to know of the misconduct at the time the misconduct was ongoing, or profited from the misconduct, meeting this threshold should require removal of the chief compliance officer regardless of that individual's direct involvement in the misconduct or whether the officer knew of it. The Department notes that, by virtue of their duties and purview, key management leaders can often set the stage for misconduct whether or not they are directly culpable. Moreover, it can be difficult to establish a direct causal link between misconduct conducted at lower levels and key management leaders. The Department is concerned that, ultimately, it may be immaterial if a key management leader like a chief compliance officer is unaware of misconduct, since their role is to establish controls and oversight to prevent such misconduct, and the existence of misconduct may be proof of failure in that regard. Accordingly, the Department is seeking comment regarding whether meeting the Section II eligibility threshold should require the automatic removal of the chief compliance officer or other compliance officials responsible for overseeing the conduct of the Reliance QPAM, regardless of whether they knew of the misconduct or were directly involved.
Section II(b)(3) requires that neither the Reliance QPAM nor any Related QPAM or Affiliated QPAM of the Misconduct Entity exercised authority over any ERISA-covered plan or IRA assets in a manner that it knew or should have known would further the misconduct, or caused the Reliance QPAM or its Affiliates, or any officers, employees or partners to directly or indirectly profit from the misconduct.
Further, Section II(b)(4) through (6) require that, as of the Reliance Date: the Reliance QPAM must not use its authority to direct an Investment Fund to enter into any transaction with a Misconduct Entity; the Reliance QPAM's asset management decisions must be independent of the management and business activities of the Misconduct Entity; and the Misconduct Entity may not act as a fiduciary under ERISA or the Code with respect to ERISA-covered Plan and IRA assets, except that it may act as an ERISA fiduciary with respect to employee benefit plans sponsored for its own employees or employees of an Affiliate. Section II(b)(7) requires that the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct must not have involved assets of any Plan or fund subject to ERISA Title 1, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975. Finally, Section II(b)(8) requires ongoing compliance by the Reliance QPAM with the applicable conditions of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, and of the QPAM Class Exemption.
Section II(c)(1) Policies
Section II(c)(1) requires the Reliance QPAM to implement, maintain (with necessary adjustments), and follow written policies (the Policies) requiring that: (1) the asset management decisions of the Reliance QPAM are conducted independently of the asset management and business activities of the Misconduct Entity; (2) the Reliance QPAM fully complies with ERISA's fiduciary duties and with ERISA and the Code's prohibited transaction provisions; (3) any filings or statements made by the Reliance QPAM to regulators on behalf of or in relation to Covered Plans are materially accurate and complete; (4) the Reliance QPAM does not make material misrepresentations or omissions in its communications with regulators with respect to Covered Plans or in its communications with Covered Plans; (5) the Reliance QPAM adheres to the Training requirements specified in the exemption; and (6) the Reliance QPAM complies with the terms of this exemption and corrects violations promptly upon discovery by the Reliance QPAM in accordance with the applicable terms of this exemption.
Section II(c)(2) Training
Section II(c)(2) requires the Reliance QPAM to conduct at least annually a program of training (the Training) for all relevant Reliance QPAM asset/portfolio management, trading, legal, compliance, and internal audit personnel. The Training must be set forth in the Policies and conducted by a professional who has been prudently selected. At a minimum, the Training must cover the Policies, ERISA and Code compliance, ethical conduct, the consequences for not complying with the exemption, and prompt reporting of wrongdoing (including resources on how to report suspected wrongdoing within the Reliance QPAM, and to EBSA and other relevant Federal oversight agencies).
The purpose of this Training is twofold. First, it ensures that everyone working in the above-identified job categories understands their obligations under relevant law. Second, it reinforces a culture of compliance by ensuring relevant Reliance QPAM personnel understand the importance of ethical conduct, the consequences of noncompliance with applicable rules, and the need to promptly report instances of noncompliance.
Section II(d) Independent Fiduciary
Section II(d) of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption requires the Reliance QPAM to prudently select an Independent Fiduciary to review the Reliance QPAM's eligibility for relief under Section II and determine whether the Reliance QPAM has developed the Policies required under this section. The Reliance QPAM must select an Independent Fiduciary that has appropriate technical training and proficiency with ERISA and the Code and must grant the Independent Fiduciary unfettered access to all the information that the Independent Fiduciary deems necessary in its sole discretion to make its required findings. Within 90 days of the Reliance Date, the Independent Fiduciary must submit a written report to the Reliance QPAM that details its processes and procedures and certifies that, to the best of the Independent Fiduciary's knowledge and belief, all of the representations made in such report are true and correct and whether the Reliance QPAM is in
(
printed page 74443)
compliance with the conditions in Section II(a) and (b)(1) through (7) and all of the Policies required by Section II(c) have been established.
Relief in this exemption is contingent on the Independent Fiduciary report containing clear, unambiguous statements that: the Independent Fiduciary has prudently performed its duties as an ERISA fiduciary on behalf of all affected Covered Plans; and all of the conditions in Section II(a) and (b)(1) through (7) have been met and the Policies required by Section II(c) have been established. Given the importance of the requirement that no person who knew or had reason to know of the misconduct that gave rise to a violation of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption, whether or not such person was ultimately convicted for participating in the crime, the report must contain an express statement confirming that, to the best of the Independent Fiduciary's knowledge, no person who knew or had reason to know of the misconduct that gave rise to a violation of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption currently works at the QPAM or any party engaged on behalf of the Reliance QPAM. The Independent Fiduciary's report must be made publicly available on the Reliance QPAM's website upon completion. It is the Department's expectation that the Independent Fiduciary's report will not contain privileged or confidential business information, however under the narrow circumstance where such information may exist in the report, the Reliance QPAM may redact such information for purposes of posting on the website. In accordance with the Recordkeeping condition in Section V, the Reliance QPAM must retain an unredacted copy of the Independent Fiduciary's report which can be reviewed by the Department upon request. The Independent Fiduciary's report also must include a certification by the head of compliance of the Reliance QPAM stating that to the best of their knowledge and belief, such head of compliance has diligently investigated the misconduct that gave rise to the violation of Section I(g), shared all material information regarding that investigation with the Independent Fiduciary, and avers that the Independent Fiduciary's report is accurate and complete.
Section II(e) Notice to the Department and Covered Plan Fiduciaries
Section II(e) requires the Reliance QPAM to send notices to the Department and to its Covered Plan clients. This condition is based on notice conditions that the Department has consistently included in recent individual exemptions involving violations of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. However, unlike such individual exemptions, Section II of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption requires that Reliance QPAMs provide a one-time notice within 90 calendar days of the Reliance Date, rather than repeatedly providing notices throughout the Exemption Period.
The Department notes that some in the regulated community have suggested that disclosures from ineligible QPAMs to Covered Plan fiduciaries would be sufficiently protective of Covered Plans. The Department disagrees. It is the Department's responsibility, not that of Covered Plan fiduciaries, to ensure that the QPAM Class Exemption is in the interest of, and protective of, affected Covered Plans, and administratively feasible. Disclosures to Covered Plan fiduciaries by asset managers interested in retaining their clients are not, by themselves, sufficient grounds for the Department to allow those asset managers to continue to engage in prohibited transactions covered by the QPAM Class Exemption. The conditions in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, taken as a whole, are intended to strike the appropriate balance that ensures Covered Plans are informed and protected while also ensuring QPAMs place their ERISA fiduciary responsibilities and integrity at the forefront of their compliance structure.
Under Section II(e), the notice must include a representation from the Reliance QPAM's head of compliance and general counsel (or their functional equivalent) that, to the best of their knowledge and belief, the Reliance QPAM is compliant with the eligibility requirements of Section II(a) and (b) and has established the Policies and Training required by Section II(c). In addition, to ensure all Covered Plans understand why the QPAM became ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption, the notice must include a detailed description of the circumstances, conduct, and entities that Participated In the Criminal Conviction and/or the Prohibited Misconduct. Lastly, the notice must include instructions on how to retrieve the certified written report of the Independent Fiduciary required by Section II(d) and the Policies required by Section II(c) from the Reliance QPAM's website once available. The Reliance QPAM must send the notices to the Department via email to
QPAM@dol.gov
,
and to Covered Plans, in a manner that ensures receipt by the ERISA fiduciary of each Covered Plan.
Section II(f) Subsequent Criminal Convictions or Prohibited Misconduct Events
Section II(f) requires that the Reliance QPAM comply with each condition of Section II for each Criminal Conviction or instance of Prohibited Misconduct that otherwise qualifies for relief under Section II, beginning on the Reliance Date corresponding to each ineligibility event. This means that under the facts in Example 2 above, when Misconduct Entity A receives a Foreign Conviction, Bank B is still eligible for the relief in Section II (as stated in Example 2), but has a new Reliance Date and will need to make sure all conditions are met for the new Reliance Date, including that notices be sent within 90 days of the Reliance Date. If the Misconduct Entity enters into the NPA with DOJ on yet another date, the Reliance QPAM will have a third Reliance Date. In other words, each ineligibility event begins a new 10-year ineligibility period.
Section II(g) Special Rule for Related QPAMs That Are Reliance QPAMs
Related QPAMs that are Reliance QPAMs can rely on the relief in Section II, subject to fewer conditions. Specifically, a Related QPAM that is a Reliance QPAM must satisfy the eligibility conditions in Section II(b)(1) through (8) requiring independence, and, if any additional Criminal Conviction or instance of Prohibited Misconduct occurs, the Related QPAM must follow the requirements of Section II(f) described above.
Section III: Exemptive Relief Under a Control Relationship Between the Reliance QPAM and the Misconduct Entity
Section III extends relief to an Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM that is ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption, where ineligibility is the result of: (1) a single U.S. Conviction of a Misconduct Entity that is not a QPAM, where the Misconduct Entity, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or (2) collectively, up to two U.S. Convictions by one or more Misconduct Entities, if no Misconduct Entity is a QPAM and where no more than one U.S. Conviction involves a Misconduct Entity that, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or (3) one or more Foreign Convictions, including where the Misconduct Entity is a QPAM; and/or (4) one or more instances of Prohibited
(
printed page 74444)
Misconduct, including where the Misconduct Entity is a QPAM.
Section III Examples
Example 4:
Assume the same facts as in Example 2 above, except that subsequently (but within ten years of the original U.S. Conviction) Misconduct Entity A receives a second U.S. Conviction for tax evasion that also did not involve assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975. The underlying facts and circumstances of the second Criminal Conviction are unrelated to Misconduct Entity A's previous Convictions or Prohibited Misconduct. Under these facts, Bank B, the QPAM, is not eligible to rely on Section II due to the second U.S. Conviction of Entity A. However, Bank B would be eligible to rely on the relief in Section III of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, as a Reliance QPAM if the definitions in Section I and the conditions in Section III are met.
Example 5:
Misconduct Entity C (not a QPAM) receives a Foreign Conviction for fraud that did not involve assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975. Bank D (a QPAM) is an Affiliate of and Controlled by Misconduct Entity C. Notwithstanding the misconduct, Bank D would be eligible to rely on the relief in Section III of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, as a Reliance QPAM if the definitions in Section I and the conditions in Section III are met.
Example 6:
Assume the same facts as in Example 5 above. Bank D, the QPAM, subsequently (but within ten years of the Foreign Conviction) enters into a deferred prosecution agreement (DPA) with the DOJ (thereby becoming itself a Misconduct Entity) that does not involve assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975, and the underlying facts and circumstances are unrelated to Misconduct Entity C's Foreign Conviction. Notwithstanding the collective misconduct, Bank D, now a Misconduct Entity, would be eligible to rely on the relief in Section III of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, as a Reliance QPAM if the definitions in Section I and the conditions in Section III are met.
Example 7:
Assume the same facts as in Example 6 above. Misconduct Entity C subsequently (but within ten years of the original Foreign Conviction) is convicted of criminal tax evasion in the U.S., and that U.S. Conviction does not involve assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975 and the facts and circumstances are unrelated to either of Misconduct Entity C's Foreign Conviction or Bank D's Prohibited Misconduct. Notwithstanding the collective misconduct, Bank D (the QPAM) would be eligible to rely on the relief in Section III of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, as a Reliance QPAM if the definitions in Section I and the conditions in Section III are met.
Department's Note:
A Reliance QPAM must meet each definition in Section I and each condition in Section III for each Criminal Conviction and instance of Prohibited Misconduct to obtain relief under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.
Section III Conditions
Section III(b) Eligibility
This section generally imposes the same eligibility conditions as in Section II(b) on the Reliance QPAM with regards to: knowledge of, and participation and compensation in connection with, the misconduct; the use of authority over any ERISA-covered plan or IRA assets; profiting from the misconduct; the independence of its asset management decisions; and the Misconduct Entity's ability to act as an ERISA fiduciary. This Section also requires that misconduct did not involve assets of any Plan or fund subject to ERISA Title 1, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975 and requires ongoing compliance with the applicable conditions of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted, and of the QPAM Class Exemption.
Section III(c) Policies and Training
This section generally imposes the same conditions as Section II(c). The policies and training conditions are similar to conditions in the Department's recent individual exemptions involving violations of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption.
Section III(d) Independent Fiduciary
To ensure the Reliance QPAM is eligible to rely on Section III and in compliance with the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, this section imposes the same requirement that is in Section II(d) to engage an Independent Fiduciary to submit a written report certifying to the Reliance QPAM's eligibility and compliance with Sections II(b)(1)-(7), III(a), and establishment of Policies under Section III(c).
Section III(e) Audit Requirement

With respect to any arrangement, agreement, or contract between the Reliance QPAM and a Covered Plan (or in an addendum thereto), the Reliance QPAM must agree and warrant: (1) to comply with ERISA and the Code, including the standards of prudence and loyalty set forth in ERISA Section 404, as applicable, and refrain from engaging in non-exempt prohibited transactions; (2) to indemnify and hold harmless the Covered Plan for any “actual losses”

Section III(i) Subsequent Criminal Convictions or Prohibited Misconduct Events
Like Section II(f), Section III(i) requires that the Reliance QPAM comply with each condition of Section III for each Criminal Conviction or instance of Prohibited Misconduct beginning on the Reliance Date corresponding to each ineligibility event.
Section IV: Phase Out Period Due to Noncompliance
This section provides a phase out period (the QROAD Phase Out Period) to prevent the QPAM from immediately losing exemptive relief if a Reliance QPAM fails to comply with a condition of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. The Department designed the QROAD Phase Out Period to mitigate the costs, disruptions, and uncertainties to Covered Plans, their participants and beneficiaries, and IRA owners that can occur when a Reliance QPAM becomes ineligible for relief under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.
The QROAD Phase Out Period lasts for a period of one year and begins on the date the Reliance QPAM knew or reasonably should have known of the noncompliance (Noncompliance Date). QPAMs that are not compliant with this exemption may find it beneficial to utilize the QROAD Phase Out Period while seeking exemptive relief under the Department's individual exemption process, as described below. Relief under the QROAD Phase Out Period requires the Reliance QPAM to, among other things, provide a notice of noncompliance to each of its Covered Plan clients and the Department at
QPAM@dol.gov
within 60 calendar days after the Noncompliance Date, and manage Covered Plan assets prudently and loyally during the QROAD Phase Out Period.
After the QROAD Phase Out Period expires, the QPAM will cease to be a Reliance QPAM, and will once again be ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption until the expiration of its 10-year ineligibility period, unless it obtains an individual exemption (or the applicable Criminal Conviction or

Example 8:

Section V: Recordkeeping
Reliance QPAMs must maintain records demonstrating compliance with this exemption, if granted, for six years following the date of any transaction for which the Reliance QPAM relies upon the relief in this exemption.
[
37
]
The Department generally imposes recordkeeping requirements in exemptions so that parties relying on the exemption can demonstrate, and the Department can verify, compliance with the conditions of the exemption. Under this exemption, the Reliance QPAM must make the records available upon request, to the extent permitted by law, to any authorized employee of the Department or the Internal Revenue Service or another State or Federal regulator; any ERISA fiduciary of a Covered Plan; any contributing employer and any employee organization whose members are covered by a Covered Plan; and any participant or beneficiary of a Covered Plan.
No party other than the Reliance QPAM would be subject to the civil penalty that may be assessed under ERISA Section 502(i) or the excise tax imposed by Code Section 4975(a) and (b), if applicable, if the Reliance QPAM did not maintain or make available the records as required by the exemption. A Reliance QPAM's failure to maintain the records necessary to determine whether the conditions of this exemption have been met would result in the Reliance QPAM losing relief provided under this exemption only for the transaction or transactions for which such records are missing or have not been maintained.
Section VI: Dates
If granted, under Section VI(a), the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption will be effective 60 calendar days after publication of the final exemption in the
Federal Register
, consistent with other class exemptions.
An Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM that currently relies on an individual exemption to engage in transactions described in the QPAM Class Exemption notwithstanding a violation of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption may continue to rely on that individual exemption. Under Section VI(b), if that QPAM prefers instead to rely on this exemption, if granted, it can do so, provided it satisfies all applicable terms and conditions of this exemption based on the circumstances of the original ineligibility. However, as discussed above, many conditions described in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption are based on conditions included in existing individual exemptions. Therefore, an Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM currently relying upon an individual exemption already may be performing tasks that satisfy the conditions of this exemption. For instance, a QPAM may have already appointed an auditor who is conducting regular audits, incorporated warranty provisions into written management agreements, and appointed a compliance officer.
If a QPAM that is not a Misconduct Entity is acquired by a Misconduct Entity or an Affiliate of a Misconduct Entity and thus becomes an Affiliated QPAM or Related QPAM after the Misconduct Entity's Ineligibility Date as a result of that acquisition, Section VI(c) of this exemption would give the newly acquired QPAM six months after the acquisition to become a Reliance QPAM by coming into full compliance with the conditions of this exemption, if granted. If a newly acquired QPAM becomes an Affiliate of another Reliance QPAM that is subject to an ongoing audit under Section III(e) of this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, this exemption permits the newly acquired QPAM to have the same audit period as that other Reliance QPAM. For the first audit, the auditor's review of the newly acquired QPAM must cover the period that begins six months after the acquisition date and continues to the end of the audit period. The Department believes that this six-month period would provide sufficient time for newly acquired QPAMs to adjust their internal processes and bring them into compliance with the requirements of this exemption as a Reliance QPAM, while also providing important protections to their Covered Plan participants and beneficiaries.

Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects; distributive impacts; and equity).

emphasizes the importance of quantifying costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility.
Under

(1) Have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities (also referred to as “economically significant”);
(2) Create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action taken or planned by another agency;
(3) Materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof; or
(4) Raise novel legal or policy issues arising out of legal mandates, the President's priorities, or the principles set forth in this Executive order.

requires that the new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations. A significant regulatory action (as defined in section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
) that would impose total costs greater than zero is considered an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action. As discussed in the analysis below, the Department expects that this proposal would result in cost savings. Therefore, if finalized as proposed, this action would be considered deregulatory under

2. Introduction and Need for Regulation
Section 408(a) of ERISA permits the Department to grant exemptions from certain prohibited transaction provisions. Under the current framework, QPAMs that are ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption due to noncompliance with Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption may seek individual exemptions. This process can be time-consuming and costly for QPAMs. The individual exemption application process typically involves consulting outside legal counsel, internal legal review, preparing and submitting a detailed exemption application, Department review and potential revisions, and possible operational disruptions during the review period.
The Department proposes to create a complementary exemption framework that provides an alternative to the individual exemption process that also promotes greater regulatory clarity, reduces uncertainty and reliance on individual exemptions, and improves administrative efficiency. The proposed exemption is intended to establish clear eligibility criteria and compliance obligations that will reduce the burdens applicable to certain otherwise ineligible QPAMs.
3. Baseline
Under the baseline, QPAMs must comply with the conditions of the QPAM Class Exemption to maintain eligibility (except for the Section I(g) condition that necessitated reliance on this exemption). If a QPAM becomes ineligible under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption but does not qualify for (or elects not to rely on) the relief in this proposed exemption, it may apply for an individual exemption. If granted, QPAMs relying on an individual exemption generally must also be subject to an independent audit.
4. Proposed Class Exemption
The Department is proposing a new class exemption, as an alternative to an individual exemption, for QPAMs experiencing ineligibility events under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. Rather than amending the QPAM Class Exemption, the proposal establishes a new, complementary framework that creates two compliance methods that depend on, among other things, whether a relationship with Control exists between the Misconduct Entity and the Reliance QPAM. This approach is intended to standardize relief while tailoring conditions based on: the number and/or type of triggering events; the type of assets involved in the misconduct; and/or the relationship between the Misconduct Entity and the Reliance QPAM. Benefits and costs presented in the analysis reflect the compliance methods contained in the proposed exemption relative to the existing framework in which QPAMs must seek an individual exemption. The proposed compliance methods and how they differ from the requirements for an individual exemption are summarized below.
4.1. Misconduct Entity Is Not a QPAM and Is an Affiliate That Does Not Control nor Is Controlled by the QPAM (Section II of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption)
First, in the case where a Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM but is an Affiliate that does not Control nor is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM, the proposed exemption would require the Reliance QPAM to establish and maintain certain policies and procedures, provide a one-time notice to the Department and the Reliance QPAM's clients, and obtain a certification from an Independent Fiduciary of the QPAM's compliance with Section II compliance method, which is not required by the Department's QPAM Section I(g) individual exemptions. The one-time notice must include representations
(
printed page 74448)
from the Reliance QPAM regarding the Reliance QPAM's compliance with Section II and information on how to obtain the certification report of the Independent Fiduciary. The Department notes that under the baseline, QPAMs in this group seeking an individual exemption would have been required to notify their clients and perform audits. Under this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, while QPAMs must still notify their clients, they are no longer required to perform audits, which results in a burden reduction for QPAMs qualifying to use this compliance method. More information about the notice content in the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption can be found in the preamble.
4.2. Misconduct Entity Is Not a QPAM and Is an Affiliate That Controls or Is Controlled by the QPAM; or Is an Affiliate Without a Control Relationship but With Certain Multiple Convictions; or Is the QPAM but no U.S. Conviction (Section III of the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption)
Section III addresses where there is: (1) A single U.S. Conviction of a Misconduct Entity that is not a QPAM, where the Misconduct Entity, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or (2) collectively, up to two U.S. Convictions by one or more Misconduct Entities, if no Misconduct Entity is a QPAM and where no more than one U.S. Conviction involves a Misconduct Entity that, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or (3) one or more Foreign Convictions, including where the Misconduct Entity is a QPAM; and/or (4) one or more instances of Prohibited Misconduct, including where the Misconduct Entity is a QPAM.
Under any of these circumstances, the Reliance QPAM must comply with certain conditions under the Section III compliance method that are structured similarly to current individual Section I(g) exemptions. These conditions include: (1) notifying clients and the Department; (2) making certain warranties in any agreement with a Covered Plan that the Reliance QPAM will comply with ERISA and Code and protect Covered Plans from harm due to the ineligibility; (3) establishing and maintaining Policies; and (4) designating a Compliance Officer to be responsible for compliance with the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.
Under the baseline, QPAMs relying on an individual exemption also would be subject to audits conducted on an annual or biennial basis. Alternatively, under the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, all QPAMs using this compliance method would undergo biennial audits performed by an independent auditor. The proposed exemption would therefore result in a burden reduction for QPAMs that previously were subject to an annual audit.
4.3. Misconduct Entity Is the QPAM With a U.S. Conviction; or Certain Subsequent/Multiple Ineligibility Events by Affiliates; or Misconduct Involves Plan Assets
As detailed in the discussions above on Section II and III of the proposed exemption and as illustrated in the above individual exemption examples, where the Misconduct Entity is the QPAM with a U.S. Conviction, and for certain subsequent/multiple ineligibility events by an Affiliate of the QPAM, and/or where the misconduct involved assets of any Plan or Investment Fund subject to ERISA Title I, Part 4 and/or Code Section 4975, the Reliance QPAM is not eligible to use the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, though QPAMs may apply for an individual exemption. This group is unimpacted by the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.

8. Benefits
The Department expects that the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption may provide several benefits for QPAMs, Covered Plans, and Covered Plan participants. By establishing clearer eligibility standards and structured compliance methods following ineligibility events, the proposal may reduce reliance on individual exemption applications, improve regulatory certainty, and reduce operational disruption for plans and investment managers. In addition, clearer requirements may reduce legal and administrative burdens associated with seeking individualized relief and support more timely compliance decisions. The following discussion describes several potential benefits associated with this proposal.
8.1. Reduced Reliance on Individual Exemptions
The proposal may reduce the number of individual exemption applications that QPAMs will submit when an ineligibility event occurs. Under the current framework, affected QPAMs typically prepare lengthy applications with the assistance of outside counsel, and then must wait on the Department's review and grant of relief. This process may be costly.
[
53
]
By establishing clear, predefined methods with standard conditions, certain QPAMs may rely on the structured process described in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, instead of applying for an individual exemption. This could lower legal and administrative costs, reduce delays, and make it easier for firms to respond promptly to misconduct events while still ensuring the required safeguards are in place to protect Covered Plans, and their participants and beneficiaries.
8.2. Greater Regulatory Certainty
The proposal provides clearer guidance about what steps QPAMs that face Section I(g) ineligibility must take to remain eligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption. Specifically, the proposal helps Reliance QPAMs better understand their obligations and reduce uncertainty about how Affiliate misconduct affects their status. Without clearer standards, a Plan may attempt to retain an asset manager that no longer qualifies for the QPAM Class Exemption while waiting to determine whether the manager can obtain an individual exemption with retroactive relief.
[
54
]
This approach can result in uncertainty and create significant risk for Plan sponsors. By clarifying the expectations for continued eligibility, the proposal reduces ambiguity and supports more timely decision-making. Moreover, with more defined requirements, Reliance QPAMs may be able to train staff more effectively and address issues earlier.
8.3. Reduced Operational Disruption
When a QPAM becomes ineligible to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption due to a violation of Section I(g) of that class exemption, Covered Plans may face uncertainty about whether their assets can continue to be managed without interruption. In particular, failure to obtain timely individual exemptive relief could bar new transactions that are dependent on the exemption, which may result in Covered Plan clients being unable to retain their investment positions, thus negatively impacting those plans and their participants and beneficiaries.
[
55
]
This proposal aims to reduce that uncertainty by providing defined conditions that permit continued, uninterrupted operation in certain cases to help avoid abrupt transitions to new asset managers, reduce potential transaction costs associated with switching managers, and support stability in long-term investment strategies.
8.4. Summary of Benefits
The proposal would increase regulatory clarity, reduce reliance on individual exemptions, and limit operational disruption following ineligibility events under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. By establishing clearer standards and defined compliance methods in certain circumstances, the proposal also would reduce uncertainty for a QPAM and its Affiliates, and lower legal and administrative costs associated with seeking an individual exemption. Taken together, the proposal also may promote continuity in asset management and reduce transaction costs associated with switching managers, while maintaining protections for Covered Plans, and their participants and beneficiaries.

10. Regulatory Alternatives
10.1. No New PTE and Continue Requiring Individual Exemptions
Under this alternative, the Department would not issue a new class exemption and would continue requiring QPAMs that become ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption to seek individual prohibited transaction exemptions. This approach would preserve case-by-case review and would continue the imposition of significant compliance costs on the affected QPAMs. As reflected in the cost analysis, preparing an individual exemption application requires substantial outside ERISA counsel time, internal legal drafting, and external oversight. If that application is successful, compliance with the individual exemption imposes ongoing costs, including to provide training, policies, disclosures and regular audits. These costs are largely fixed per applicant and do not benefit from economies of scale.
In addition to direct compliance costs, reliance on individual exemptions may introduce uncertainty and potential transition costs for Covered Plans relying on QPAM-managed entities. Smaller or mid-sized asset managers may face disproportionate burden relative to larger firms, which could reduce competition in the plan asset management market. While individualized reviews allow tailored conditions, the Department believes this alternative would likely result in higher aggregate administrative costs and greater market disruption relative to a class-based approach.
10.2. Modify PTE 84-14 Section I(g)
The Department considered amending the QPAM Class Exemption by narrowing the scope of Section I(g) regarding what events may make a QPAM ineligible for relief. This would result in fewer QPAMs becoming ineligible under Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption. However, after carefully considering this option, the Department determined that, at the present time, it is not appropriate to narrow the scope of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption in this way. As noted above, the records supporting several individual exemption requests clearly demonstrate that a misconduct event by a “far flung” affiliate of a QPAM, with no apparent Control over the QPAM, may nonetheless involve numerous personnel spread across the QPAM's organizational structure. The Department continues to believe that the complexity of most criminal convictions and the behavior associated therewith, particularly those involving prolonged misconduct, warrants the protections described in this proposal. Accordingly, this proposal preserves the scope of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption and protects Covered Plans by requiring certain determinations by a qualified Independent Fiduciary regarding whether a QPAM is eligible for the relief provided under the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption.
10.3. Propose This Exemption With a Narrower Section II
The Department considered publishing this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption but limiting Section II and Section III relief to a total of two Foreign Convictions or instances of Prohibited Misconduct (including NPAs and DPAs). This would ensure the same treatment of all conduct that the Department has identified as raising serious integrity concerns. However, after carefully considering this option, the Department determined that, at the present time, it is appropriate to treat Foreign Convictions and Prohibited Misconduct differently than U.S. Convictions, in recognition of the different systems and processes that result in Foreign Convictions and Prohibited Misconduct. Accordingly, this proposal acknowledges that Foreign Convictions and Prohibited Misconduct are relevant to QPAM integrity and do trigger ineligibility under Section I(g) but allows a QPAM to continue relying on Section II or III despite multiple Foreign Convictions and/or instances of Prohibited Misconduct.
10.4. Propose This Exemption With a Provision That Each Audit Report Must Be Made Publicly Available
Section III(e) requires The Reliance QPAM must provide the Audit Report to the Department within forty-five (45) calendar days of completion, and the Department will make the Audit Report available to the public upon request. The Department considered making the Audit Report publicly available as soon as practicable after the Reliance QPAM provides it or requiring the Reliance QPAM itself to make the Audit Report public. However, the Department tentatively believes this would impose undue burdens on Reliance QPAMs without significant protection for plans and participants.
11. Uncertainty
11.1. Number of Affected QPAMs That May Become Ineligible
There is uncertainty regarding the number of QPAMs that may become ineligible under the QPAM Class Exemption and how many will use the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption. The frequency and distribution of triggering events may vary over time depending on enforcement activity, firm conduct, market conditions, and evolving compliance practices. As a result, the total number of entities that may rely on the proposed modified exemption framework cannot be predicted with complete precision.
If fewer entities are affected than estimated, aggregate compliance cost savings associated with the proposed exemption would be lower than projected. Conversely, if more entities are affected than estimated, the potential cost savings associated with the proposed exemption would increase.
11.2. Frequency of Individual Exemption Applications
There is also uncertainty regarding how frequently affected QPAMs would otherwise seek individual exemptions in the absence of a class-based exemption. Some QPAMs may apply for individual relief, while others may restructure operations, transfer assets, or exit the QPAM market. These behavioral responses affect both direct administrative costs and broader market impacts.
The cost estimates in this RIA assume that QPAMs that historically sought individual exemptions would rely instead on the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption when available. However, actual application behavior may differ depending on firm size, reputational considerations, and the perceived likelihood of approval of an individual exemption. Variations in these assumptions could materially affect the estimated cost differentials across alternatives.
(
printed page 74457)
11.3. Impact on Fully Compliant QPAMs
Additionally, there is uncertainty regarding the extent to which this proposal may indirectly affect QPAMs that remain fully compliant. To the extent that fully compliant QPAMs incur additional internal compliance costs, the aggregate burden associated with the proposal could be higher than estimated. At the same time, greater regulatory clarity and more standardized expectations may reduce compliance costs over time.
11.4. Estimates of Burden
Finally, there is uncertainty regarding the estimates of burden. Compliance costs may vary significantly depending on firm size, operational complexity, and the availability of internal legal expertise. The estimates presented in this analysis rely on representative wage rates and assumed labor hours; however, actual costs may differ across firms.
If affected entities rely more heavily on outside counsel than assumed, compliance costs under the individual exemption alternative would increase. Conversely, firms with greater internal compliance capacity may experience lower costs. These variations contribute to uncertainty in the overall magnitude of projected cost savings.

The Department has prepared this initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) and requests data or other information that would prevent it from certifying that a final class exemption would not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.
1. Need for the Proposed Exemption
As discussed above, the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would revise and standardize the framework governing ineligibility events under the QPAM Class Exemption. Under current regulatory conditions, QPAMs that become ineligible due to violations of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption must apply for individual exemptions if they intend to continue to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption. The process of applying for individual exemptions can be time-consuming and costly. This proposal establishes two structured compliance methods designed to clarify eligibility standards and reduce reliance on individualized applications.
2. Affected Small Entities
The Proposed QROAD Class Exemption would affect QPAMs. Under Small Business Administration (SBA) size standards, the relevant threshold for investment advisers registered under the Advisers Act and similar entities is $47 million in annual receipts.
[
69
]
The relevant NAICS codes include Investment Banking and Securities Dealing (523150), Insurance Carriers (524113), and Portfolio Management (523940).
The QPAM Class Exemption was premised on the QPAM being an entity of sufficient size to withstand undue influence from parties in interest. These size standards would limit the number of small entities that would be impacted. For example, the preamble to the 1982 proposal of the QPAM Class Exemption stated:
“The minimum capital and funds-undermanagement standards of the proposed exemption are intended to assure that the eligible fiduciaries managing the accounts or funds (“investment funds”), consisting of the assets of one or more plans, are established institutions which are large enough to discourage the exercise of undue influence upon their decision-making processes by parties in interest.”
[
70
]
Additionally, the Department has sought revenue information on the parent companies of QPAMs that have obtained individual exemptions in the past. The parent companies for whom the Department could identify revenues have annual revenues in the billions or hundreds of billions of dollars. While the Department does not have complete data on all QPAMs that could use the Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, it expects that few would fall below SBA's revenue threshold of $47 million.
The QPAM Class Exemption sets size thresholds a firm must meet in order to be a QPAM. The minimum capital and funds-under-management standards are intended to ensure that the eligible fiduciaries managing the accounts or investment funds are established institutions which are large enough to discourage the exercise of undue influence upon their decision-making processes by parties in interest. Therefore, the Department believes that this proposal would not affect a significant number of small entities. If a QPAM did meet the SBA definition of a small entity, the per-entity cost for the Section II and Section III compliance methods are both $3,125,
[
71
]
which are less than 0.01 percent of the SBA revenue threshold of $47 million. The Section II compliance cost of $3,125 would represent 1 percent of annual revenue for an entity with approximately $312,500 in annual revenue. There are also per-entity cost-savings of $37,075 for both compliance methods.
(
printed page 74459)
3. Cost of Proposed Exemption
The Proposed QROAD Class Exemption establishes two structured compliance methods designed to clarify eligibility standards and reduce reliance on individualized applications. Under the proposal, Reliance QPAMs must prepare notices to clients and the Department, and meet other requirements such as certifications or audits, to utilize the exemption. The proposal may reduce reliance on costly individual exemption applications, and the need for or frequency of audits. Increased compliance costs related to the notice and certification are expected to be modest relative to the revenues of affected entities.
To provide context for the magnitude of these costs, the Department compares the estimated per-entity compliance cost to the SBA size standard for Investment Banking and Securities Dealing (523150), Insurance Carriers (524113), and Portfolio Management (523940) which is $47 million in annual revenue. As shown in Tables 9 and 10, the estimated per-entity cost for the Section II and Section III compliance methods are both $3,125, which represents a very small share of revenues. A cost of $3,125 would represent 1 percent of annual revenue for an entity with approximately $312,500 in annual revenue.
The proposal also may generate cost savings by reducing reliance on individual exemption applications and a reduction in the need for, or frequency of, audits. As shown in Tables 9 and 10, the estimated gross cost savings from forgoing an audit and an application for an individual exemption for QPAMs using the Section II or Section III compliance methods is $37,075, which represents a larger share of revenues than the estimated compliance costs across all revenue levels examined. Accordingly, the Department expects that the proposed exemption could result in net cost savings for affected entities in circumstances where firms would otherwise seek an individual exemption. In addition, relatively few QPAMs are expected to experience ineligibility events in any given year and therefore few would need to rely on the structured compliance methods established by the proposal.
(
printed page 74460)
4. Alternative
As an alternative, the Department considered taking no action and continuing to require QPAMs that experience ineligibility events to apply for individual exemptions. However, the individual exemption process can be time-consuming and costly for affected entities and may create uncertainty for QPAMs and their affiliated entities during the review period. The proposed exemption is intended to provide clearer standards and reduce reliance on individualized applications while maintaining appropriate safeguards.

There are no duplicate, overlapping, or relevant Federal rules.

Executive Order 13132
outlines fundamental principles of federalism, and requires the adherence to specific criteria by Federal agencies in the process of their formulation and implementation of policies that have “substantial direct effects” on the States, the relationship between the Federal Government and States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

Federal agencies promulgating regulations that have federalism implications must consult with State and local officials and describe the extent of their consultation and the nature of the concerns of State and local officials in the preamble to the proposed exemption.
The proposed exemption does not have federalism implications because it has no substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Section 514 of ERISA provides, with certain exceptions specifically enumerated, that the provisions of Titles I and IV of ERISA supersede any and all laws of the States as they relate to any employee benefit plan covered under ERISA.
General Information
The attention of interested persons is directed to the following:
(1) The fact that a transaction is the subject of an exemption under ERISA Section 408(a) and Code Section 4975(c)(2) does not relieve an ERISA fiduciary, or other party in interest or disqualified person with respect to a Plan, from certain other provisions of ERISA and the Code, including any prohibited transaction provisions to which the exemption does not apply and the general fiduciary responsibility provisions of ERISA Section 404 which require, among other things, that an ERISA fiduciary act prudently and discharge their duties respecting the Plan solely in the interests of the participants and beneficiaries of the Plan. Additionally, the fact that a transaction is the subject of an exemption does not affect the requirement of Code Section 401(a) that the Plan must operate for the exclusive benefit of the employees of the employer maintaining the Plan and their beneficiaries.
(2) Before the exemption may be granted under ERISA Section 408(a) and Code Section 4975(c)(2), the Department must find that it is administratively feasible; in the interests of Plans, their participants and beneficiaries, and IRA owners; and protective of the rights of participants and beneficiaries of Plans and IRA owners.
(3) If granted, the exemption is applicable to a particular transaction only if the transaction satisfies the conditions specified in the exemption.
(4) The proposed exemption, if granted, is supplemental to, and not in derogation of, any other provisions of ERISA and the Code, including statutory or administrative exemptions and transitional rules. Furthermore, the fact that a transaction is subject to an administrative or statutory exemption is not dispositive of whether the transaction is in fact a prohibited transaction.

Section II—Exemptive Relief Where No Control Relationship Exists Between the Reliance QPAM and the Misconduct Entity
(a) Covered Transactions
A Reliance QPAM may continue to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption during the Exemption Period notwithstanding:
(1) A single Criminal Conviction described in Section VI(r)(1) of the QPAM Class Exemption (a U.S. Conviction) of a Misconduct Entity, where the Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM and, at any time, neither Controls nor is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or
(2) One or more Criminal Convictions described in Section VI(r)(2) of the QPAM Class Exemption (Foreign Convictions) by one or more Misconduct Entities, where, in each instance, the Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM and, at any time, neither Controls nor is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; and/or
(3) One or more instances of Prohibited Misconduct by one or more Misconduct Entities, where, in each instance, the Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM and, at any time, neither Controls nor is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM.
(b) Eligibility
(1) As of the Reliance Date, no officer, director, agent (other than the Misconduct Entity), or employee of the Reliance QPAM knew of or had reason to know of, or Participated In, the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct, during the time the conduct was ongoing. Further, as of the Reliance Date, no officer, director, agent (other than the Misconduct Entity) or employee of a party engaged on behalf of the Reliance QPAM, who has responsibility for, or exercises authority in connection with, the management of Covered Plan assets, knew of or had reason to know of, or Participated In the conduct that was the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct, during the time the conduct was ongoing;
(2) As of the Reliance Date, no officer, director, agent (other than the Misconduct Entity) or employee of the Reliance QPAM received direct compensation, or knowingly received indirect compensation, in connection with the conduct that underlies the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct. Further, as of the Reliance Date, no officer, director, agent (other than the Misconduct Entity) or employee of a party engaged on behalf of the Reliance QPAM who had responsibility for, or exercised authority in connection with, the management of plan assets, received direct compensation, or knowingly received indirect compensation, in connection with the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct;
(3) The Reliance QPAM (and any other Related QPAMs and Affiliated QPAMs of the Misconduct Entity) did not exercise authority over the assets of
(
printed page 74462)
any Investment Fund or plan subject to Part 4 of Title I of ERISA (an ERISA-covered plan) or Code Section 4975 (an IRA) in a manner that it knew, or should have known, would further the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct, or cause the Reliance QPAM (or its Affiliates or any officers, employees or partners) to directly or indirectly profit from the conduct that is the subject of the Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct;
(4) As of the Reliance Date, the Reliance QPAM will not use its authority or influence to direct an Investment Fund that is subject to ERISA or the Code and managed by such QPAM with respect to one or more Covered Plans to enter into any transaction with a Misconduct Entity or to engage a Misconduct Entity to provide any service to such Investment Fund for a direct or indirect fee borne by such Investment Fund, regardless of whether such transaction or service may otherwise be within the scope of relief provided by an administrative or statutory exemption;

Notwithstanding the above, if the Reliance QPAM is a Related QPAM, then the Reliance QPAM may rely on the QPAM Class Exemption during the Exemption Period for a covered transaction described in Section II(a) and III(a) if the conditions in Section II(b)(1)-(8) and (f) are satisfied. Related QPAMs are not otherwise required to satisfy the conditions in Section II(c), (d) and (e).
Section III—Exemptive Relief Under a Control Relationship Between the Reliance QPAM and the Misconduct Entity
(a) Covered Transactions
A Reliance QPAM may continue to rely on the QPAM Class Exemption during the Exemption Period, notwithstanding:
(1)(A) A single U.S. Conviction of a Misconduct Entity, where the Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM; or
(B) Collectively, up to two U.S. Convictions by one or more Misconduct Entities, where in each instance, the Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM and no more than one U.S. Conviction involves a Misconduct Entity is not a QPAM that, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by Reliance QPAM; and/or
(2) One or more Foreign Convictions by one or more Misconduct Entities, where any Misconduct Entity, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM including where any Misconduct Entity is a QPAM; and/or
(3) One or more instances of Prohibited Misconduct by one or more Misconduct Entities, where any Misconduct Entity, at any time, either Controls or is Controlled by the Reliance QPAM including where any Misconduct Entity is a QPAM.

(2) The Reliance QPAM implements the Training, conducted in accordance with the requirements in Section II(c)(2)(A)-(B) above.
(d) Independent Fiduciary
(1) The Reliance QPAM must prudently appoint an Independent Fiduciary with appropriate technical training and proficiency with ERISA and the Code, to determine the Reliance QPAM's compliance with Sections II(b)(1)-(7), III(a), and that the Policies required under Section III(c) have been established. The Independent Fiduciary must be granted unfettered access to all the information and documents it deems necessary in its sole discretion to make its required findings.
(2) Within 90 days of the Reliance Date, the Independent Fiduciary must submit a written report to the Reliance QPAM's head of compliance and general counsel (or their functional equivalent) that contains a detailed description of the Independent Fiduciary's processes and procedures. The written report must also contain a certification as to whether, to the best of the Independent Fiduciary's knowledge and belief: all of the representations made in such report are true and correct; all of the conditions in Sections II(b)(1)-(7), III(a) have been met; and all of the Policies required under Section III(c) have been established. The Independent Fiduciary's report must contain:
(A) An express statement confirming that, to the best of the Independent Fiduciary's knowledge, no person who knew or had reason to know of the misconduct that gave rise to a violation of Section I(g) of the QPAM Class Exemption currently works at the Reliance QPAM or any party engaged on behalf of the Reliance QPAM; and
(B) A certification by the head of compliance of the Reliance QPAM, stating that to the best of their knowledge and belief: such head of compliance has diligently investigated the misconduct that gave rise to the violation of Section I(g); shared all material information regarding that investigation with the Independent Fiduciary; and the Independent Fiduciary's report is accurate and complete.
The Independent Fiduciary's written report must be made available on the Reliance QPAM's website upon completion.
(e) Audit
(1) The Reliance QPAM undergoes an audit by an independent auditor who has been prudently selected and who has appropriate technical training and proficiency with ERISA and the Code to evaluate the adequacy of and the Reliance QPAM's compliance with the Policies and Training conditions in Section III(c) and the eligibility conditions in Section III(a) and (b). The audit requirement must be incorporated into the Policies. Each audit must cover twelve (12) consecutive months. The first audit must cover the 12-month period beginning on the earlier of the start date of the One Year Transition under Section I(i) of the QPAM Class Exemption (if applicable), or the Reliance Date. The audit must be completed within 6 months of the end of the 12-month period to which it relates. The audit must be completed within 6 months of the end of the twelve-month period to which it relates. Each successive biennial audit must cover a one-year period that begins 12 months after the end of the most recent audit period, and must be completed within 6 months of the end of the audit period;
(2) Within the scope of the audit and to the extent necessary for the auditor, in its sole opinion, to complete its audit and comply with the conditions for relief described herein, the Reliance QPAM and any applicable Affiliates will grant the auditor unfettered access to its businesses, including, but not limited to its computer systems, business records, transactional data, workplace locations, training materials, and personnel. Such access must be provided only to the extent that it is not prevented by State or Federal statute or does not involve communications subject to attorney client privilege, and may be limited to information relevant to the auditor's objectives as specified by the terms of this exemption;
(3) The auditor's engagement must specifically require the auditor to determine whether the Reliance QPAM has developed, implemented, maintained, and followed the Policies in accordance with the conditions of this exemption, and has developed and implemented the Training, as required herein;
(4) The auditor's engagement must specifically require the auditor to test the QPAM's operational compliance with the Policies and Training conditions. In this regard, the auditor must test a sample of the Reliance QPAM's transactions involving Covered Plans. The sample must include transactions that are sufficient in size, number and nature to afford the auditor a reasonable basis to determine the extent of the Reliance QPAM's operational compliance with the Policies and Training conditions. The auditor also must review each Compliance Report issued by the Compliance Officer as described in Section III(h) since the previous Audit Report was issued;
(5) On or before the end of the relevant period for completing each audit, the auditor must issue a written report (the Audit Report) to the Reliance QPAM that describes the procedures performed by the auditor during its examination. (A) the adequacy of the Reliance QPAM's Policies and Training; the Reliance QPAM's compliance with this exemption; the need, if any, to strengthen the Policies and Training required by Section III(c); and any instance of the Reliance QPAM's noncompliance with the Policies and Training. The Reliance QPAM must promptly address any noncompliance by preparing a written plan of action to address any determination by the auditor regarding the adequacy of the Policies and Training and the auditor's recommendations (if any) with respect to strengthening the Policies and Training. Any determination by the auditor that the Reliance QPAM has implemented, maintained, and followed sufficient Policies and Training must not be based solely or in substantial part on an absence of evidence indicating noncompliance. Any finding that the Reliance QPAM has complied with the requirements under this subparagraph

(f) Warranties
As of the Reliance Date, with respect to any arrangement, agreement, or contract between a Reliance QPAM and a Covered Plan, the Reliance QPAM agrees and warrants:
(1) To comply with ERISA and the Code, as applicable, with respect to the Covered Plan; to refrain from engaging in prohibited transactions that are not otherwise exempt (and to promptly correct any prohibited transactions in accordance with applicable rules under ERISA and the Code); and to comply with the standards of prudence and loyalty set forth in ERISA Section 404 with respect to the Covered Plan, to the extent that section is applicable;
(2)(A) To indemnify and hold harmless the Covered Plan for any actual losses resulting directly from: the Reliance QPAM's violation of the conditions of this exemption; loss of QPAM relief due to failure to satisfy Section I(g); prohibited transactions or ERISA fiduciary breaches connected to the misconduct that gave rise to reliance on this exemption. The term “actual losses” includes, but is not limited to, losses and related costs arising from prudently unwinding transactions with third parties and from prudently transitioning Plan assets to an alternative asset manager as well as costs associated with exposure to excise taxes under Code Section 4975 as a result of the Reliance QPAM's inability to rely on the relief in the QPAM Class Exemption; and
(B) To develop and maintain written processes that clearly describe: (i) how the Reliance QPAM identifies and quantifies “actual losses” for purposes of Section III(f)(2)(A); and (ii) how Covered Plans may recover or avoid incurring the losses that the Reliance QPAM must indemnify or hold Covered Plans harmless from incurring pursuant to Section III(f)(2)(A);
(3) Not to require (or otherwise cause) the Covered Plan to waive, limit, or qualify the liability of the Reliance QPAM for violating ERISA or the Code or engaging in prohibited transactions;
(4) Not to restrict the ability of the Covered Plan to terminate or withdraw from its arrangement with the Reliance QPAM with respect to any investment in a separately managed account or pooled fund subject to ERISA and managed by the Reliance QPAM, with the exception of reasonable restrictions, appropriately disclosed in advance, that are specifically designed to ensure equitable treatment of all investors in a separately managed account or pooled fund, in the event such withdrawal or termination may have adverse consequences for all other investors. In connection with any such arrangement involving investments in pooled funds subject to ERISA entered into after the Ineligibility Date, the adverse consequences must relate to a lack of liquidity of the underlying assets, valuation issues, or regulatory reasons that prevent the fund from promptly redeeming a Covered Plan's investment, and such restrictions must be applicable to all such investors in the pooled fund on equal terms and effective no longer than reasonably necessary to avoid the adverse consequences;
(5) Not to impose any fees, penalties, or charges for such termination or withdrawal with the exception of reasonable fees, appropriately disclosed in advance, that are specifically designed to prevent generally recognized abusive investment practices or specifically designed to ensure equitable treatment of all investors in a pooled fund, in the event the withdrawal or termination may have adverse consequences for all other investors, provided that such fees are applied consistently and in like manner to all such investors;
(6) Not to include exculpatory provisions disclaiming or otherwise limiting the liability of the Reliance QPAM for a violation of such agreement's terms. To the extent consistent with ERISA Section 410, however, this provision does not prohibit disclaimers for liability caused by an error, misrepresentation, or misconduct of an ERISA plan fiduciary or other party hired by the ERISA plan fiduciary who is independent of the Reliance QPAM and its Affiliates, officers, employees or partners, or damages arising from acts outside the control of the Reliance QPAM; and

Section IV—Phase Out Period Due to Noncompliance
A Reliance QPAM that relies on the relief in Section II or III but subsequently fails to comply with a condition in this exemption may rely on the relief in this Section IV and continue to rely on the relief in Section II or III of this exemption, as applicable, for up to one year (the QROAD Phase Out Period) following the date the Reliance QPAM knew of or should have reasonably known of the noncompliance (Noncompliance Date). Relief is available only with respect to the Reliance QPAM's Covered Plans that had a pre-existing written management agreement with the Reliance QPAM, as required under QPAM Class Exemption Section VI(a), as of the Noncompliance Date. A Reliance QPAM must manage Covered Plan assets prudently and loyally during the QROAD Phase Out Period. During the QROAD Phase Out Period, the QPAM must comply with the conditions of Section II or III of this exemption and the following conditions:
Within 60 days after the Noncompliance Date, the Reliance QPAM must provide notice to the Department via email at

(1) Its failure to satisfy the terms of this exemption and the starting date of the QROAD Phase Out Period; and
(2) That during the QROAD Phase Out Period, the Reliance QPAM:
(A) Agrees not to restrict the ability of a Covered Plan to terminate or withdraw from its arrangement with the Reliance QPAM, with the exception of reasonable restrictions, appropriately disclosed in advance, that are specifically designed to ensure equitable treatment of all investors in a pooled fund in the event such withdrawal or termination may have adverse consequences for all other investors. In connection with any of these arrangements involving investments in pooled funds subject to ERISA, the adverse consequences must relate to a lack of liquidity of the underlying assets, valuation issues, or regulatory reasons that prevent the fund from promptly redeeming a Covered Plan's investment, and such restrictions must be applicable to all investors in the pooled fund on equal terms and effective no longer than reasonably necessary to avoid the adverse consequences;
(B) Will not impose any fees, penalties, or charges on Covered Plans in connection with the process of terminating or withdrawing from an Investment Fund managed by the Reliance QPAM except for reasonable fees, appropriately disclosed in advance, that are specifically designed to: (i) prevent generally recognized abusive investment practices, or (ii) ensure equitable treatment of all investors in a pooled fund in the event such withdrawal or termination may have adverse consequences for all other investors, provided that such fees are applied consistently and in a like manner to all such investors; and
(C) Agrees to indemnify, hold harmless, and promptly restore actual losses to the client Plans for any damages that directly result to them from a violation of applicable laws, a breach of contract, or any claim arising out of the conduct that is the subject of any Criminal Conviction or Prohibited Misconduct causing reliance on this exemption. Actual losses specifically include losses and costs arising from unwinding transactions with third parties and from transitioning Plan assets to an alternative asset manager as well as costs associated with any exposure to excise taxes under Code Section 4975 as a result of a Reliance QPAM's inability to rely upon the relief in the QPAM Class Exemption.

(a) The Reliance QPAM maintains the records necessary to enable the persons described in subsection (a)(2) below to determine whether the conditions of this exemption have been met with respect to a transaction for a period of six years from the date of the transaction in a manner that is reasonably accessible for examination. AGENCY:
Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Council.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Council (Council) publishes notice of a proposed subaward from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to Ducks Unlimited, a nonprofit organization, for the purpose of constructing a breakwater along the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway at McFaddin National Wildlife Refuge in order to prevent wetland loss, and constructing interior ditches and levees at J.D. Murphee Wildlife Management Area in order to enhance wetlands, in accordance with the FY26 RESTORE CHENIER BKT2 Award as approved in the Council's Funded Priorities List 3b (FPL).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Please send questions by email to Bridget Zachary at
bridget.zachary@restorethegulf.gov
or (504) 232-3750
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 1321(t)(2)(E)(ii)(III) of the
Resources and Ecosystems Sustainability, Tourist Opportunities, and Revived Economies Act of 2012
(
33 U.S.C. 1321(t)
and
note
) (RESTORE Act) and the Department of the Treasury's implementing regulation at
31 CFR 34.401(b)
set forth certain notice and publication requirements. They require that for purposes of awards made under the Comprehensive Plan Component of the RESTORE Act, a State or Federal award recipient may make a subaward to or enter into a cooperative agreement with a nongovernmental entity that equals or exceeds 10 percent of the total amount of the award only if at least 30 days before the State or Federal award recipient enters into such an agreement, the Council publishes in the
Federal Register
and delivers to specified Congressional committees the name of the recipient and subrecipient; a brief description of the activity, including its purpose; and the amount of the award. This notice accomplishes the
Federal Register
publication requirement.
Description of Proposed Action
As specified in FPL 3b, which is available on the Council's website at
https://www.restorethegulf.gov/​our-work/​fpl/​fpl-3/​
,
RESTORE Act funds in the amount of $15,889,993 will support the FY26 RESTORE CHENIER BKT2 Award to TCEQ. TCEQ will provide a subaward in the amount of $9,245,570 to Ducks Unlimited to construct a breakwater along the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway at McFaddin National Wildlife Refuge in order to prevent wetland loss, and construct interior ditches and levees at J.D. Murphee Wildlife Management Area in order to enhance wetlands.
Keala J. Hughes,
Director of External Affairs & Tribal Relations, Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Council.

I. General Information
Written Comments
Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2020-0312, at
https://www.regulations.gov

ADDRESSES

i.e.,
